\begin{definition}[Improper Integrals over an Unbounded Domain]\label{analysis-unit-0178}
    Suppose \(\functiondomain{f}{\cointv{a}{\plusinfty}}{\RR}\) is integrable on \(\ccintv{a}{R}\), for all \(R \in \cointv{a}{\plusinfty}\). We let
    \[
        \function{F}{\cointv{a}{\plusinfty}}{\RR}{R}{\int_{a}^{R} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}}.
    \]

    Then we say the \emph{improper integral}
    \[
        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}
    \]
    exists/converges, if \(L = \lim_{R \to \plusinfty} F\pqty{R}\) exists and is finite, and we set
    \[
        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = L.
    \]

    Similarly, we may define \(\int_{\minusinfty}^{b} g\pqty{x} \dd{x}\).

    If \(\functiondomain{f}{\RR}{\RR}\) is such that \(\int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = L_1\) and \(\int_{\minusinfty}^{a} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = L_2\), for some \(a \in \RR\), then we say the improper integral
    \[
        \int_{\minusinfty}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}
    \]
    exists, and we set
    \[
        \int_{\minusinfty}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = \int_{\minusinfty}^{a} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} + \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = \lim_{R_1 \to \plusinfty} \int_{a}^{R_1} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} + \lim_{R_2 \to \minusinfty} \int_{R_2}^{a} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}.
    \]
\end{definition}
title: Improper Integrals over an Unbounded Domain

label: analysis-unit-0179
latex:
\begin{remark}\label{analysis-unit-0179}
    This is different from taking the limit
    \[
        \lim_{R \to \plusinfty} \bqty{\int_{-R}^{R} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}}.
    \]

    If the above improper integral exists, then this new limit (the Cauchy principal value) exists and is equal -- but not necessarily otherwise.
\end{remark}

label: analysis-unit-0180
latex:
\begin{examples}[Improper Integrals over Unbounded Intervals]\label{analysis-unit-0180}
    \label{ex:improper-integrals-unbounded-intervals}%
    \begin{itemize}
        \item The integral
        \[
            \int_{1}^{\plusinfty} \frac{1}{x^p} \dd{x} = \lim_{R \to \plusinfty} \int_{1}^{R} \frac{1}{x^p} \dd{x}
        \]
        exists, if and only if \(p > 1\).

        \item We have
        \[
            \int_{2}^{\plusinfty} \frac{1}{x \pqty{\log x}^2} \dd{x} = \lim_{R \to \plusinfty} \int_{2}^{R} \frac{\dd{x}}{x \pqty{\log x}^2} = \frac{1}{\log 2}.
        \]

        \item The \emph{Gaussian Integral} is given by
        \[
            \int_{\minusinfty}^{\plusinfty} e^{- x^2} \dd{x}.
        \]

        However, its antiderivative is difficult to calculate (and is in fact non-elementary). We can use alternative methods to show this converges.
    \end{itemize}
\end{examples}
title: Improper Integrals over Unbounded Intervals

label: analysis-unit-0181
latex:
\begin{remark}\label{analysis-unit-0181}
    Recall the \(n\)th term test for series, introduced in \autoref{prop:ser-test-nth-term}. However, this does not necessarily work for improper integrals, even if the function is continuous. Formally,
    \[
        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} \text{ exists} \notimplies \lim_{x \to \plusinfty} f\pqty{x} = 0.
    \]

    Indeed, if the limit exists, then it must be zero, but the limit does not necessarily exist.
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Monotone Convergence Theorem for Functions]\label{analysis-unit-0182}
    \label{prop:fn-monotone-convergence-theorem}%
    Let \(\functiondomain{f}{\cointv{a}{\plusinfty}}{\RR}\) be increasing.

    \begin{itemize}
        \item If \(f\) is bounded above, then we have
        \[
            \lim_{x \to \plusinfty} f\pqty{x} = \sup_{x \geq a} f\pqty{x}.
        \]
        \item If \(f\) is not bounded above, then we have
        \[
            \lim_{x \to \plusinfty} f\pqty{x} = \plusinfty.
        \]
    \end{itemize}

    Similarly, let \(\functiondomain{g}{\cointv{a}{\plusinfty}}{\RR}\) be decreasing.

    \begin{itemize}
        \item If \(g\) is bounded below, then we have
        \[
            \lim_{x \to \plusinfty} g\pqty{x} = \inf_{x \geq a} g\pqty{x}.
        \]
        \item If \(g\) is not bounded below, then we have
        \[
            \lim_{x \to \plusinfty} g\pqty{x} = \minusinfty.
        \]
    \end{itemize}
\end{proposition}

section_path.title: Tests on Convergence of Improper Integrals

title: Monotone Convergence Theorem for Functions

latex:
\begin{proof}
    We prove this for increasing functions, and the decreasing case is similar.

    Let \(\epsilon > 0\). If \(f\pqty{x}\) is bounded above, by the definition of the supremum, there is some \(R \in \cointv{a}{\plusinfty}\), such that
    \[
        \sup_{x \geq a} f\pqty{x} - \epsilon < f\pqty{R} \leq \sup_{x \geq a} f\pqty{x}.
    \]

    This means that for all \(x > R\), we have
    \[
        \sup_{x \geq a} f\pqty{x} - \epsilon < f\pqty{R} \leq f\pqty{x} \leq \sup_{x \geq a} f\pqty{x},
    \]
    so in particular,
    \[
        \abs{f\pqty{x} - \sup_{x \geq a} f\pqty{x}} < \epsilon,
    \]
    showing the limit as desired.

    However, if \(f\pqty{x}\) is not bounded above, for any threshold \(M > 0\), there is some \(R \in \cointv{a}{\plusinfty}\), such that
    \[
        f\pqty{R} > M.
    \]

    Hence, for all \(x > R\), we have
    \[
        f\pqty{x} \geq f\pqty{R} > M,
    \]
    which shows divergence to \(\plusinfty\) as desired.
\end{proof}

latex:
\begin{proposition}[Cauchy Criteria for Function Limit at Infinity]\label{analysis-unit-0183}
    \label{prop:cauchy-criteria-funciton-limit-infinity}%
    Let \(\functiondomain{f}{X \subseteq \CC}{\CC}\) be such that \(\infty\) is an accumulation point of \(X\). Then \(f\pqty{x}\) converges to some finite limit as \(x \to \infty\), if and only if
    \[
        \forall \epsilon > 0, \exists R > 0, \forall x_1, x_2 \in X, \abs{x_1}, \abs{x_2} > R: \abs{f\pqty{x_1} - f\pqty{x_2}} < \epsilon.
    \]
\end{proposition}

section_path.title: Tests on Convergence of Improper Integrals

title: Cauchy Criteria for Function Limit at Infinity

latex:
\begin{proof}
    Suppose that \(f\pqty{x} \to L \in \CC\) as \(x \to \infty\), and let \(\epsilon > 0\) be arbitrary. By the definition of a limit, for some \(R > 0\), we have
    \[
        \forall x \in X, \abs{x} > R: \abs{f\pqty{x} - L} < \frac{\epsilon}{2}.
    \]

    Hence, for all \(x_1, x_2 \in X, \abs{x_1}, \abs{x_2} > R\), we have
    \begin{align*}
        \abs{f\pqty{x_1} - f\pqty{x_2}} &\leq \abs{f\pqty{x_1} - L} + \abs{f\pqty{x_2} - L} \\
        &< \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \\
        &= \epsilon
    \end{align*}
    as desired.

    On the other hand, suppose that the Cauchy criteria holds. Let \(\pqty{z_n}_{n \in \NN}\) be a sequence on \(X\) with limit \(\infty\). Then, the sequence \(\pqty{f\pqty{z_n}}_{n \in \NN}\) is Cauchy, and hence tends to some limit \(L \in \CC\).

    Now, let \(\epsilon > 0\) be arbitrary, and let \(R > 0\) be such that
    \[
        \forall x_1, x_2 \in X, \abs{x_1}, \abs{x_2} > R: \abs{f\pqty{x_1} - f\pqty{x_2}} < \frac{\epsilon}{2},
    \]
    and let \(n > 0\) be sufficiently large, such that
    \[
        \abs{z_n} > R \qand \abs{f\pqty{z_n} - L} < \frac{\epsilon}{2}
    \]  

    For any \(x \in X, \abs{x} > R\), we have
    \begin{align*}
        \abs{f\pqty{x} - L} &\leq \abs{f\pqty{x} - f\pqty{z_n}} + \abs{f\pqty{z_n} - L} \\
        &< \frac{\epsilon}{2} + \frac{\epsilon}{2} \\
        &= \epsilon
    \end{align*}
    as desired.
\end{proof}

title: Comparison Test for Integrals

latex:
\begin{proof}
    Let
    \[
        F\pqty{R} = \int_{a}^{R} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} \qand G\pqty{R} = \int_{a}^{R} g\pqty{x} \dd{x}.
    \]

    Note that \(F\) and \(G\) are both increasing, with
    \[
        0 \leq F\pqty{R} \leq G\pqty{R}.
    \]

    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Since \(G\) converges, it is bounded above, and therefore so is \(F\). Hence, \(F\) converges, and since limit preserve weak inequalities, we have
        \[
            \lim_{R \to \plusinfty} F\pqty{R} = \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} \leq \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} g\pqty{x} \dd{x} = \lim_{R \to \plusinfty} G\pqty{R}.
        \]
        

        \item Since \(f \geq 0\), from \autoref{prop:fn-monotone-convergence-theorem}, we have
        \[
            \lim_{R \to \plusinfty} F\pqty{R} = \plusinfty
        \]
        necessarily, and in particular, \(F\) is not bounded above.

        But we have \(G\pqty{R} \geq F\pqty{R}\), so \(G\) is not bounded above either, and hence
        \[
            \lim_{R \to \plusinfty} G\pqty{R} = \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} g\pqty{x} \dd{x} = \plusinfty.
        \]
    \end{enumerate}
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Application of Direct Comparison Test]\label{analysis-unit-0185}
    \label{ex:app-direct-comparison-test}%
    We return to the Gaussian integral. For \(x \geq 1\), we have \(x^2 \geq x\), so \(e^{-x^2} \leq e^{-x}\).

    Therefore, we have
    \[
        \int_{1}^{\plusinfty} e^{-x^2} \dd{x} \leq \int_{1}^{\plusinfty} e^{-x} \dd{x} = \bqty{- \frac{1}{e^x}}^{\plusinfty}_{1} = \frac{1}{e}.
    \]

    Hence,
    \[
        \int_{\minusinfty}^{\plusinfty} e^{-x^2} \dd{x} = 2 \int_{0}^{\plusinfty} e^{-x^2} \dd{x} = 2 \int_{1}^{\plusinfty} e^{-x^2} \dd{x} + 2 \int_{0}^{1} e^{-x^2} \dd{x}
    \]
    so the improper integral converges, as desired.
\end{example}

\begin{proposition}[Limit Comparison (Ratio) Test for Integrals]\label{analysis-unit-0186}
    \label{prop:int-test-ratio}%
    Let \(\functiondomain{f, g}{\cointv{a}{\plusinfty}}{\RR}\) be integrable over any finite interval \(\ccintv{a}{R}\) for \(R \geq a\), satisfying \(f(x)\ge0\) and \(g(x)\ge0\) everywhere, with \(g(x)>0\) for all sufficiently large \(x\), and
    \[
        \lim_{x \to \plusinfty} \frac{f\pqty{x}}{g\pqty{x}} = L \in \oointv{0}{\plusinfty}.
    \]

    Then,
    \[
        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} \text{ exists} \iff \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} g\pqty{x} \dd{x} \text{ exists}.
    \]
\end{proposition}

title: Limit Comparison (Ratio) Test for Integrals

latex:
\begin{proof}
    By definition of the limit, we have for sufficiently large \(a\), say \(a > R\), that
    \[
        \frac{L}{2} \leq \frac{f\pqty{x}}{g\pqty{x}} \leq \frac{3L}{2},
    \]
    by taking \(\epsilon = \frac{L}{2}\) in the definition. Hence,
    \[
        0 \leq g\pqty{x} \leq \frac{2}{L} f\pqty{x}
    \]
    and
    \[
        0 \leq f\pqty{x} \leq \frac{3L}{2} g\pqty{x}
    \]

    The result follows from \autoref{prop:int-test-comparison} (Comparison Test).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{analysis-unit-0187}
    If \(\lim_{x \to \plusinfty} \frac{f\pqty{x}}{g\pqty{x}} = 0\), then \(f\pqty{x} \leq g\pqty{x}\) for sufficiently large \(x\), and hence by comparison test,
    \[
        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} g\pqty{x} \dd{x} \text{ exists} \implies \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} \text{ exists},
    \]
    but not necessarily the other direction.

    Similarly, if \(\lim_{x \to \plusinfty} \frac{f\pqty{x}}{g\pqty{x}} = \plusinfty\), then \(f\pqty{x} \geq g\pqty{x}\) for sufficiently large \(x\), and hence by comparison test,
    \[
        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} \text{ exists} \implies \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} g\pqty{x} \dd{x} \text{ exists},
    \]
    but not necessarily the other direction either.
\end{remark}

title: Root Test for Integrals

latex:
\begin{proof}
    Note that \(L \geq 0\).

    \begin{itemize}
        \item Suppose \(0 \leq L < 1\). Let \(0 \leq L < r < 1\). For some \(R \geq a\), we have
        \[
            \forall x > R: f\pqty{x}^{\flatfrac{1}{x}} < r,
        \]
        and hence
        \[
            \forall x > R: 0 \leq f\pqty{x} < r^x.
        \]

        Since \(0 < r < 1\), the improper integral of \(r^x\) to infinity converges by direct integration. Therefore, by the direct comparison test, the improper integral of \(f\pqty{x}\) converges.

        \item Now, suppose \(L > 1\). Let \(L > r > 1\). For some \(R \geq a\), we have
        \[
            \forall x > R: f\pqty{x}^{\flatfrac{1}{x}} > r > 0,
        \]
        and hence
        \[
            \forall x > R: f\pqty{x} > r^x > 0.
        \]

        Since \(r > 1\), the improper integral of \(r^x\) to infinity diverges by direct integration. Hence, by the direct comparison test, the improper integral of \(f\pqty{x}\) diverges.
    \end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Cauchy-Ness is Equivalent to Convergence of Improper Integrals]\label{analysis-unit-0191}
    \label{prop:int-cauchy}%
    Let \(\functiondomain{f}{\cointv{a}{\plusinfty}}{\RR}\) be integrable on \(\ccintv{a}{R}\) for any \(R \geq a\). Then the improper integral
    \[
        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}
    \]
    converges, if and only if for any \(\epsilon > 0\), there is some \(R \geq a\), such that for all \(R \leq x_1 \leq x_2\), we have
    \[
        \abs{\int_{x_1}^{x_2} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}} < \epsilon.
    \]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Absolute Convergence implies Convergence for Improper Integrals]\label{analysis-unit-0192}
    \label{prop:int-absolute-convergence}%
    Let \(\functiondomain{f}{\cointv{a}{\plusinfty}}{\RR}\) be integrable on \(\ccintv{a}{R}\) for any \(R \geq a\). Then if the improper integral of its absolute value

        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}.
    \]
\end{proposition}

latex:
\begin{proof}[\proofname\ using \autoref{prop:int-cauchy} (Cauchy is equivalent to Convergence)]
    Let
    \[
        F\pqty{x} = \int_{a}^{x} f\pqty{t} \dd{t}, \quad G\pqty{x} = \int_{a}^{x} \abs{f\pqty{t}} \dd{t}.
    \]

    Hence, we have for \(x_1, x_2 \geq a\).
    \begin{align*}
        \abs{F\pqty{x_2} - F\pqty{x_1}} &= \abs{\int_{x_1}^{x_2} f\pqty{t} \dd{t}} \\
        &\leq \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \abs{f\pqty{t}} \dd{t} \\
        &= G\pqty{x_2} - G\pqty{x_1}.
    \end{align*}

    This shows that if \(G\) Cauchy, then \(F\) is as well. But by \autoref{prop:int-cauchy}, this means if \(G\) converges, then \(F\) converges as well, finishing the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Dirichlet Test for Improper Integrals]\label{analysis-unit-0193}
    \label{prop:int-test-dirichlet}%
    Let \(f \in \contClass{0} \pqty{\cointv{a}{\plusinfty}}\) be continuous, and suppose it has a bounded antiderivative
    \[
        F\pqty{x} = \int_{a}^{x} f\pqty{t} \dd{t}.
    \]

    Let \(g \in \contClass{1} \pqty{\cointv{a}{\plusinfty}}\) be continuously differentiable, monotone, and satisfies
    \[
        \lim_{x \to \plusinfty} g\pqty{x} = 0.
    \]

    Then the improper integral
    \[
        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{x} g\pqty{x} \dd{x}
    \]
    converges.
\end{proposition}

latex:
\begin{proof}[\proofname\ using \autoref{prop:int-absolute-convergence} (Absolute Convergence)]
    We let
    \[
        F\pqty{x} = \int_{a}^{x} f\pqty{t} \dd{t}, \quad H\pqty{x} = \int_{a}^{x} f\pqty{t} g\pqty{t} \dd{t}.
    \]

    Both \(F\) and \(G\) are continuously differentiable. Hence, using  integration by parts, we have
    \begin{align*}
        H\pqty{x} &= \int_{a}^{x} F'\pqty{t} g\pqty{t} \dd{t} \\
        &= F\pqty{x} g\pqty{x} - F\pqty{a} g\pqty{a} - \int_{a}^{x} F\pqty{t} g'\pqty{t} \dd{t}
    \end{align*}

    Let \(M = \sup_{x \geq a} \abs{F\pqty{x}}\). For the final term, we have the integral of the absolute value is
    \begin{align*}
        \int_{a}^{x} \abs{F\pqty{t} g'\pqty{t}} \dd{t} &\leq \sup_{x \geq a} \abs{F\pqty{t}} \cdot \int_{a}^{x} \abs{g'\pqty{t}} \dd{t} \\
        &= M \cdot \int_{a}^{x} \pm g'\pqty{t} \dd{t} \\
        &= M \cdot \abs{g\pqty{a} - g\pqty{x}}.
    \end{align*}

    Hence, as \(x \to \plusinfty\), we have
    \[
        \int_{a}^{\plusinfty} \abs{F\pqty{t} g'\pqty{t}} \dd{t} \leq M \cdot \abs{g\pqty{a}},
    \]
    so the improper integral of  \(\abs{F\pqty{t} g'\pqty{t}}\) converges, and hence the improper integral of \(F\pqty{t} g'\pqty{t}\) converges, by \autoref{prop:int-absolute-convergence} (Absolute Convergence of Improper Integral).

    Hence, as \(x \to \infty\), \(F\pqty{x}\) is bounded while \(g\pqty{x} \to 0\), so \(F\pqty{x} g\pqty{x} \to 0\), and the final improper integral converges. So \(H\) converges, as desired.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Improper Integrals over Isolated Singularity]\label{analysis-unit-0194}
    \label{def:improper-integral-isolated-singularity}%
    Let \(\functiondomain{f}{\ocintv{a}{b}}{\RR}\), and suppose that \(f\) is integrable over all \(\ccintv{a + \delta}{b}\) for all \(0 < \delta \leq b - a\). Then, let
    \[
        \function{F}{\ocintv{0}{b - a}}{\RR}{\delta}{\int_{a + \delta}^{b} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}}.
    \]

    We say the \emph{improper integral} \(\int_{a}^{b} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}\) exists/converges, if the limit
    \[
        \lim_{\delta \to 0^+} F\pqty{\delta}
    \]
    exists and is finite, and we denote this value as
    \[
        \int_{a}^{b} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = \lim_{\delta \to 0^+} F\pqty{\delta},
    \]
    and we say it does not exist/diverges otherwise.

    We may similarly define this for \(\functiondomain{f}{\cointv{a}{b}}{\RR}\).

    Let \(\functiondomain{f}{\ccintv{B}{b} \setminus \Bqty{a}}{\RR}\) is such that
    \[
        \int_{B}^{a} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = l_1 \qand \int_{a}^{b} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = l_2
    \]
    both converges, then we say the improper integral \(\int_{B}^{b} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}\) exists, and we denote this value as
    \[
        \int_{B}^{b} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = l_1 + l_2.
    \]
\end{definition}
title: Improper Integrals over Isolated Singularity

label: analysis-unit-0195
latex:
\begin{remark}\label{analysis-unit-0195}
    Similar to the improper integral from \(\minusinfty\) to \(\plusinfty\) case, we are in fact taking two separate limits
    \[
        \int_{B}^{b} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = \lim_{\delta_1 \to 0^+} \int_{B}^{a - \delta_1} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} + \lim_{\delta_2 \to 0^+} \int_{a + \delta_2}^{b} f\pqty{x} \dd{x}.
    \]

    The symmetric limit with \(\delta_1=\delta_2=\delta\downarrow0\) is the Cauchy
principal value; it need not imply convergence of either one-sided improper integral.
For example, \(1/(x-a)\) has symmetric principal value zero on \([a-1,a+1]\),
because the truncated integrals cancel, although each one-sided integral diverges.
\end{remark}

label: analysis-unit-0196
title: Improper Integrals over Isolated Singularity

latex: From the examples, we see that we may use some substitution to change the improper integral with the isolated point to some improper integral to infinity. This is formally expressed in \autoref{lem:conversion-types-improper-integrals}, but this should only be regarded as a broad idea rather than a concrete lemma.

label: analysis-unit-0197
latex:
\begin{lemma}[Conversion between Types of Improper Integrals]\label{analysis-unit-0197}
    \label{lem:conversion-types-improper-integrals}%
    Let \(\functiondomain{f}{\ocintv{a}{b}}{\RR}\) be continuous on \((a,b]\), hence Riemann integrable on every \([a+\delta,b]\) with \(0<\delta<b-a\). For some continuously differentiable bijection
    \[
        \functiondomain{\phi}{\cointv{c}{\plusinfty}}{\ocintv{a}{b}}
    \]
    which is strictly decreasing with \(\phi\pqty{c} = b\) and \(\lim_{t \to \plusinfty} \phi\pqty{t} = a\). Then
    \[
        \int_{a}^{b} f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = \int_{c}^{\plusinfty} f\pqty{\phi\pqty{t}} \pqty{- \phi'\pqty{t}} \dd{t},
    \]
    in the sense that they either both converge (to the same value) or both diverge.
\end{lemma}
title: Conversion between Types of Improper Integrals

latex:
\begin{proof}[Proof of the conversion lemma]
For every finite \(R>c\), substitution on a compact interval gives
\(\int_{\phi(R)}^b f(x)\,dx=\int_c^R f(\phi(t))(-\phi'(t))\,dt\).
As \(R\to\infty\), the lower endpoint \(\phi(R)\) approaches \(a\) and ranges
over a full one-sided neighbourhood of \(a\), because \(\phi\) is a decreasing
bijection. The two defining limits therefore exist together and are equal.
\end{proof}
title: Proof of the conversion lemma

latex:
\begin{definition}[Series of Functions]\label{analysis-unit-0200}
    \label{def:series-of-functions}%
    Let \(\pqty{f_n}_{n}\) be a sequence of functions. We call the infinite sum
    \[
        \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n = f_1 + f_2 + \cdots
    \]
    as a \emph{series} of \(\CC\)-valued functions on \(X\).

    If the infinite sum converges for all \(x \in Y \subseteq X\), then we define the function
    \[
        \function{f}{Y}{\CC}{x}{\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} f_n \pqty{x}}
    \]
    as the series.
\end{definition}
title: Series of Functions

latex:
If we know the integrability, continuity, or differentiability of \(f_n\), can we say anything about \(f\) in that respect? The answer is non-trivial, since we only know before that they work for finite sums -- while for infinite sums we are dealing with two limits. In other words, we are studying whether we may swap limit/differentiation/integration/infinite summation operators. For example, as we have seen before, we can only swap limits with function operations when the function is continuous.

As an example, if we want to show that \(f\) is continuous at some \(a\), then we want to show
\[
    \lim_{x \to a} \lim_{n \to \infty} f_n \pqty{x} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \lim_{x \to a} f_n \pqty{x}.
\]

But a counterexample may be constructed. For example, reducing our perspective to sequences, we define
\[
    s_{m, n} = \frac{m}{m + n}.
\]

We have
\[
    \lim_{n \to \infty} \lim_{m \to \infty} s_{m, n} = \lim_{n \to \infty} 1 = 1,
\]
while swapping limits gives
\[
    \lim_{m \to \infty} \lim_{n \to \infty} s_{m, n} = \lim_{m \to \infty} 0 = 0.
\]

We will focus on an easier case where our functions \(f_n\) are always given in the form
\[
    f_n \pqty{x} = c_n \pqty{x - a}^n
\]
where \(a\) is the \emph{centre}, and \(c_n\) as the \emph{coefficients}.

label: analysis-unit-0201
latex:
\begin{definition}[Power Series]\label{analysis-unit-0201}
    \label{def:power-series}%
    Let \(a \in \CC\) and \(\pqty{c_n}_{n\ge0}\) be a numerical sequence in \(\CC\). We call
    \[
        \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \pqty{x - a}^n
    \]
    a \emph{power series} \emph{centred at \(a\)}, and with \emph{coefficients} \(\pqty{c_n}_n\).
\end{definition}
title: Power Series

label: analysis-unit-0202
latex:
\begin{example}[Taylor Series is Power Series]\label{analysis-unit-0202}
    \label{ex:taylor-series}%
    If \(f\) is smooth at \(a\), then its Taylor series at \(a\) is a power series with coefficients
    \[
        c_n = \frac{f^{\pqty{n}} \pqty{a}}{n!}.
    \]
\end{example}
title: Taylor Series is Power Series

latex:
Every power series trivially converges at its centre where \(x = a\).

We first study the convergence of power series, i.e., the set
\[
    Y = \set{x \in \CC}{\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n} \text{ converges at }x}.
\]

label: analysis-unit-0203
title: Convergence at one Point implies Absolute Convergence in Smaller Radius

latex:
\begin{proof}
    We conduct a comparison test to geometric series. Let
    \[
        r = \frac{\abs{y - a}}{\abs{x - a}} < 1.
    \]

    Then the power series about \(y\) satisfies
    \[
        \abs{c_n \pqty{y - a}^{n}} \leq \abs{c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n}} \cdot \abs{\frac{y - a}{x - a}}^n = \abs{c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n}} \cdot r^n
    \]
    for \(r < 1\).

    Now, since the series converges at \(x\), we have
    \[
        \lim_{n \to \infty} c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n} = 0,
    \]
    and in particular this sequence is bounded., so there is some \(M > 0\), such that
    \[
        \abs{c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n}} \leq M.
    \]

    Hence,
    \[
        \abs{c_n \pqty{y - a}^n} \leq M r^n
    \]
    for \(r < 1\), and comparing to the geometric series, we see that the series
    \[
        \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \abs{c_n \pqty{y - a}^{n}}
    \]
    converges, and hence the desired series is absolutely convergent.
\end{proof}

label: analysis-unit-0204
title: Existence of Radius of Convergence

label: analysis-unit-0205

latex:
\begin{proof}
    We look at the set
    \[
        A = \set{r \geq 0}{\exists x \in \CC, \abs{x - a} = r: \text{ the power series converges at }x}.
    \]

    Trivially, \(0 \in A\). This tells us that \(A\) is non-empty. Set
    \[
        R = \sup A \in \ccintv{0}{\plusinfty}.
    \]

    If \(R = \plusinfty\), this means we have points converging at arbitrarily large radius, so by \autoref{lem:convergence-one-point-implies-convergence-smaller-radius}, this means the power series converge absolutely for any \(x \in \CC\).

    Now, if \(R\) is finite, by definition of the supremum, we know that the power series diverges for any point strictly further away from \(a\) than \(R\).
    
    For any \(\abs{y - a} < R\), then by the definition of the supremum, there is some \(r \in A\) with \(\abs{y - a} < r \leq R\). Then some point \(x\in\mathbb C\) with \(|x-a|=r\) gives convergence. So since \(\abs{y - a} < r = \abs{x - a}\), by \autoref{lem:convergence-one-point-implies-convergence-smaller-radius}, the power series converges absolutely at \(y\).
\end{proof}

label: analysis-unit-0206
latex:
\begin{proposition}[Root Test for Power Series]\label{analysis-unit-0206}
    \label{prop:power-series-test-root}%
    Let \(\pqty{c_n}_n\) be a sequence in \(\CC\), such that
    \[
        L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\abs{c_n}}
    \]
    exists (or is \(\plusinfty\)). Then the radius of convergence is given by
    \[
        R = \frac{1}{L}.
    \]
\end{proposition}
title: Root Test for Power Series

label: analysis-unit-0207
latex:
\begin{proposition}[Ratio Test for Power Series]\label{analysis-unit-0207}
    \label{prop:power-series-test-ratio}%
    Let \(\pqty{c_n}_n\) be a sequence in \(\CC\), with \(c_n\ne0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), such that
    \[
        L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \abs{\frac{c_{n + 1}}{c_n}}
    \]
    exists (or is \(\plusinfty\)). Then the radius of convergence is given by
    \[
        R = \frac{1}{L}.
    \]
\end{proposition}
title: Ratio Test for Power Series

label: analysis-unit-0208
latex:
\begin{remark}\label{analysis-unit-0208}
    The general formula uses the \emph{root} limsup:
\[
\frac1R=\limsup_{n\to\infty}|c_n|^{1/n}=:L.
\]
To verify it, fix \(r=|x-a|>0\). If \(rL<1\), choose \(q\) with \(rL<q<1\).
Eventually \(|c_n|r^n\le q^n\), giving absolute convergence. If \(rL>1\), choose
\(1<q<rL\); infinitely many terms satisfy \(|c_n|r^n>q^n\), so they do not tend
to zero. The same arguments cover \(L=0\) and \(L=+\infty\) with the stated
reciprocal conventions; the centre \(r=0\) always gives convergence.
A ratio limsup cannot generally replace the root limsup in the radius formula.
For example, \(c_{2k}=1\) and \(c_{2k+1}=2\) have root limsup one, hence \(R=1\),
but \(\limsup|c_{n+1}/c_n|=2\).
\end{remark}

label: analysis-unit-0209
latex:
\begin{examples}[Radius of Convergence]\label{analysis-unit-0209}
    \label{ex:radius-of-convergence}%
    \begin{itemize}
        \item The series
        \[
            \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n!}
        \]
        converges absolutely on all of \(\CC\), i.e., \(R = \plusinfty\). Indeed, the coefficients are given by \(c_n = \frac{1}{n!}\), and \autoref{prop:power-series-test-ratio} gives
        \[
            L = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\flatfrac{1}{\pqty{n + 1}!}}{\flatfrac{1}{n!}} = \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{1}{n + 1} = 0.
        \]
        
        \item The series
        \[
            \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} n! x^n
        \]
        has a zero radius of convergence.

        \item We investigate the convergence of the series
        \[
            \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n^2}.
        \]

        The ratio test gives
        \[
            \lim_{n \to \infty} \abs{\frac{\frac{1}{\pqty{n + 1}^2}}{\frac{1}{n^2}}} = 1
        \]
        which gives \(R = 1\). Therefore, the power series converges absolutely with \(\abs{x} < 1\), and diverges with \(\abs{x} > 1\).

        For \(\abs{x} = 1\), we note that
        \[
            \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \abs{\frac{x^n}{n^2}} = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}
        \]
        converges absolutely.

        Therefore, this power series converges absolutely for \(\abs{x} \leq 1\), and diverges \(\abs{x} > 1\).

        \item Now investigating the series
        \[
            \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n}.
        \]

        The radius of convergence remains to be \(1\). However, with \(\abs{x} = 1\), the behaviour is more subtle.

        If \(x = 1\), this gives divergence since this is the harmonic series. However, if \(x = -1\), this gives (conditional) convergence since this is the alternating harmonic series.
    \end{itemize}
\end{examples}
title: Radius of Convergence

label: analysis-unit-0210
latex:
\begin{remark}\label{analysis-unit-0210}
    The set of convergence points
    \[
        Y = \set{x \in \CC}{\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \pqty{x - a}^n \text{ converges}}
    \]
    and hence gives a possible domain for the function of the power series. It must contain the set
    \[
        \set{x \in \CC}{\abs{x - a} < R}.
    \]

    However, it may or may not contain the points
    \[
        \set{x \in \CC}{\abs{x - a} = R},
    \]
    and definitely does not contain
    \[
        \set{x \in \CC}{\abs{x - a} > R}.
    \]
\end{remark}

Given that the terms of the sums are polynomials, this means they are continuous, integrable, and differentiable. We would like to study these properties of the infinite sum as well. Formally, if we have the function
\[
    \function{f}{Y}{\CC}{x}{\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \pqty{x - a}^n,}
\]
then for example, can we conclude that
\[
    \dv{x} f\pqty{x} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \dv{x} \pqty{x - a}^n,
\]
and can we conclude that
\[
    \int f\pqty{x} \dd{x} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \int \pqty{x - a}^{n} \dd{x}?
\]

label: analysis-unit-0211
title: Differentiating Power Series Term-by-Term

latex: Clearly, we need to be careful: term-by-term operations might not hold on the \emph{entire} set of convergence of power series. But we may show that they do converge within the radius of convergence. We first introduce two notations to help us.

label: analysis-unit-0212
latex:
\begin{definition}[Open Ball and Closed Disk]\label{analysis-unit-0212}
    \label{def:open-ball-closed-disk}%
    Let \(a \in \CC\) be the \emph{centre} and \(R > 0\) be the \emph{radius}. Then the \emph{open ball} with centre \(a \in \CC\) and radius \(R > 0\) is defined as
    \[
        B_R \pqty{a} = \set{x \in \CC}{\abs{x - a} < R}
    \]
    and the \emph{closed disk} as
    \[
        D_R \pqty{a} = \set{x \in \CC}{\abs{x - a} \leq R}.
    \]
\end{definition}
title: Open Ball and Closed Disk

label: analysis-unit-0213
title: Continuity of Power Series

latex:
\begin{proof}[\proofname\ (Supplementary)]
    We introduce the notation
    \[
        S_N\pqty{x} = \sum_{n \leq N} c_n \pqty{x - a}^n, \quad T_N\pqty{x} = \sum_{n > N} c_n \pqty{x - a}^n
    \]
    and notice the tail may be bounded above by
    \[
        \abs{T_N\pqty{x}} \leq \sum_{n > N} \abs{c_n} \abs{x - a}^n \leq \sum_{n > N} \abs{c_n} r^n
    \]
    for all \(x \in D_r\pqty{a}\) with \(r < R\). By the definition of radius of convergence, for all \(\epsilon > 0\), there is some \(N = N \pqty{\epsilon} \in \NN\), such that
    \[
        \sum_{n > N} \abs{c_n} r^n < \epsilon,
    \]
    and hence
    \[
        \forall x \in D_r\pqty{a}: \abs{T_N\pqty{x}} < \epsilon
    \]

    Take \(x_0 \in D_r\pqty{a}\). We want to show that \(f\) is continuous at \(x_0\). By the triangular inequality, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \abs{f\pqty{x} - f\pqty{x_0}} &\leq \abs{S_N\pqty{x} - S_N\pqty{x_0}} + \abs{T_N\pqty{x}} + \abs{T_N \pqty{x_0}} \\
        &\leq \abs{S_N\pqty{x} - S_N\pqty{x_0}} + 2 \epsilon
    \end{align*}
    for all \(x \in D_r\pqty{a}\). To conclude the proof, we use the fact that polynomials are continuous, and choose some \(\delta = \delta\pqty{\epsilon}\) such that
    \[
        \abs{S_N\pqty{x} - S_N\pqty{x_0}} < \epsilon.
    \]

    This finishes the proof.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Integrability of Real Power Series, Term-by-Term]\label{analysis-unit-0214}
    \label{prop:integrability-of-power-series-term-by-term}%
    Let
    \[
        \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \pqty{x - a}^n
    \]
    be a real power series, with radius of convergence \(R > 0\). Then the function
    \[
        \function{f}{\oointv{a - R}{a + R}}{\RR}{x}{\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \pqty{x - a}^n}  
    \]
    is integrable on every \(\ccintv{a - r}{a + r}\) for every \(r < R\), and
    \[
        \int_{a}^{x} f\pqty{t} \dd{t} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \frac{\pqty{x - a}^{n + 1}}{n + 1}
    \]
    for any \(a - R < x < a + R\).
\end{proposition}
title: Integrability of Real Power Series, Term-by-Term

latex:
\begin{proof}[\proofname\ (Supplementary)]
    Continuity implies integrability, so it remains to show the formula for integration. We use the same idea, by splitting up the power series into a polynomial and a tail. We have
    \begin{align*}
        \abs{\int_{a}^{x} f\pqty{t} \dd{t} - \sum_{n \leq N} \frac{c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n + 1}}{n + 1}} &= \abs{\int_{a}^{x} f\pqty{t} \dd{t} - \int_{a}^{x} S_N\pqty{t} \dd{t}} \\
        &= \abs{\int_{a}^{x} T_N\pqty{t} \dd{t}} \\
        &\leq \sup_{\abs{t - a} < r} \abs{T_N \pqty{t}} \abs{\int_{a}^{x} \dd{t}} \\
        &\leq r \sup_{\abs{t - a} < r} \abs{T_N \pqty{t}} \\
        &\leq r \epsilon
    \end{align*}
    for some sufficiently large \(N = N\pqty{\epsilon}\). Hence,
    \[
        \int_{a}^{x} f\pqty{t} \dd{t} = \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n = 0}^{N} \frac{c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n + 1}}{n + 1} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n + 1}}{n + 1}.
    \]
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Differentiability of Power series, Term-by-Term]\label{analysis-unit-0215}
    \label{prop:differentiability-of-power-series-term-by-term}%
    Let
    \[
        \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n}
    \]
    be a power series, with a non-zero radius of convergence \(R > 0\). Then the function
    \[
        \function{f}{B_R \pqty{a}}{\CC}{x}{\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} c_n \pqty{x - a}^n}
    \]
    is differentiable on the whole of its domain, and we have
    \[
        f'\pqty{x} = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} n c_n \pqty{x - a}^{n - 1}.
    \]
\end{proposition}
title: Differentiability of Power series, Term-by-Term
\proofname\ (Supplementary, Using Integrability, Real Power Series)

latex:
\begin{proof}[\proofname\ (Supplementary, Direct, Complex Power Series)]
    Consider \(x_0 \in B_R\pqty{a}\). Let \(\abs{x_0 - a} < r < R\) and \(\abs{x - a} < r\).

    Recall the identity
    \[
        \frac{\pqty{x - a}^n - \pqty{x_0 - a}^n}{x - x_0} = \sum_{k = 0}^{n - 1} \pqty{x - a}^k \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1 - k}.
    \]

    Subtracting the target derivative term \(n \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1}\), we have
    \begin{align*}
        \frac{\pqty{x - a}^n - \pqty{x_0 - a}^n}{x - x_0} - n \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1} &= \sum_{k = 0}^{n - 1} \pqty{\pqty{x - a}^k \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1 - k} - \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1}} \\
        &= \sum_{k = 0}^{n - 1} \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1 - k} \pqty{\pqty{x - a}^k - \pqty{x_0 - a}^k} \\
        &= \pqty{x - x_0} \sum_{k = 0}^{n - 1} \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1 - k} \sum_{j = 0}^{k - 1} \pqty{x - a}^{j} \pqty{x_0 - a}^{k - 1 - j}.
    \end{align*}

    We have
    \[
        \abs{x - a}, \abs{x_0 - a} < r,
    \]
    and hence
    \[
        \abs{\frac{\pqty{x - a}^n - \pqty{x_0 - a}^n}{x - x_0} - n \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1}} \leq \abs{x - x_0} \binom{n}{2} r^{n - 2}.
    \]

    We may check that
    \[
        \sum_{n = 2}^{\infty} \abs{c_n} \binom{n}{2} r^{n - 2}
    \]
    converges, and let this sum be \(M\).
    
    Now we investigate the difference of the power series. Since both series converge, we may subtract them term-by-term, giving
    \[
        \frac{f\pqty{x} - f\pqty{x_0}}{x - x_0} - \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} n c_n \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1} = \sum_{n = 2}^{\infty} c_n \pqty{\frac{\pqty{x - a}^n - \pqty{x_0 - a}^n}{x - x_0} - n \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1}},
    \]
    and hence
    \[
        \abs{\frac{f\pqty{x} - f\pqty{x_0}}{x - x_0} - \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} n c_n \pqty{x_0 - a}^{n - 1}} \leq \abs{x - x_0} \sum_{n = 2}^{\infty} \abs{c_n} \binom{n}{2} r^{n - 2} = M \abs{x - x_0}.
    \]

    Taking \(x \to x_0\) gives us the desired result.
\end{proof}
title: \proofname\ (Supplementary, Direct, Complex Power Series)

\begin{examples}[Differentiating and Integrating Power Series]\label{analysis-unit-0216}
    \label{ex:differentiating-integrating-power-series}%
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Consider \(\sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n!}\) which converges on all of \(\CC\). Term-by-term differentiation and integration gives us
        \[
            \dv{x} \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n!} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \dv{x} \pqty{x^n} \frac{1}{n!} = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n - 1}}{\pqty{n - 1}!} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n!}
        \]
        and
        \[
            \int_{0}^{x} \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n!} \dd{t} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \int_{0}^{x} \frac{t^n}{n!} \dd{t} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n + 1}}{\pqty{n + 1}!} = \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n!} - 1.
        \]
        \item Consider \(\sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n^2}\) has radius of convergence \(1\). For all \(\abs{x} < 1\), we have
        \[
            \dv{x} \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{x^n}{n^2} = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n - 1}}{n}
        \]
        and
        \[
            \int_{0}^{x} \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{t^n}{n^2} \dd{t} = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n + 1}}{n^2 \pqty{n + 1}}.
        \]
    \end{itemize}
\end{examples}

    The first two properties arise from differentiating/dividing the power series.

    For the third property, we set
    \[
        f_{a, b} \pqty{z} = \exp\pqty{a + b - z} \cdot \exp\pqty{z}.
    \]

    Then we have
    \begin{align*}
        f'\pqty{z} &= - \exp'\pqty{a + b - z} \exp\pqty{z} + \exp\pqty{a + b - z} \exp'\pqty{z} \\
        &= - f\pqty{z} + f\pqty{z} \\
        &= 0
    \end{align*}
    and hence \(f\) is constant on \(\CC\). Therefore,
    \[
        \exp\pqty{a} \exp\pqty{b} = f\pqty{b} = f\pqty{0} = \exp\pqty{a + b}.
    \]
\end{proof}

title: Properties of Exponential Function on \(\RR\)

latex:
\begin{proof}
    The first two properties follow from \autoref{lem:properties-exp}.

    For \(x > 0\), note that every term in the infinite series is positive, and in particular,
    \[
        \exp\pqty{x} \geq 1 + x > 0
    \]
    for all \(x > 0\), with \(\exp\pqty{x} \to \plusinfty\) as \(x \to \plusinfty\).

    On the other hand, for \(x < 0\), note we have
    \[
        \exp\pqty{-x} \cdot \exp\pqty{x} = \exp\pqty{0} = 1,
    \]
    so since \(\exp\pqty{-x} > 0\), we must have \(\exp\pqty{x} > 0\). Furthermore,
    \[
        \exp\pqty{x} = \frac{1}{\exp\pqty{-x}} \to 0
    \]
    as \(x \to \minusinfty\), since \(\exp\pqty{-x} \to \plusinfty\).

    Since \(\exp'\pqty{x} = \exp\pqty{x} > 0\), it is strictly increasing, and hence injective into \(\oointv{0}{\plusinfty}\). Now given any
    \[
        y \in \oointv{0}{\plusinfty} = \oointv{\lim_{x \to \minusinfty} \exp\pqty{x}}{\lim_{x \to \plusinfty} \exp\pqty{x}},
    \]
    we have some \(a, b \in \RR\), with \(\exp a < y < \exp b\), so by \autoref{thm:intermediate-value} (Intermediate Value Theorem), there is some \(x \in \ccintv{a}{b}\) such that \(\exp\pqty{x} = y\). This shows that it is surjective, hence finishing the proof.
\end{proof}

label: analysis-unit-0222
title: Properties of Logarithm Functions

latex:
\begin{proof}
    The first property is by definition.

    For any \(y = \exp u \in \oointv{0}{\plusinfty}\) and \(z = \exp v \in \oointv{0}{\plusinfty}\), we have
    \[
        \log \pqty{yz} = \log \pqty{\exp u \cdot \exp v} = \log \pqty{\exp \pqty{u + v}} = u + v = \log y + \log z
    \]
    as desired.

    For the third property, we may apply \autoref{thm:inverse-fn-thm-differentiable} (Inverse Function Theorem) to get
    \[
        \log'\pqty{y} = \frac{1}{\exp'\pqty{\log y}} = \frac{1}{y}.
    \]

    For the fourth property, the first point comes from \(\exp 0 = 1\), and hence by \autoref{thm:ftc-1} (Fundamental Theorem of Calculus), we have
    \[
        \log y = \int_1^y \log' t \dd{t} = \int_1^y \frac{1}{t} \dd{t}.
    \]

    The final part inherits from the limit properties of the exponential function.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{analysis-unit-0223}
    We have, for \(y \in \oointv{-1}{1}\), that
    \begin{align*}
        \log\pqty{1 + y} &= \int_0^y \frac{\dd{t}}{1 + t} \\
        &= \int_0^y \frac{\dd{t}}{1 - \pqty{-t}} \\
        &= \int_0^y \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \pqty{-1}^n t^n \dd{t} \\
        &= \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \int_0^y \pqty{-1}^n t^n \dd{t} \\
        &= \sum_{n = 0}^{\infty} \frac{\pqty{-1}^{n} y^{n + 1}}{n + 1}.
    \end{align*}

    In particular, using Analysis II techniques (Abel's Theorem), or quite some tedious integral comparison, we may show that in the case for \(y = 1\), that
    \[
        \log 2 = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty} \frac{\pqty{-1}^{n - 1}}{n}.
    \]

    We have
    \begin{align*}
        \abs{\log 2 - \sum_{n = 0}^{N} \int_{0}^{1} \pqty{-1}^n t^n \dd{t}} &= \abs{\int_{0}^{1} \frac{\dd{t}}{1 + t} - \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1 - \pqty{-t}^{N + 1}}{1 + t} \dd{t}} \\
        &\leq \int_{0}^{1} \abs{\frac{1}{1 + t} - \frac{1 - \pqty{-t}^{N + 1}}{1 + t}} \dd{t} \\
        &\leq \int_{0}^{1} t^{N + 1} \dd{t} \\
        &= \frac{1}{N + 2} \\
        &\to 0
    \end{align*}
    as \(N \to \infty\)
\end{remark}

As a corollary, we see that for natural numbers \(p, q \in \NN\) and \(x > 0\), we have
\[
    \Gamma_p \pqty{x} = \underbrace{\Gamma_1 \pqty{x} \cdots \Gamma_1 \pqty{x}}_{p \text{ terms}} = x^p,
\]
and
\[
    \Gamma_{-p} \pqty{x} = \underbrace{\Gamma_{-1} \pqty{x} \cdots \Gamma_{-1} \pqty{x}}_{p \text{ terms}} = x^{-p}.
\]

Furthermore, we have
\[
    \pqty{\Gamma_{\flatfrac{1}{p}} \pqty{x}}^{p} = \underbrace{\Gamma_{\flatfrac{1}{p}} \pqty{x} \cdots \Gamma_{\flatfrac{1}{p}} \pqty{x}}_{p \text{ terms}} = \Gamma_{\flatfrac{1}{p} + \cdots + \flatfrac{1}{p}} \pqty{x} = \Gamma_1 \pqty{x} = x,
\]
and hence
\[
    \Gamma_{\flatfrac{1}{p}} \pqty{x} = x^{\flatfrac{1}{p}}.
\]

Hence,
\[
    x^{\flatfrac{p}{q}} = \Gamma_{\flatfrac{p}{q}} \pqty{x},
\]
and we have
\[
    \Gamma_{\alpha} \pqty{x} = x^\alpha
\]
for all \(\alpha \in \QQ\).

As for the agreement with the exponential function, we have
\[
    \exp\pqty{x} = \exp\pqty{x \log e} = \Gamma_x \pqty{e} = e^x.
\]

We now study some limit properties on monomials, exponentials and logarithms.

latex:
\begin{proof}
    For the first limit, we let \(x > 1\). Then, since \(x > 0\), we have
    \[
        \exp x = \sum_{k = 0}^{\infty} \frac{x^k}{k!} > \frac{x^n}{n!},
    \]  
    for all \(n \in \NN\).

    We pick \(n\) such that \(n - r \geq 1\), then
    \[
        0 \leq \frac{x^r}{\exp x} \leq \frac{n!}{x^{n - r}} \leq \frac{n!}{x}.
    \]

    Taking the limit as \(x \to \plusinfty\), and using the sandwich theorem gives us the result as desired.

    For the second limit, we have \(t^{-1} \leq t^{\epsilon - 1}\) for all \(t \geq 1\) and \(\epsilon > 0\). Pick \(\epsilon\) such that \(r > \epsilon\), then
    \[
        0 \leq x^{-r} \log x = x^{-r} \int_{1}^{x} \frac{\dd{t}}{t} \leq x^{-r} \int_{1}^{x} t^{\epsilon - 1} \dd{t} = \frac{x^{\epsilon - r}}{\epsilon}
    \]
    and take \(x \to \plusinfty\) with the sandwich theorem gives the result as desired.

    For the limit where \(x \to 0^+\), we note
    \begin{align*}
        \lim_{x \to 0^+} \pqty{x^r \log x} &= - \lim_{t \to \plusinfty} \pqty{t \exp \pqty{- rt}} && x = e^{-t} \\
        &= - \lim_{y \to \plusinfty} \pqty{\frac{y e^{-y}}{r}} && y = rt \\
        &= 0
    \end{align*}
    by the first limit.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
    Once we showed the existence of the smallest \(\pi > 0\), the remaining three propositions follow from the additions formulae.

    We look at \(x \in \oointv{0}{2}\), since by differentiating, we have
    \[
        \cos' x = - \sin x = - \bqty{\pqty{x - \frac{x^3}{3!}} + \pqty{\frac{x^5}{5!} - \frac{x^7}{7!}} + \cdots} < 0,
    \]
    since all the terms in the brackets are positive, using that the series is absolutely convergent, and hence bracketing of terms is allowed. Thus, \(\cos\) has at most one root \(\oointv{0}{2}\). To see that the existence of the root, we have
    \[
        \cos \pqty{\sqrt{2}} = \pqty{1 - \frac{\pqty{\sqrt{2}}^2}{2!}} + \pqty{\frac{\pqty{\sqrt{2}}^4}{4!} - \frac{\pqty{\sqrt{2}}^6}{6!}} + \cdots > 0
    \]
    and
    \[
        \cos \pqty{\sqrt{3}} = \pqty{1 - \frac{\pqty{\sqrt{3}}^2}{2!} + \frac{\pqty{\sqrt{3}}^4}{4!}} - \pqty{\frac{\pqty{\sqrt{3}}^6}{6!} - \frac{\pqty{\sqrt{3}}^8}{8!}} - \cdots < 0.
    \]
    
    By intermediate value theorem, \(\cos\) has a root \(\flatfrac{\pi}{2} \in \oointv{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}} \subset \oointv{0}{2}\). Now, we have
    \[
        \sin^2\pqty{\frac{\pi}{2}} = 1 - \cos^2 \pqty{\frac{\pi}{2}} = 1
    \]
    tells us that \(\sin \pqty{\flatfrac{\pi}{2}} = \pm 1\). But since \(\flatfrac{\pi}{2} \in \oointv{0}{2}\), we have \(\sin \pqty{\flatfrac{\pi}{2}} > 0\), so \(\sin \pqty{\flatfrac{\pi}{2}} = 1\).

\begin{lemma}[Perimeter of Unit Circle]\label{analysis-unit-0234}
    \label{lem:perimeter-unit-circle}%
    \(2\pi\) is the perimeter of the unit circle
    \[
        \mathcal{S}^1 = \set{z \in \CC}{\abs{z} = 1}.
    \]
\end{lemma}
title: Perimeter of Unit Circle

latex:
\begin{proof}
    If we can show the map
    \[
        \function{\gamma}{\cointv{0}{2\pi}}{\mathcal{S}^1}{t}{\exp \pqty{it}}
    \]
    is a bijection, then we get that
    \begin{align*}
        \text{perimeter of }\mathcal{S}^1 &= \text{length of }\gamma \\
        &= \int_{0}^{2 \pi} \abs{\gamma' \pqty{t}} \dd{t} \\
        &= \int_{0}^{2 \pi} \abs{i \exp \pqty{it}} \dd{t} \\
        &= \int_{0}^{2 \pi} \dd{t} \\
        &= 2 \pi.
    \end{align*}

    \textbf{Surjectivity.} Take \(z \in \mathcal{S}^1\), and we write \(z = a + ib\), with \(a^2 + b^2 = 1\), with \(a, b \in \RR\). The restriction
    \[
        \functiondomain{\cos}{\ccintv{0}{\pi}}{\ccintv{-1}{1}}
    \]
    is continuous and strictly monotone. Hence, there is some \(t \in \ccintv{0}{\pi}\) with \(\cos t = a\).

    Furthermore, the restriction
    \[
        \functiondomain{\sin}{\ccintv{0}{\pi}}{\ccintv{0}{1}}
    \]
    is non-negative, so \(\sin t = \sqrt{1 - a^2}\).
    
    \begin{itemize}
        \item If \(b = \sqrt{1 - a^2}\), we get \(\sin t = b\).
        \item If \(b = - \sqrt{1 - a^2}\), we have \(b = - \sin t\), which is to say \(b = \sin \pqty{2 \pi - t}\). But \(\cos t = \cos \pqty{-t} = \cos \pqty{2\pi - t}\).
    \end{itemize}

    Hence, there is some \(t \in \cointv{0}{2\pi}\), such that \(z = \exp \pqty{it}\).

    \textbf{Injectivity.} The earlier positivity proof gives \(\sin t>0\) on \((0,\pi/2]\).
For \(\pi/2<t<\pi\), the addition identities give \(\sin t=\sin(\pi-t)>0\),
so \(\cos' t=-\sin t<0\) throughout \((0,\pi)\). Therefore \(\cos\) is injective
on \([0,\pi]\). On \((\pi,2\pi)\), \(\sin t<0\); this distinguishes the lower
semicircle from the upper one, and reflection \(t\mapsto2\pi-t\) gives injectivity
there as well. The only real-axis endpoints are \(t=0,\pi\), with distinct images.
Hence \(t\mapsto e^{it}\) is injective on \([0,2\pi)\).
\end{proof}

section_path.title: Why an infinitesimal is not zero

latex:
For nonzero \(h\), ordinary algebra gives
\[
\frac{(x+h)^2-x^2}{h}=2x+h.
\]
Taking a real limit as \(h\to0\), or taking a standard part for a nonzero
hyperreal infinitesimal \(h\), gives the derivative \(2x\). Cancelling \(h\)
uses its nonzero value. The later standard-part operation does not assert
that \(h=0\). The title ``without limits'' refers to an alternative formulation
of calculus, not an exemption from precise definitions or an assertion that
classical limit concepts have become invalid.

section_path.title: Why an infinitesimal is not zero

label: def:ultrafilter
latex:
\begin{definition}[Free ultrafilter]\label{def:ultrafilter}
A free ultrafilter \(\U\) on \(\NN=\{1,2,\ldots\}\) is a family of subsets
containing \(\NN\), not containing the empty set, closed under finite intersections
and under passing to supersets, such that exactly one of \(A\) and
\(\NN\setminus A\) belongs to \(\U\) for every \(A\subseteq\NN\), and no
finite set belongs to \(\U\). Consequently every cofinite set belongs to \(\U\).
\end{definition}
title: Free ultrafilter

label: rem:choice
latex:
\begin{remark}[Existence assumption]\label{rem:choice}
Start with the cofinite filter and apply Zorn's lemma to the proper filters
containing it. The union of a chain is a proper filter, so a maximal one exists.
If neither \(A\) nor its complement belonged to this maximal filter, adjoining
\(A\) would still generate a proper filter: otherwise an existing filter member
would be disjoint from \(A\), forcing its complement into the filter.
This contradicts maximality. The resulting ultrafilter cannot contain a finite
set, since it already contains its cofinite complement.
Fix one such \(\U\) throughout this document.
\end{remark}
title: Existence assumption

label: def:ultrapower
latex:
\begin{definition}[Ultrapower]\label{def:ultrapower}
For real sequences \((x_n),(y_n)\), set
\[
(x_n)\sim(y_n)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\{n:x_n=y_n\}\in\U.
\]
Define \(\HR=\RR^{\NN}/\!\sim\), with elements written \([x_n]\).
Arithmetic is coordinatewise, and
\[
[x_n]<[y_n]\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\{n:x_n<y_n\}\in\U.
\]
Embed \(r\in\RR\) as the constant class \([r,r,\ldots]\).
\end{definition}
title: Ultrapower

label: prop:field
title: Ordered-field extension

latex:
\begin{proof}
Changing representatives on a set whose complement belongs to \(\U\) does not
change any coordinatewise identity on the intersection of the relevant
\(\U\)-large sets. This proves well-definedness and the field identities.
Exactly one of \(\{x_n<y_n\},\{x_n=y_n\},\{x_n>y_n\}\) belongs to \(\U\),
which gives trichotomy; order compatibility follows coordinatewise.
If \(X=[x_n]\ne0\), the set \(A=\{n:x_n\ne0\}\) belongs to \(\U\).
Take \(y_n=1/x_n\) on \(A\), and \(y_n=0\) elsewhere. Then \(XY=1\).
Distinct constant sequences remain distinct, so the real embedding is injective.
\end{proof}

label: def:sizes
latex:
\begin{definition}[Finite, infinitesimal and infinite]\label{def:sizes}
A hyperreal \(X\) is finite if \(|X|<M\) for some positive standard real \(M\).
It is infinitesimal if \(|X|<r\) for every positive standard real \(r\).
Zero is infinitesimal; a nonzero infinitesimal is explicitly required when dividing.
A hyperreal is infinite if \(|X|>M\) for every positive standard real \(M\).
Write \(X\approx Y\) when \(X-Y\) is infinitesimal.
\end{definition}
title: Finite, infinitesimal and infinite

label: ex:reciprocal
latex:
\begin{example}[Reciprocal infinite and infinitesimal elements]\label{ex:reciprocal}
Let \(H=[n]\) and \(\varepsilon=[1/n]\). Then \(H\) is positive infinite,
\(\varepsilon\) is positive infinitesimal, and \(H\varepsilon=1\).
Indeed, each required inequality holds eventually in \(n\), hence on a
cofinite set in \(\U\). More generally, if \(\omega\) is positive infinite,
\(1/\omega\) is positive infinitesimal. An arbitrary infinitesimal and an
arbitrary infinite element need not have product one; that relation must be imposed.
\end{example}
title: Reciprocal infinite and infinitesimal elements

label: def:extension
latex:
\begin{definition}[Extensions of sets and functions]\label{def:extension}
For \(A\subseteq\RR\), define
\[
\ext A=\{[x_n]:\{n:x_n\in A\}\in\U\}.
\]
For \(f:\RR\to\RR\), define \(\ext f([x_n])=[f(x_n)]\).
For \(f:D\to\RR\), the same definition on \(\ext D\) uses representatives
in \(D\) on a \(\U\)-large set; values outside that set may be chosen arbitrarily.
Finite-arity relations and operations are extended coordinatewise in the same way.
In particular, \(\ext\NN\) and \(\ext\QQ\) are defined, and \(H=[n]\in\ext\NN\).
\end{definition}

section_path.title: Natural extensions and the scope of transfer

title: Extensions of sets and functions

label: thm:transfer
latex:
\begin{theorem}[First-order transfer in the chosen structure]\label{thm:transfer}
Consider the real ordered field together with any specified real functions,
relations and named constants. For every first-order formula \(\varphi\) of
this structure and hyperreal parameters \([a_n^1],\ldots,[a_n^k]\),
\[
\HR\models\varphi([a_n^1],\ldots,[a_n^k])
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\{n:\RR\models\varphi(a_n^1,\ldots,a_n^k)\}\in\U,
\]
where the functions and relations on the left are their natural extensions.
In particular a sentence true in the real structure remains true in its
ultrapower. This is the form of \L o\'s's theorem used here.
\end{theorem}

section_path.title: Natural extensions and the scope of transfer

title: First-order transfer in the chosen structure

latex:
\begin{proof}
Atomic formulas follow from the coordinatewise definitions. Intersections and
the ultrafilter dichotomy prove the steps for conjunction and negation.
For an existential formula, a hyperreal witness gives real coordinate witnesses
on a \(\U\)-large set by induction. Conversely, if real witnesses exist on
such a set, choose one at each index there and an arbitrary real elsewhere.
Their class is a hyperreal witness by induction. Universal quantification follows
from negation and existential quantification. Structural induction proves the formula.
\end{proof}

section_path.title: Natural extensions and the scope of transfer

label: rem:scope
latex:
\begin{remark}[What is not being transferred]\label{rem:scope}
This theorem is about first-order formulas in the specified structure.
It does not allow unrestricted quantification over all subsets of \(\HR\),
nor does it introduce predicates meaning ``standard'' or ``infinitesimal''.
A fixed real function, even a discontinuous one, may be named and extended.
The fact that a real function is continuous can also be expressed using
quantifiers over numbers. Quantifiers in its transferred formula range over
hyperreals, not just standard reals.
\end{remark}

section_path.title: Natural extensions and the scope of transfer

title: What is not being transferred

label: ex:transfer
latex:
\begin{example}[Arithmetic and Archimedean quantifiers]\label{ex:transfer}
Commutativity and cancellation hold in the hyperreal field. For a nonzero
infinitesimal \(\varepsilon\),
\[
\frac1{1+\varepsilon}=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{1-\varepsilon^2},
\]
since multiplying numerator and denominator by \(1-\varepsilon\) is legitimate.
The real assertion \(\forall x\in\RR\ \exists n\in\NN\ (n>x)\) transfers to
\(\forall X\in\HR\ \exists N\in\ext\NN\ (N>X)\).
It does not assert that a standard natural number exceeds every hyperreal.
Thus transfer is compatible with the infinite element \(H\).
\end{example}

label: thm:st
title: Existence and uniqueness of the standard part

latex:
\begin{proof}
The real set \(A=\{a\in\RR:a<X\}\) is nonempty and bounded above because
\(X\) is finite. Put \(r=\sup A\). For each real \(\delta>0\), some
\(a\in A\) satisfies \(r-\delta<a<X\). Also \(X<r+\delta\), since otherwise
\(r+\delta/2\in A\), contradicting the supremum. Hence \(|X-r|<\delta\).
If \(X\approx s\) for another real \(s\), then \(r-s\) is a real infinitesimal
by the triangle inequality, and is zero by Lemma~\ref{lem:algebra}.
\end{proof}

label: prop:st-arithmetic
latex:
\begin{proposition}[Standard-part arithmetic]\label{prop:st-arithmetic}
For finite \(X,Y\),
\[
\st(X+Y)=\st X+\st Y,\qquad \st(XY)=(\st X)(\st Y).
\]
If \(\st Y\ne0\), then \(X/Y\) is finite and
\(\st(X/Y)=\st X/\st Y\).
\end{proposition}
title: Standard-part arithmetic

label: ex:scales
latex:
\begin{example}[Scales and the microscope interpretation]\label{ex:scales}
For real \(a\), nonzero infinitesimal \(\varepsilon\), and each fixed standard
integer \(k\), \(a+k\varepsilon\approx a\). Thus
\(\st(2+\varepsilon)=2\) and \(\st(3-\varepsilon+\varepsilon^4)=3\).
At an infinite scale, \(4H\), \(4H+1\) and \(4H+1+\varepsilon\) are all infinite,
so none has a real standard part. However
\((4H+1+\varepsilon)-(4H+1)=\varepsilon\), so the last two are infinitely close.
A finite drawing of these scales is schematic, not an exhaustive real coordinate
model of the hyperreal line. There is no smallest positive infinitesimal: if
\(\varepsilon>0\) is infinitesimal, so is \(\varepsilon/2\).
\end{example}
title: Scales and the microscope interpretation

label: def:limit
latex:
\begin{definition}[Classical finite limit]\label{def:limit}
Let \(D\subseteq\RR\), let \(a\) be an accumulation point of \(D\), and
let \(f:D\to\RR\). The assertion \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L\in\RR\) means
\[
\forall r>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall x\in D:
\quad0<|x-a|<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x)-L|<r.
\]
All quantifiers here are over real numbers.
\end{definition}

section_path.title: Limits and continuity: all infinitesimal probes

title: Classical finite limit

label: thm:limit
latex:
\begin{theorem}[Nonstandard criterion for a finite limit]\label{thm:limit}
In Definition~\ref{def:limit}, the limit equals \(L\) if and only if
\[
\ext f(X)\approx L\quad\hbox{for every }X\in\ext D
\hbox{ with }X\approx a\hbox{ and }X\ne a.
\]
Equivalently all these values are finite and have standard part \(L\).
\end{theorem}

section_path.title: Limits and continuity: all infinitesimal probes

title: Nonstandard criterion for a finite limit

latex:
\begin{proof}
Suppose the real limit holds. Fix a standard \(r>0\) and its real \(\delta>0\).
Transfer the implication with these fixed parameters. Every admissible \(X\)
is within \(\delta\) of \(a\), giving \(|\ext f(X)-L|<r\). As this holds for
all standard \(r>0\), the difference is infinitesimal.
Conversely, failure gives a real \(r_0>0\) and, for each integer \(n\), a point
\(x_n\in D\) with \(0<|x_n-a|<1/n\) and \(|f(x_n)-L|\ge r_0\).
The class \(X=[x_n]\) is infinitely close to \(a\), distinct from it, and
\(|\ext f(X)-L|\ge r_0\), contradicting the asserted criterion.
\end{proof}

section_path.title: Limits and continuity: all infinitesimal probes

label: prop:other-limits
latex:
\begin{proposition}[One-sided and infinite-endpoint limits]\label{prop:other-limits}
If the real domain contains a right neighbourhood of \(a\),
\(\lim_{x\downarrow a} f(x)=L\in\RR\) precisely when
\(\ext f(a+h)\approx L\) for every positive infinitesimal \(h\).
For a left neighbourhood use every negative infinitesimal \(h\).
If the domain contains a ray \((b,\infty)\), then
\(\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=L\in\RR\) precisely when
\(\ext f(W)\approx L\) for every positive infinite \(W\).
For a negative ray use every negative infinite \(W\).
\end{proposition}

section_path.title: Limits and continuity: all infinitesimal probes

title: One-sided and infinite-endpoint limits

latex:
\begin{proof}
The one-sided proofs restrict the choices in Theorem~\ref{thm:limit} to the
appropriate side. At \(+\infty\), transfer each real tail estimate. If the
limit fails, choose \(x_n>\max\{b,n\}\) with a fixed positive error from \(L\).
Then \([x_n]\) is a positive infinite counterexample. Reflect the variable
for \(-\infty\).
\end{proof}

section_path.title: Limits and continuity: all infinitesimal probes

title: Continuity criterion

latex:
\begin{proof}
Transfer the epsilon--delta continuity estimate as in Theorem~\ref{thm:limit}.
If continuity fails, choose \(x_n\in D\) with \(|x_n-a|<1/n\) and a fixed
positive lower bound for \(|f(x_n)-f(a)|\). The resulting class contradicts
the criterion. At an isolated point the condition also holds: a real gap around
\(a\) transfers, forcing any such \(X\) to equal \(a\).
\end{proof}

label: thm:derivative
title: Derivative criterion

label: ex:polynomial
latex:
\begin{example}[Polynomial derivative]\label{ex:polynomial}
For a fixed standard integer \(m\ge1\) and \(f(x)=x^m\), the binomial formula gives
\[
\frac{(a+h)^m-a^m}{h}
=ma^{m-1}+\sum_{j=2}^m\binom mj a^{m-j}h^{j-1}.
\]
The sum is finite, with real coefficients and positive powers of an infinitesimal,
so it is infinitesimal. The criterion proves \(f'(a)=ma^{m-1}\).
For \(m=0\), the constant function has derivative zero directly.
For \(m=1\), the remainder is an empty sum. The fixed standard value of \(m\)
is essential to this finite-sum argument.
\end{example}
title: Polynomial derivative

label: ex:abs
title: Why the sign of the infinitesimal matters

latex:
Define the real exponential by the absolutely convergent series
\(E(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}t^k/k!\), and set \(e=E(1)\).
The ratio test proves convergence for each real \(t\). The Cauchy product and
binomial theorem give \(E(x+t)=E(x)E(t)\); this uses absolute convergence.
Below \(e^x\) denotes \(E(x)\) for real \(x\); for hyperreal arguments it means
\(\ext E\), not a new unproved operation on infinitesimals.

section_path.title: The exponential: retaining the required precision

title: Exponential derivative

latex:
\begin{proof}
Transfer Lemma~\ref{lem:exp-error}. For every nonzero infinitesimal \(h\),
\[
\left|\frac{\ext E(h)-1}{h}-1\right|\le e|h|,
\]
so this quotient is infinitely close to one. The transferred addition law gives
\[
\frac{\ext E(a+h)-E(a)}h
=E(a)\frac{\ext E(h)-1}h\approx E(a).
\]
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:derivative}. No replacement of a base by an approximately
equal base under an infinite exponent is used.
\end{proof}

section_path.title: The exponential: retaining the required precision

label: prop:e-sequence
latex:
\begin{proposition}[The classical sequence for \(e\)]\label{prop:e-sequence}
With \(e=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}1/k!\), one has
\(\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+1/n)^n=e\). Consequently, for every positive infinite
hypernatural \(N\in\ext\NN\),
\[
\st\big((1+1/N)^N\big)=e.
\]
The hypernatural power denotes the natural extension of the integer-power function.
\end{proposition}

section_path.title: The exponential: retaining the required precision

title: The classical sequence for \(e\)

latex:
\begin{proof}
Expand
\[
(1+1/n)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\frac1{k!}
 \prod_{j=0}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac jn\right).
\]
Every factor in each product lies in \([0,1]\), so this is at most \(e\).
For any fixed integer \(K\), the first \(K+1\) terms tend to
\(\sum_{k=0}^K1/k!\) and form a lower bound for \(n\ge K\).
Choosing \(K\) with a sufficiently small factorial-series tail proves convergence.
Transfer the resulting real tail estimates to \(N\); every infinite hypernatural
exceeds the standard threshold. The standard-part formula follows.
\end{proof}

section_path.title: The exponential: retaining the required precision

label: rem:precision
latex:
\begin{remark}[What an approximation permits]\label{rem:precision}
The exact exponential at an infinitesimal argument is generally not \(1+h\).
For \(h>0\), transfer of \(E(t)\ge1+t+t^2/2\) for real \(t\ge0\) gives
\(\ext E(h)>1+h\). The derivative proof works because the error divided by
\(h\) is still infinitesimal, as shown above.
In general, \(X\approx Y\) alone does not permit replacing \(X\) by \(Y\)
inside a quotient by an infinitesimal: \(h\approx0\), but \(h/h=1\).
Similarly, standard-part equality of two bases is not an exact equality that
can be substituted under a variable or infinite exponent. Indeed,
\(1+1/H\approx1\), but Proposition~\ref{prop:e-sequence} gives
\(\st((1+1/H)^H)=e\), whereas \(1^H=1\). Since the series defining \(e\)
has positive terms and begins with \(1+1+1/2\), these standard parts differ.
\end{remark}

title: Discontinuity is preserved

\begin{proof}
By density, choose rationals \(q_n\) and irrationals \(r_n\), both distinct
from \(a\), with \(|q_n-a|<1/n\) and \(|r_n-a|<1/n\).
Then \(Q=[q_n]\) and \(R=[r_n]\) are distinct from \(a\) and infinitely close
to it, but \(\ext D(Q)=1\) and \(\ext D(R)=0\).
No real \(L\) can be infinitely close to both zero and one. Apply

\end{proof}

label: rem:wrong-extension
latex:
\begin{remark}[A different map obtained from standard parts]\label{rem:wrong-extension}
On finite hyperreals one may define \(G(X)=D(\st X)\), but this is not
\(\ext D\). For example, \(\st(\sqrt2/H)=0\), so \(G(\sqrt2/H)=D(0)=1\),
whereas \(\ext D(\sqrt2/H)=0\).
A nonstandard continuity test using this different map would not test continuity
of \(D\). The standard-part operation is not among the transferred real
operations of Theorem~\ref{thm:transfer}.
\end{remark}

label: prop:improper
title: Improper integrals through an extended primitive

latex:
\begin{proof}
By definition convergence of this improper integral is precisely
\(\lim_{t\to+\infty}F(t)=L\). Apply Proposition~\ref{prop:other-limits}.
Thus one may use an infinite cutoff in the extended \(F\), but equality of
standard parts must hold for all such cutoffs. In particular \(W\) and \(2W\)
have the same standard part of \(\ext F\) when the integral converges.
\end{proof}

label: ex:integrals
latex:
\begin{example}[A convergent and a divergent cutoff]\label{ex:integrals}
For \(f(x)=x^{-2}\) on \([1,\infty)\), the real identity \(F(t)=1-1/t\)
transfers to \(\ext F(W)=1-1/W\). Every positive infinite \(W\) gives
standard part one, so the improper integral is one.
For \(f(x)=1\), \(F(t)=t-1\) and \(\ext F(W)=W-1\) is infinite; no real
standard part exists and the improper integral does not converge to a finite value.
\end{example}
title: A convergent and a divergent cutoff
