title: $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},\cdot)$ is NOT a group

latex:
\begin{wex}{$a\ast b=a+b+ab$ on $\mathbb{R}$: identity $0$, but $-1$ has no inverse}
On $\mathbb{R}$ define $a\ast b=a+b+ab$. Decide whether $(\mathbb{R},\ast)$ is a group, and whether $(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$ is.
\wrec The clean trick is the factorization $a\ast b=(1+a)(1+b)-1$, which turns $\ast$ into ordinary multiplication after the shift $a\mapsto 1+a$. Recognition: whenever an exotic operation can be rewritten as $f(a)f(b)$ for a bijection-like $f$, transport the question to a familiar group/monoid. The forbidden value will be the preimage of $0$.
\wsol
\emph{Set up the shift.} Let $u=1+a$, $v=1+b$. Then
\[
a\ast b=a+b+ab=(1+a)(1+b)-1=uv-1,\qquad\text{so } 1+(a\ast b)=(1+a)(1+b).
\]
(G0) Closed on $\mathbb{R}$: $a\ast b\in\mathbb{R}$.
(G1) Associativity: $1+\big((a\ast b)\ast c\big)=(1+(a\ast b))(1+c)=(1+a)(1+b)(1+c)$, symmetric in the grouping, so $(a\ast b)\ast c=a\ast(b\ast c)$. Associative.
(G2) Identity $e$: need $a+e+ae=a$, i.e.\ $e(1+a)=0$ for all $a$, forcing $e=0$. Check: $a\ast0=a+0+0=a$. Identity is $0$.
(G3) Inverse of $a$: need $x$ with $(1+a)(1+x)=1+0=1$, i.e.\ $1+x=\dfrac1{1+a}$, so $x=\dfrac1{1+a}-1=\dfrac{-a}{1+a}$. This requires $1+a\ne0$, i.e.\ $a\ne-1$.
At $a=-1$: $(-1)\ast x=-1+x-x=-1\ne0$ for all $x$, so $-1$ has \emph{no} inverse. Hence $(\mathbb{R},\ast)$ is \textbf{not} a group.
On $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\}$ the map $a\mapsto 1+a$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}=\mathbb{R}^\times$, and it carries $\ast$ to multiplication. Since $(\mathbb{R}^\times,\cdot)$ is an abelian group, so is $(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$: closed (if $a,b\ne-1$ then $(1+a)(1+b)\ne0$ so $a\ast b\ne-1$), identity $0$, inverse $\dfrac{-a}{1+a}$.
\textit{Check.} Take $a=2$: $x=\dfrac{-2}{3}$, and $2\ast(-\tfrac23)=2-\tfrac23+2\cdot(-\tfrac23)=2-\tfrac23-\tfrac43=2-2=0$. Correct.
The transport of structure is exactly the commuting square
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\})\times(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\}) \arrow[r, "\ast"] \arrow[d, "(1+\,\cdot\,)\times(1+\,\cdot\,)"'] & \mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\} \arrow[d, "1+\,\cdot\,"] \\
\mathbb{R}^\times\times\mathbb{R}^\times \arrow[r, "{(u,v)\mapsto uv}"'] & \mathbb{R}^\times
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four nodes, all groups. Top-left: the Cartesian product $(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\})\times(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\})$, where pairs of inputs for the operation $\ast$ live. Top-right: $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\}$, the group under $\ast$ whose group structure we are establishing. Bottom-left: $\mathbb{R}^\times\times\mathbb{R}^\times$, pairs of nonzero reals, i.e.\ inputs for ordinary multiplication. Bottom-right: $\mathbb{R}^\times$, the abelian group of nonzero reals under multiplication. All four are abelian groups (the bottom row is classical; the top row is what we are proving).
\dgi{Arrows:} Top horizontal: the operation $\ast$, sending $(a,b)$ to $a\ast b=a+b+ab$. Bottom horizontal: ordinary multiplication $\cdot$, sending $(u,v)$ to $uv$. Left vertical: the map $(1+\,\cdot\,)\times(1+\,\cdot\,)$, sending $(a,b)$ to $(1+a,1+b)$; it is a bijection $(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\})^2\to(\mathbb{R}^\times)^2$. Right vertical: the shift $1+\,\cdot\,$, sending $a$ to $1+a$; it is a bijection $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\}\to\mathbb{R}^\times$.
\dgi{What commutes:} Down-then-right equals right-then-down: $(1+(a\ast b))=(1+a)(1+b)$. That is, $(1+\,\cdot\,)\circ\ast = \cdot\circ((1+\,\cdot\,)\times(1+\,\cdot\,))$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase $(a,b)$ along both paths. \emph{Top then right:} first apply $\ast$ to get $a+b+ab$, then shift to get $1+(a+b+ab)=1+a+b+ab=(1+a)(1+b)$. \emph{Left then bottom:} first shift each factor to get $(1+a,1+b)$, then multiply to get $(1+a)(1+b)$. These are identical by the factorization $1+a+b+ab=(1+a)(1+b)$, which is just the elementary algebraic identity $(1+a)(1+b)=1+a+b+ab$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram encodes the algebraic reason why $(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$ is a group: the shift $a\mapsto 1+a$ is an isomorphism from $(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$ to $(\mathbb{R}^\times,\cdot)$. Every group axiom for $\ast$ can be read off from the diagram by transporting it from $\mathbb{R}^\times$ through the bijection. The proof that $(\mathbb{R},\ast)$ fails to be a group is also recorded: $a=-1$ maps to $0$, which is the missing element of $\mathbb{R}^\times$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $a=2$, $b=3$. Top path: $2\ast3=2+3+6=11$, shift to $1+11=12$. Left-then-bottom: shift to $(3,4)$, multiply to $12$. Equal: $12=12$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the right vertical arrow $1+\,\cdot\,$ as a group homomorphism in the sense that $1+(a+b)=(1+a)+(1+b)$, which is false. The shift is a homomorphism from $(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$ to $(\mathbb{R}^\times,\cdot)$, not from $(\mathbb{R},+)$ to $(\mathbb{R}^\times,\cdot)$. The diagram says the shift intertwines $\ast$ with $\cdot$, not $+$ with $\cdot$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the exotic operation $\ast$ is secretly ordinary multiplication in disguise, with the bijection $a\mapsto 1+a$ as the dictionary, so $(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1\},\ast)$ inherits all of $(\mathbb{R}^\times,\cdot)$'s group structure for free.
\end{dgx}
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{Using cancellation to solve $axb=c$ for $x$}
In any group $G$, solve $a\,x\,b=c$ for $x$ in terms of $a,b,c$, and prove the solution is unique.
\wrec This is the equation-solving corollary of cancellation (Proposition~\ref{p:cancel@c1}): isolate $x$ by peeling off the outer factors with their inverses, respecting the side each sits on. Trigger: an equation with the unknown sandwiched between known group elements; multiply on the matching side and use associativity, never division.
\wsol
Start from $axb=c$. Left-multiply by $a^{-1}$:
\[
a^{-1}(axb)=a^{-1} c\ \Longrightarrow\ (a^{-1} a)xb=a^{-1} c\ \Longrightarrow\ xb=a^{-1} c.
\]
Now right-multiply by $b^{-1}$:
\[
(xb)b^{-1}=(a^{-1} c)b^{-1}\ \Longrightarrow\ x(bb^{-1})=a^{-1} c b^{-1}\ \Longrightarrow\ x=a^{-1} c\,b^{-1}.
\]
\emph{Existence:} substitute back, $a\,(a^{-1} c b^{-1})\,b=(aa^{-1})c(b^{-1} b)=c$. \emph{Uniqueness:} if $axb=ax'b$ then left-cancel $a$ and right-cancel $b$ to get $x=x'$. So $x=a^{-1} cb^{-1}$ is the unique solution.
\textit{Check (in $D_8=\langle r,s\st r^4=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1} s\rangle$).} Solve $r\,x\,s=r^2$. Here $a=r$, $b=s$, $c=r^2$, so $x=a^{-1} c\,b^{-1}=r^{-1} r^2 s^{-1}$. Now $r^{-1}=r^3$ and $s^{-1}=s$, hence
\[
x=r^3\,r^2\,s=r^{5}s=r^{5-4}s=r\,s=rs.
\]
Verify: $r(rs)s=r^2 s^2=r^2$. Correct.
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{Socks--shoes in a nonabelian group ($S_3$ and $D_8$)}
Verify $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1} a^{-1}$ concretely, and show that the ``naive'' $a^{-1} b^{-1}$ is wrong, in a nonabelian group.
\wrec Proposition~\ref{p:invlaws@c1}(b) is forced by associativity, but the order reversal only \emph{matters} when $ab\ne ba$. Trigger: any time you invert a product in a noncommutative setting (permutations, matrices, dihedral symmetries), reverse the factors. Test the law against a case where reversing changes the answer.
\wsol
\emph{In $S_3$ (compose right-to-left).} Let $a=(1\,2\,3)$, $b=(1\,2)$.
First $ab$: apply $b$ then $a$. $1\xrightarrow{b}2\xrightarrow{a}3$, $2\xrightarrow{b}1\xrightarrow{a}2$, $3\xrightarrow{b}3\xrightarrow{a}1$. So $ab=(1\,3)$, a transposition, hence $(ab)^{-1}=(1\,3)$.
Now $b^{-1} a^{-1}$: $b^{-1}=(1\,2)$, $a^{-1}=(1\,3\,2)$. Apply $a^{-1}$ then $b^{-1}$: $1\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}3\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}3$, $2\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}1\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}2$, $3\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}2\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}1$. So $b^{-1} a^{-1}=(1\,3)=(ab)^{-1}$. Law confirmed.
The wrong order $a^{-1} b^{-1}$: apply $b^{-1}=(1\,2)$ then $a^{-1}=(1\,3\,2)$: $1\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}2\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}1$, $2\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}1\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}3$, $3\xrightarrow{b^{-1}}3\xrightarrow{a^{-1}}2$. So $a^{-1} b^{-1}=(2\,3)\ne(1\,3)$. The naive order fails, exactly because $S_3$ is nonabelian.

\emph{In $D_8$.} Let $a=r$, $b=s$, so $ab=rs$. Since $(rs)(rs)=r(sr)s=r(r^{-1} s)s=s^2=1$, the element $rs$ is its own inverse: $(rs)^{-1}=rs$. Socks--shoes gives $b^{-1} a^{-1}=s^{-1} r^{-1}=s\,r^3$. Reduce $sr^3=r^{-3}s=r s$ (using $sr=r^{-1} s$ thrice, equivalently $sr^k=r^{-k}s$). So $b^{-1} a^{-1}=rs=(ab)^{-1}$. Consistent.
\textit{Check.} In both groups we recovered $(ab)^{-1}$ on the nose, and in $S_3$ the reversed and naive orders gave genuinely different permutations $(1\,3)$ vs $(2\,3)$, dramatizing why order reversal is mandatory.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{The square--root subtlety: cancellation does not give $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$}
In a group, deduce from $x^2=e$ together with $xy=e$ what $y$ must be, and contrast with trying to ``cancel a square.''
\wrec Cancellation removes a \emph{matched} factor from both sides; it does not let you halve an exponent. Trigger: students write $x^2=y^2\Rightarrow x=y$ by ``cancelling,'' which is false in general. Use cancellation only as Proposition~\ref{p:cancel@c1} licenses it.
\wsol
From $xy=e$, no extra multiplication is needed: $xy=e$ already says $y=x^{-1}$ by uniqueness of inverses. If also $x^2=e$, then $x^{-1}=x$, so $y=x$.
Now the contrast: $x^2=y^2$ does \emph{not} imply $x=y$. In $\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z}$ under $+$ (so the group operation is addition, and ``$x^2$'' means $x+x=2x$): $2\cdot\bar1=\bar2$ and $2\cdot\bar5=\overline{10}=\bar2$, so $2\bar1=2\bar5$ but $\bar1\ne\bar5$. The reason: cancelling the $2$ would require multiplying by an ``inverse of doubling,'' which is not a group element. Cancellation (Proposition~\ref{p:cancel@c1}) only cancels the \emph{same} group element $a$ appearing on the \emph{same side}, as in $ab=ac\Rightarrow b=c$; it never cancels a repeated factor that equals the variable.
\textit{Check.} In $\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z}$, $\bar1+\bar1=\bar2=\bar5+\bar5$ indeed, yet $\bar1\ne\bar5$: so $2x=2y$ is consistent with $x\ne y$, and ``cancelling the $2$'' is illegitimate. By contrast, legitimate cancellation cancels a fixed group element on a fixed side: from $\bar3+\bar1=\bar3+\bar5$ left cancellation of $\bar3$ would give $\bar1=\bar5$; since $\bar1\ne\bar5$, the premise must be false, and indeed $\bar3+\bar1=\bar4\ne\bar0=\bar3+\bar5$. No contradiction arises -- the legitimate law is never violated.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Confirming $V_4$ is an abelian group from its table}
Use the table above to verify all axioms except associativity, confirm commutativity, and read off each inverse.
\wrec Apply the table-reading method: closure (no stray symbols), identity (header-matching row/column), inverses (where $e$ occurs), Latin-square (cancellation), and symmetry across the diagonal (abelian). Associativity is the one axiom the table cannot show, so cite the model $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$.
\wsol
\emph{Closure:} all $16$ body entries are among $e,a,b,c$. Yes.
\emph{Identity:} row $e$ is $e\,a\,b\,c$ and column $e$ is $e\,a\,b\,c$; so $e\ast x=x\ast e=x$. Identity $=e$.
\emph{Inverses:} $e$ appears at positions $(e,e),(a,a),(b,b),(c,c)$ -- once in every row/column -- so $e^{-1}=e$, $a^{-1}=a$, $b^{-1}=b$, $c^{-1}=c$.
\emph{Latin square:} row $a$ is $a\,e\,c\,b$ (a permutation of $e,a,b,c$); rows $b,c$ likewise; columns likewise. So left/right cancellation hold.
\emph{Abelian:} the table is symmetric across the main diagonal -- e.g.\ entry $(a,b)=c=(b,a)$, $(b,c)=a=(c,b)$, $(a,c)=b=(c,a)$. So $\ast$ is commutative.
\emph{Associativity:} inherited from $V_4\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ via $e\mapsto(0,0)$, $a\mapsto(1,0)$, $b\mapsto(0,1)$, $c\mapsto(1,1)$, where the operation is coordinatewise addition mod $2$ (associative).
\textit{Check.} Test one associativity instance directly against the table: $(a\ast b)\ast c=c\ast c=e$ and $a\ast(b\ast c)=a\ast a=e$. Equal, as the model predicts.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{A defective table: spotting the broken axiom}
Decide whether the following table on $\{e,a,b,c\}$ defines a group:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\ast & e & a & b & c\\\hline
e & e & a & b & c\\
a & a & b & c & e\\
b & b & c & e & a\\
c & c & a & a & b
\end{array}
\]
\wrec Run the table-reading checklist and stop at the first violated condition. Trigger: a proposed finite operation -- always test the Latin-square property first, since a repeated entry in a row or column instantly kills the cancellation laws, which every group satisfies (they follow from (G1)--(G3)).
\wsol
Closure: all entries in $\{e,a,b,c\}$. OK.
Identity: row/column $e$ match the headers, so $e$ is an identity. OK.
Latin square: examine row $c$: it reads $c,a,a,b$ -- the symbol $a$ appears \emph{twice} and $e$ does \emph{not} appear at all. Two failures follow:
(i) $e$ is missing from row $c$, so there is no $x$ with $c\ast x=e$: element $c$ has \emph{no right inverse}, violating (G3).
(ii) The repeat $c\ast a=a=c\ast b$ with $a\ne b$ violates left cancellation, which a group must satisfy.
Either observation alone shows this is \textbf{not} a group.
\textit{Check.} In a genuine group every row is a permutation of the elements (rearrangement theorem); row $c=(c,a,a,b)$ is not a permutation, confirming the defect without even testing associativity.
\end{wex}

\begin{remark}[Why the table cannot show associativity, and a diagram for cancellation]
The Latin-square property is equivalent to both cancellation laws but is \emph{strictly weaker} than being a group: there exist Latin squares (``quasigroups'') that are not associative. The cancellation law $ab=ac\Rightarrow b=c$ is exactly the statement that left translation $L_a:x\mapsto ax$ is injective, which on a finite set forces it to be a bijection -- this is the rearrangement theorem. As a commuting square, the inverse map intertwines left and right translations:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=6em]
G \arrow[r, "L_a:\,x\mapsto ax"] \arrow[d, "(\cdot)^{-1}"'] & G \arrow[d, "(\cdot)^{-1}"] \\
G \arrow[r, "R_{a^{-1}}:\,y\mapsto y a^{-1}"'] & G
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four copies of the same group $G$, arranged at the four corners of the square. The top-left and top-right are $G$ viewed as a set of inputs before inversion; the bottom-left and bottom-right are $G$ viewed as the set of outputs after inversion.
\dgi{Arrows:} Top horizontal: left translation $L_a$, the map $x\mapsto ax$, acting on $G$ from the left by the fixed element $a$. Bottom horizontal: right translation $R_{a^{-1}}$, the map $y\mapsto ya^{-1}$, acting from the right by $a^{-1}$. Left vertical: the inversion map $(\cdot)^{-1}$, sending $x$ to $x^{-1}$. Right vertical: the same inversion map $(\cdot)^{-1}$, sending $ax$ to $(ax)^{-1}$. All four maps are bijections of $G$ to itself.
\dgi{What commutes:} Down-then-right equals right-then-down: $R_{a^{-1}}\circ(\cdot)^{-1}=(\cdot)^{-1}\circ L_a$. Explicitly, for every $x\in G$: $(ax)^{-1}=(x^{-1})a^{-1}$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase a generic $x\in G$ along both paths. \emph{Right then down:} first apply $L_a$ to get $ax$, then invert to get $(ax)^{-1}=x^{-1} a^{-1}$ by Proposition~\ref{p:invlaws@c1}(b). \emph{Down then right:} first invert $x$ to get $x^{-1}$, then apply $R_{a^{-1}}$ to get $x^{-1} a^{-1}$. Both paths yield $x^{-1} a^{-1}$, and they agree because $(ab)^{-1}=b^{-1} a^{-1}$ holds in any group.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The remark uses this square to explain the rearrangement theorem in a conceptual way: $L_a$ is a bijection because the square writes it as $L_a=(\cdot)^{-1}\circ R_{a^{-1}}\circ(\cdot)^{-1}$, a composite of bijections (inversion is its own inverse and $R_{a^{-1}}$ has inverse $R_a$), so its inverse as a set-map is $(\cdot)^{-1}\circ R_a\circ(\cdot)^{-1}=L_{a^{-1}}$; i.e.\ the diagram displays how inversion converts left multiplication into right multiplication. It also shows that the cancellation-law content ($L_a$ injective) is captured by a simple conjugation via the inversion involution.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $G=S_3$, take $a=(1\,2)$. Then $L_a$ maps $(1\,3)$ to $(1\,2)(1\,3)=(1\,3\,2)$. Inverting: $((1\,2)(1\,3))^{-1}=(1\,3\,2)^{-1}=(1\,2\,3)$. Other path: invert $(1\,3)$ to get $(1\,3)$ (a transposition is its own inverse), then right-multiply by $a^{-1}=(1\,2)$: $(1\,3)(1\,2)=(1\,2\,3)$. Both yield $(1\,2\,3)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes expect inversion to intertwine $L_a$ with $L_{a^{-1}}$ (left-multiply by $a^{-1}$), but the socks-shoes law reverses the side: $(ax)^{-1}=x^{-1} a^{-1}$ is right multiplication by $a^{-1}$, not left. The diagram makes this reversal of side unavoidable and visible.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that inversion in a group converts left multiplication by $a$ into right multiplication by $a^{-1}$, so the two translations are intertwined by the inversion involution rather than being related by a naive left-to-left substitution.
\end{dgx}
Commutativity of this square is the identity $(ax)^{-1}=x^{-1} a^{-1}$ from Proposition~\ref{p:invlaws@c1}(b), now read as ``inverting turns left multiplication by $a$ into right multiplication by $a^{-1}$.''
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Additive number groups]\label{r:addnumber-mrg@c1}
Each of
\[
(\mathbb{Z},+),\quad(\mathbb{Q},+),\quad(\mathbb{R},+),\quad(\mathbb{C},+)
\]
is an abelian group: addition is associative and commutative, the identity is $0$, and the inverse of $x$ is $-x$. They sit inside one another, $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{Q}\subset\mathbb{R}\subset\mathbb{C}$, each a subgroup of the next under the same $+$. Note $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ is the only one of the four in which a single element, namely $1$ (or $-1$), generates the whole group: $\mathbb{Z}=\langle 1\rangle$.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Multiplicative number groups, and what gets deleted]\label{r:multnumber-mrg@c1}
Under multiplication the picture is more delicate because $0$ is never invertible. Writing $A^{\times}=A\setminus\{0\}$ for a field $A$:
\[
(\mathbb{Q}^{\times},\cdot),\quad(\mathbb{R}^{\times},\cdot),\quad(\mathbb{C}^{\times},\cdot)
\]
are abelian groups (identity $1$, inverse $x^{-1}=1/x$), but $(\mathbb{Q},\cdot),(\mathbb{R},\cdot),(\mathbb{C},\cdot)$ are \emph{not}, since $0$ has no inverse. By contrast $(\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\},\cdot)$ is still not a group: e.g.\ $2$ has no integer inverse (axiom (G3) fails, not merely the deletion of $0$). The positive reals and positive rationals form groups under multiplication,
\[
(\mathbb{R}^{+},\cdot),\qquad(\mathbb{Q}^{+},\cdot),
\]
because a product of positives is positive (closure) and $1/x>0$ when $x>0$ (inverses); these are the multiplicative analogues of the additive groups above, and $x\mapsto\log x$ is a bijection $\mathbb{R}^{+}\to\mathbb{R}$ carrying $\cdot$ to $+$.
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Integer powers]\label{d:powers-mrg@c1}
Let $G$ be a group, $x\in G$. Define $x^0=1$ (the identity), and for $n\ge1$
\[
x^n=\underbrace{x\,x\cdots x}_{n\text{ factors}},\qquad x^{-n}=(x^{-1})^n=(x^n)^{-1} .
\]
By generalized associativity (Remark~\ref{r:genassoc@c1}) the usual laws of exponents hold for all integers $m,n$:
\[
x^m x^n=x^{m+n},\qquad (x^m)^n=x^{mn}.
\]
In additive notation (e.g.\ in $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},+)$ or $(\mathbb{Z},+)$) one writes $nx$ in place of $x^n$, so ``$x^n=1$'' reads ``$nx=0$''.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[When $x^k=1$]\label{p:orderdivides-mrg@c1}
Let $x\in G$ have finite order $n=\ord{x}$. For an integer $k$,
\[
x^k=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\mid k.
\]
Consequently $x^a=x^b$ iff $a\equiv b\pmod n$, and the distinct powers of $x$ are exactly $1,x,x^2,\dots,x^{n-1}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{wex}{Orders in $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{R}^{\times}$, and $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$}
Compute the order of each element in several of the book's standard groups, distinguishing finite from infinite order.
\wrec Apply Definition~\ref{d:order-mrg@c1} directly: hunt for the least $n$ with $x^n=1$ (additively $nx=0$). The trigger is ``order of an element''; in the infinite groups below ($\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{R}^{\times}$, $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$) most elements have infinite order, and finite order signals a root of unity or a torsion phenomenon.
\wsol
\emph{In $(\mathbb{Z},+)$.} Here $x^n$ means $nx$. For $x=0$, $\ord{0}=1$. For any $x\ne0$, $nx=0$ forces $n=0$, so no \emph{positive} $n$ works: $\ord{x}=\infty$. Every nonzero integer has infinite order.

\emph{In $(\mathbb{R}^{\times},\cdot)$.} $\ord{1}=1$ and $\ord{-1}=2$ (since $(-1)^2=1$ and $(-1)^1=-1\ne1$). Any other $x$ ($x\ne\pm1$) has $|x^n|=|x|^n\ne1$ unless $|x|=1$, so $x=\pm1$ are the only elements of finite order; all others have infinite order, e.g.\ $\ord{2}=\infty$.

\emph{In $(\mathbb{C}^{\times},\cdot)$.} The element $i$ has powers $i,i^2=-1,i^3=-i,i^4=1$, so $\ord{i}=4$. A primitive $n$th root of unity $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/n}$ has $\ord{\zeta}=n$ exactly (its powers $1,\zeta,\dots,\zeta^{n-1}$ are distinct). A complex number of modulus $\ne1$, or of modulus $1$ but with irrational angle divided by $2\pi$, has infinite order.

\textit{Check.} In $\mathbb{C}^{\times}$, $\ord{i}=4$ matches Proposition~\ref{p:orderdivides-mrg@c1}: $i^k=1\iff4\mid k$, and indeed $i^{8}=1$, $i^{6}=i^2=-1\ne1$. The four distinct powers are $1,i,-1,-i$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Orders in $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},+)$: the formula $\ord{\bar a}=n/\gcd(a,n)$}
In the additive group $\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$ find the order of $\bar a$ for several $a$, and state the general rule.
\wrec In $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},+)$ the relation $x^k=1$ is the additive $k\,\bar a=\bar 0$, i.e.\ $n\mid ka$; the least such $k>0$ is governed by $\gcd(a,n)$. Trigger: order of an element in a cyclic additive group -- reach for the gcd formula rather than listing multiples blindly.
\wsol
We seek the least $k\ge1$ with $k\,\bar a=\bar0$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$, i.e.\ $12\mid ka$.
\begin{itemize}
\item $\bar1$: least $k$ with $12\mid k$ is $k=12$, so $\ord{\bar1}=12$.
\item $\bar3$: $12\mid 3k\iff 4\mid k$, least is $k=4$, so $\ord{\bar3}=4$.
\item $\bar4$: $12\mid 4k\iff 3\mid k$, least is $k=3$, so $\ord{\bar4}=3$.
\item $\bar8$: $12\mid 8k\iff 3\mid 2k\iff 3\mid k$, least is $k=3$, so $\ord{\bar8}=3$.
\item $\bar0$: $\ord{\bar0}=1$.
\end{itemize}
In general $\ord{\bar a}=\dfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z},+)$: since $k\bar a=\bar0\iff n\mid ka\iff \dfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}\mid k$ (dividing $n\mid ka$ through by $\gcd(a,n)$ and using that $\tfrac{n}{\gcd(a,n)}$ and $\tfrac{a}{\gcd(a,n)}$ are coprime).
\textit{Check.} For $a=3,n=12$: $n/\gcd(a,n)=12/3=4$, matching $\ord{\bar3}=4$; and $4\bar3=\overline{12}=\bar0$ while $1\bar3,2\bar3,3\bar3=\bar3,\bar6,\bar9\ne\bar0$. The elements of order $12$ (the \emph{generators} of $\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$) are exactly the $\bar a$ with $\gcd(a,12)=1$, namely $\bar1,\bar5,\bar7,\overline{11}$.
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{List $(\mathbb{Z}/(15)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ and the order of each unit}
Write out $(\mathbb{Z}/(15)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ and compute $\ord{\bar a}$ (under multiplication) for every $\bar a$ in it.
\wrec ``List $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$'' triggers the gcd filter (keep $a$ with $\gcd(a,15)=1$); ``order of each'' triggers power-listing, restricted to divisors of $\varphi(15)$ by Lagrange.
\wsol $15=3\cdot5$, so $\varphi(15)=\varphi(3)\varphi(5)=2\cdot4=8$. Discard multiples of $3$ ($3,6,9,12$) and of $5$ ($5,10$). The survivors among $1,\dots,14$ are
\[
(\mathbb{Z}/(15)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar2,\bar4,\bar7,\bar8,\overline{11},\overline{13},\overline{14}\},\qquad \#=8=\varphi(15).\ \checkmark
\]
Possible orders divide $8$: i.e. $1,2,4,8$. Compute each (all mod $15$):
\[
\begin{array}{c|l|c}
\bar a & \text{powers until }\bar1 & \ord{\bar a}\\\hline
\bar1 & \bar1 & 1\\
\bar2 & \bar2,\ \bar4,\ \bar8,\ \overline{16}=\bar1 & 4\\
\bar4 & \bar4,\ \overline{16}=\bar1 & 2\\
\bar7 & \bar7,\ \overline{49}=\bar4,\ \overline{28}=\overline{13},\ \overline{91}=\bar1 & 4\\
\bar8 & \bar8,\ \overline{64}=\bar4,\ \overline{32}=\bar2,\ \overline{16}=\bar1 & 4\\
\overline{11} & \overline{11},\ \overline{121}=\bar1 & 2\\
\overline{13} & \overline{13},\ \overline{169}=\bar4,\ \overline{52}=\bar7,\ \overline{91}=\bar1 & 4\\
\overline{14} & \overline{14},\ \overline{196}=\bar1 & 2
\end{array}
\]
where e.g. $7^2=49=45+4\equiv\bar4$, $7^3=7\cdot4=28=15+13\equiv\overline{13}$, $7^4=7\cdot13=91=90+1\equiv\bar1$. Sanity check: every order is $1$, $2$, or $4$, each dividing $\varphi(15)=8$ (Lagrange).\ $\checkmark$ Note no element has order $8$, so $(\mathbb{Z}/(15)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is NOT cyclic; in fact it is $(\mathbb{Z}/(15)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\cong \mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{Order of $\bar2$ in three different unit groups}
Compute $\ord{\bar 2}$ in $(\mathbb{Z}/(7)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$, $(\mathbb{Z}/(9)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$, and $(\mathbb{Z}/(17)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$.
\wrec Each is a unit group; $\bar2$ is a unit iff $n$ is odd, which holds for $7,9,17$. Use Lagrange to limit candidate orders to divisors of $\varphi(n)$, then list powers of $2$.
\wsol \textbf{Mod $7$} ($\varphi(7)=6$, divisors $1,2,3,6$): $2,4,8\equiv1$. So $\ord{\bar2}=3\mid6$.\ $\checkmark$
\textbf{Mod $9$} ($\varphi(9)=6$): $2,4,8,16\equiv7,14\equiv5,10\equiv1$. Powers $2^1,\dots,2^6$ give $2,4,8,7,5,1$; first return at $6$, so $\ord{\bar 2}=6$ -- $\bar2$ is a generator, $(\mathbb{Z}/(9)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic.\ $\checkmark$
\textbf{Mod $17$} ($\varphi(17)=16$, divisors $1,2,4,8,16$): $2^2=4,\ 2^4=16\equiv\overline{-1},\ 2^8\equiv(-1)^2=1$. First return at $8$ (not at $4$, since $2^4\equiv16\ne1$), so $\ord{\bar 2}=8\mid16$.\ $\checkmark$ Sanity check: in each case the order divides $\varphi(n)$, as Lagrange demands.
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{Infinite order via a homomorphism to $\mathbb{Z}$}
In $(\mathbb{Q}^{\times},\cdot)$ show $\ord{3}=\infty$ by mapping to $(\mathbb{Z},+)$.
\wrec When direct power-listing is awkward, look for a homomorphism $\varphi$ into a torsion-free group: if $\varphi(x)$ has infinite order, so does $x$. The $3$-adic valuation $v_3$ is such a map.
\wsol Let $v_3:\mathbb{Q}^\times\to\mathbb{Z}$ send a rational to the exponent of $3$ in its prime factorization; it is a homomorphism: $v_3(xy)=v_3(x)+v_3(y)$. The square below commutes (top: multiply two rationals; map down by $v_3$; bottom: add the valuations):
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
  \mathbb{Q}^\times\times\mathbb{Q}^\times \arrow[r, "m"] \arrow[d, "v_3\times v_3"'] & \mathbb{Q}^\times \arrow[d, "v_3"] \\
  \mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z} \arrow[r, "+"'] & \mathbb{Z}
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four groups: $\mathbb{Q}^\times\times\mathbb{Q}^\times$ (the direct product of the multiplicative group of nonzero rationals with itself), $\mathbb{Q}^\times$ (nonzero rationals under multiplication), $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ (the direct product of the integers under addition), and $\mathbb{Z}$ (integers under addition). The top row lives in the multiplicative world; the bottom row in the additive world.
\dgi{Arrows:} $m:\mathbb{Q}^\times\times\mathbb{Q}^\times\to\mathbb{Q}^\times$ is the group multiplication $(x,y)\mapsto xy$. The left vertical $v_3\times v_3:(x,y)\mapsto(v_3(x),v_3(y))$ applies the $3$-adic valuation componentwise. The right vertical $v_3:\mathbb{Q}^\times\to\mathbb{Z}$ sends a nonzero rational to the exponent of $3$ in its prime factorization (negative for denominator factors). The bottom $+:\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ is ordinary integer addition $(a,b)\mapsto a+b$.
\dgi{What commutes:} Going right-then-down equals going down-then-right: $v_3(xy)=v_3(x)+v_3(y)$ for all $x,y\in\mathbb{Q}^\times$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} This is precisely the statement that $v_3$ is a group homomorphism from $(\mathbb{Q}^\times,\cdot)$ to $(\mathbb{Z},+)$. For any nonzero rationals $x=3^a\frac{p}{q}$ and $y=3^b\frac{r}{s}$ (with $3\nmid p,q,r,s$), the product $xy=3^{a+b}\frac{pr}{qs}$ has $v_3(xy)=a+b=v_3(x)+v_3(y)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram is used to prove $\ord{3}=\infty$ in $(\mathbb{Q}^\times,\cdot)$ without listing powers. Since $v_3$ is a homomorphism into the torsion-free group $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ and $v_3(3)=1$ has infinite additive order, $3$ itself must have infinite multiplicative order. The commutativity square makes the homomorphism property precise and visible.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $x=6=2\cdot3$ and $y=\frac{3}{5}$. Then $v_3(x)=1$, $v_3(y)=1$, and $xy=\frac{18}{5}=2\cdot3^2\cdot5^{-1}$, so $v_3(xy)=2=1+1$. The square commutes for this pair.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think $v_3$ lands in $\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$; in fact $v_3(\frac{1}{3})=-1\in\mathbb{Z}$, so the codomain must be all of $\mathbb{Z}$, not just the nonneg integers.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that a homomorphism into a torsion-free group transfers the problem of infinite order from $\mathbb{Q}^\times$ to $\mathbb{Z}$, where it is obvious.
\end{dgx}
Now $v_3(3^k)=k$. If $3^k=1$ for some $k>0$ then $k=v_3(3^k)=v_3(1)=0$, contradicting $k>0$. Hence $\ord{3}=\infty$. Sanity check: directly, $3^k\ge3>1$ for $k>0$, confirming no positive power is $1$.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

title: Infinite order via a homomorphism to $\mathbb{Z}$

latex:
For a cyclic group the assignment $k\mapsto x^k$ is the universal way orders appear. If $\ord{x}=n<\infty$, the homomorphism $\mathbb{Z}\to G$, $k\mapsto x^k$, has kernel exactly $n\mathbb{Z}$ and factors uniquely through $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$; if $\ord{x}=\infty$, the map is injective (kernel $\{0\}$), so $\langle x\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
  1 \arrow[r] & n\mathbb{Z} \arrow[r, hook] & \mathbb{Z} \arrow[r, two heads, "k\,\mapsto\,x^k"] & \langle x\rangle \arrow[r] & 1
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Five terms: the trivial group $1$, the subgroup $n\mathbb{Z}\le\mathbb{Z}$ of multiples of $n$ (a normal subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}$), the group $\mathbb{Z}$ of integers, the cyclic subgroup $\langle x\rangle\le G$ (a group generated by a single element $x$ of order $n$), and the trivial group $1$ again. This is a short exact sequence of groups.
\dgi{Arrows:} The leftmost $1\to n\mathbb{Z}$ is the unique map from the trivial group. The map $n\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}$ is the inclusion (injective), indicated by the hook arrow. The map $\mathbb{Z}\to\langle x\rangle$, $k\mapsto x^k$, is the evaluation homomorphism (surjective onto $\langle x\rangle$, indicated by the double-head). The rightmost $\langle x\rangle\to 1$ is the unique map to the trivial group.
\dgi{What commutes:} Exactness at $n\mathbb{Z}$: $\operatorname{im}(1\to n\mathbb{Z})=\{0\}=\operatorname{ker}(n\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z})$ since the inclusion is injective. Exactness at $\mathbb{Z}$: $\operatorname{im}(n\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z})=n\mathbb{Z}=\operatorname{ker}(k\mapsto x^k)$ because $x^k=1$ iff $n\mid k$. Exactness at $\langle x\rangle$: $\operatorname{im}(k\mapsto x^k)=\langle x\rangle=\operatorname{ker}(\langle x\rangle\to 1)$ since the map to the trivial group has full kernel.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The key exactness condition is at $\mathbb{Z}$: the kernel of $k\mapsto x^k$ is $\{k\in\mathbb{Z} : x^k=1\}$. Since $\ord{x}=n$, an integer $k$ satisfies $x^k=1$ if and only if $n\mid k$, i.e. $k\in n\mathbb{Z}$. This is exactly the image of the inclusion, establishing exactness.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This exact sequence packages the fundamental relationship between $\ord{x}$ and the structure of $\langle x\rangle$: it says $\langle x\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ (by the first isomorphism theorem) and makes the kernel $n\mathbb{Z}$ explicit. The diagram appears here to set up the factoring triangle below.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=\mathbb{Z}/(12)\mathbb{Z}$, $x=\bar 4$. Then $\ord{\bar 4}=3$ and $\langle\bar4\rangle=\{\bar0,\bar4,\bar8\}$. The sequence is $1\to3\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{k\mapsto k\bar4}\{\bar0,\bar4,\bar8\}\to1$; check $k\bar4=\bar0$ iff $12\mid4k$ iff $3\mid k$, so $\ker=3\mathbb{Z}$. $\checkmark$
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes confuse the subgroup $n\mathbb{Z}\le\mathbb{Z}$ with the quotient group $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$; these are different objects. The sequence records the kernel of the evaluation map as the \emph{subgroup} $n\mathbb{Z}$, not as a quotient.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the order of $x$ is the unique positive integer $n$ for which the kernel of the evaluation map $\mathbb{Z}\to\langle x\rangle$ is exactly $n\mathbb{Z}$, encoding $\langle x\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{dgx}
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
  \mathbb{Z} \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] \arrow[dr, two heads, "k\,\mapsto\,x^k"'] & \mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z} \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\varphi"] \\ & \langle x\rangle
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three groups: $\mathbb{Z}$ (integers under addition), $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}=\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ (the quotient group of residue classes mod $n$, order $n$), and $\langle x\rangle$ (the cyclic subgroup of $G$ generated by $x$, where $\ord{x}=n<\infty$).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\pi:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$, $k\mapsto\bar k$, is the canonical surjection (the quotient map killing $n\mathbb{Z}$), shown with a double-head. The diagonal $k\mapsto x^k$ is the evaluation homomorphism, a surjection onto $\langle x\rangle$ with kernel $n\mathbb{Z}$. The dashed vertical $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}\to\langle x\rangle$ is the unique induced isomorphism given by the universal property of the quotient; it sends $\bar k\mapsto x^k$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\varphi\circ\pi = (k\mapsto x^k)$, i.e., $\varphi(\bar k)=x^k$ for all $k\in\mathbb{Z}$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $\varphi$: if $\bar k=\bar k'$ then $k\equiv k'\pmod n$, so $n\mid(k-k')$, so $x^{k-k'}=1$ (since $\ord{x}=n$), giving $x^k=x^{k'}$. Hence $\varphi(\bar k):=x^k$ does not depend on the coset representative, and the universal property of $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ produces a unique such $\varphi$ making the triangle commute. Injectivity: $\varphi(\bar k)=1$ means $x^k=1$ means $n\mid k$ means $\bar k=\bar 0$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the universal-property factoring that characterizes all finite cyclic groups: any surjection $\mathbb{Z}\to\langle x\rangle$ with kernel $n\mathbb{Z}$ factors uniquely through $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$, giving an isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}\cong\langle x\rangle$. The diagram unifies the earlier short exact sequence with the explicit structure of $\langle x\rangle$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G=S_3$ and $x=(1\,2\,3)$. Then $\ord{x}=3$, $\langle x\rangle=\{e,(1\,2\,3),(1\,3\,2)\}$, and $n=3$. The induced $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}\to\langle x\rangle$ sends $\bar0\mapsto e$, $\bar1\mapsto(1\,2\,3)$, $\bar2\mapsto(1\,3\,2)$, an isomorphism.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The dashed arrow exists and is unique ONLY because $\ker(k\mapsto x^k)=n\mathbb{Z}=\ker\pi$. If $\ord{x}$ were infinite (kernel $\{0\}$), or a different finite value, the dashed arrow to $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ would not be an isomorphism (or might not exist as drawn).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that every cyclic group of finite order $n$ is canonically isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$, with the isomorphism uniquely determined by where a generator $x$ maps under the universal quotient.
\end{dgx}
Thus $\ord{x}$ is precisely the unique $n$ with $\ker(k\mapsto x^k)=n\mathbb{Z}$ (and $\ord{x}=\infty$ exactly when that kernel is $\{0\}$).

\begin{wex}{The complete addition table of $(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z},+)$}
Write out the Cayley table for $(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z},+)$ and read off the inverse of each element.
\wrec This is the defining operation $\bar a+\bar b=\overline{a+b}$ of Definition~\ref{d:zn@c1} applied to every pair; the table makes the group axioms (closure, identity row/column, a unique $\bar 0$ in each row giving inverses) visible at a glance.
\wsol Entries are $\overline{a+b}\bmod 6$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
+ & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5\\\hline
\bar0 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5\\
\bar1 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0\\
\bar2 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1\\
\bar3 & \bar3 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2\\
\bar4 & \bar4 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3\\
\bar5 & \bar5 & \bar0 & \bar1 & \bar2 & \bar3 & \bar4
\end{array}
\]
The $\bar0$ entries locate inverses: $-\bar0=\bar0$, $-\bar1=\bar5$, $-\bar2=\bar4$, $-\bar3=\bar3$, $-\bar4=\bar2$, $-\bar5=\bar1$, matching $-\bar a=\overline{6-a}$. The table is symmetric across the main diagonal, recording that $(\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z},+)$ is abelian. Sanity check: each row is a permutation of the six classes (the Latin-square property every group table has).\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{The complete multiplication table of $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$}
List $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$, write out its multiplication table, and find the order of each element.
\wrec ``List $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$'' invokes the gcd filter (Prop.~\ref{p:unit-iff-coprime@c1}); the table then exhibits the multiplicative group structure, and orders are read directly from the diagonal of squares.
\wsol $\gcd(a,8)=1$ for $a\in\{1,3,5,7\}$, so $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar3,\bar5,\bar7\}$ and $\varphi(8)=4$. Entries $\overline{ab}\bmod 8$:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
\times & \bar1 & \bar3 & \bar5 & \bar7\\\hline
\bar1 & \bar1 & \bar3 & \bar5 & \bar7\\
\bar3 & \bar3 & \bar1 & \bar7 & \bar5\\
\bar5 & \bar5 & \bar7 & \bar1 & \bar3\\
\bar7 & \bar7 & \bar5 & \bar3 & \bar1
\end{array}
\]
Every diagonal square is $\bar1$: $3^2=9\equiv\bar1$, $5^2=25\equiv\bar1$, $7^2=49\equiv\bar1$. Hence $\ord{\bar3}=\ord{\bar5}=\ord{\bar7}=2$ and $\ord{\bar1}=1$. So $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ has no element of order $4=\varphi(8)$; it is the Klein four-group, $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$, NOT cyclic. Sanity check: each element is its own inverse, consistent with $x^2=\bar1$ throughout; every order divides $\varphi(8)=4$.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ for $n=5,7,9,10$: which are cyclic}
Determine $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ and the order of a small candidate generator for $n=5,7,9,10$, and state which of these unit groups is cyclic.
\wrec D\&F use small moduli to illustrate that some $(\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ have a generator (a single power runs through all units) and some do not. Lagrange limits the orders to divisors of $\varphi(n)$.
\wsol
\textbf{$n=5$}: $(\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar2,\bar3,\bar4\}$, $\varphi(5)=4$. Powers of $\bar2$: $2,4,3,1$, so $\ord{\bar2}=4$ and $\bar2$ is a generator; $(\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic.
\textbf{$n=7$}: $(\mathbb{Z}/(7)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\dots,\bar6\}$, $\varphi(7)=6$. Powers of $\bar3$: $3,2,6,4,5,1$, so $\ord{\bar3}=6$; $(\mathbb{Z}/(7)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic.
\textbf{$n=9$}: $(\mathbb{Z}/(9)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar2,\bar4,\bar5,\bar7,\bar8\}$, $\varphi(9)=6$. Powers of $\bar2$: $2,4,8,7,5,1$, so $\ord{\bar2}=6$; $(\mathbb{Z}/(9)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic.
\textbf{$n=10$}: $(\mathbb{Z}/(10)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}=\{\bar1,\bar3,\bar7,\bar9\}$, $\varphi(10)=4$. Powers of $\bar3$: $3,9,7,1$, so $\ord{\bar3}=4$; $(\mathbb{Z}/(10)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ is cyclic.
Sanity check: in each case the listed generator's powers reproduce exactly the $\varphi(n)$ units, and every order divides $\varphi(n)$. (Contrast $(\mathbb{Z}/(8)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ above and $(\mathbb{Z}/(15)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$ earlier, which are not cyclic.)\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Orders in $S_3$}
In the symmetric group $S_3$ (permutations of $\{1,2,3\}$, composed right-to-left), compute the order of each element.
\wrec D\&F compute orders in $S_3$ soon after defining order, to show finite groups can have several different orders. Disjoint-cycle structure determines order: a single $k$-cycle has order $k$.
\wsol The six elements are the identity, three transpositions, and two $3$-cycles. As cycles:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\sigma & \text{type} & \ord{\sigma}\\\hline
\id & \text{identity} & 1\\
(1\,2),\ (1\,3),\ (2\,3) & \text{transposition} & 2\\
(1\,2\,3),\ (1\,3\,2) & 3\text{-cycle} & 3
\end{array}
\]
Check a transposition: $(1\,2)^2=\id$, and $(1\,2)\ne\id$, so order $2$. Check a $3$-cycle: $(1\,2\,3)^2=(1\,3\,2)\ne\id$, $(1\,2\,3)^3=\id$, so order $3$. Sanity check: $|S_3|=6$ and the orders $1,2,3$ all divide $6$; no element has order $6$, so $S_3$ is not cyclic.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Orders in the quaternion group $Q_8$}
In $Q_8=\{\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\}$ with $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$ and $ij=k$, find the order of every element.
\wrec D\&F present $Q_8$ as a group where, unlike $D_8$, there is a \emph{unique} element of order $2$ and every non-identity element except $-1$ has order $4$. Use $i^2=j^2=k^2=-1$ and $(-1)^2=1$.
\wsol $\ord{1}=1$. Since $(-1)^2=1$ and $-1\ne1$, $\ord{-1}=2$. For $i$: $i^2=-1$, $i^3=-i$, $i^4=(-1)^2=1$, so $\ord{i}=4$; the same computation gives $\ord{-i}=\ord{j}=\ord{-j}=\ord{k}=\ord{-k}=4$.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
g & \text{value} & \ord{g}\\\hline
1 & 1 & 1\\
-1 & -1 & 2\\
\pm i,\ \pm j,\ \pm k & \text{square to } -1 & 4
\end{array}
\]
Sanity check: all orders divide $|Q_8|=8$; there is exactly one element of order $2$ (namely $-1$), in contrast with $D_8$, which has five (the half-turn $r^2$ and the four reflections). So $D_8$ and $Q_8$ are non-isomorphic groups of the same order.\ $\checkmark$
\end{wex}

\begin{definition}[Dihedral group]\label{d:dihedral@c1}
Fix $n\ge 3$. Label the vertices of a regular $n$-gon $0,1,\dots,n-1$ counterclockwise. The \emph{dihedral group} $D_{2n}$ is the group of all rigid symmetries (rotations and reflections) of this polygon under composition. It is generated by
\[
r=\text{rotation counterclockwise by }2\pi/n,\qquad
s=\text{reflection across the axis through vertex }0,
\]
subject to the relations
\[
r^n=1,\qquad s^2=1,\qquad srs=r^{-1}\quad(\text{equivalently }sr=r^{-1} s,\ \ r^k s=s r^{-k}).
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Order and normal form]\label{p:normalform@c1}
$|D_{2n}|=2n$, and every element of $D_{2n}$ can be written \emph{uniquely} in one of the two normal forms
\[
r^i\quad(\text{a rotation}),\qquad sr^i\quad(\text{a reflection}),\qquad 0\le i<n.
\]
Thus $D_{2n}=\{1,r,\dots,r^{n-1},\,s,sr,\dots,sr^{n-1}\}$, a disjoint union of $n$ rotations and $n$ reflections.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proposition}[Orders of elements]\label{p:orders@c1}
In $D_{2n}$:
\[
\ord{r^k}=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)},\qquad \ord{sr^i}=2\ \text{ for every }i.
\]
In particular $r$ has order $n$, and all $n$ reflections are involutions.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Inside the cyclic subgroup $\langle r\rangle\cong\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ the order of $r^k$ is $n/\gcd(n,k)$ (standard cyclic-group fact). For a reflection,

(sr^i)^2=sr^i\,sr^i=s(r^i s)r^i=s(sr^{-i})r^i=s^2 r^{-i+i}=1,
\]
using $r^i s=sr^{-i}$. Since $sr^i\ne1$ (it is a reflection, not the identity), $\ord{sr^i}=2$.

\begin{wex}{Multiply two reflections: $(sr^3)(sr^5)$ in $D_{12}$}
In $D_{12}$ (so $n=6$), compute $(sr^3)(sr^5)$ and put it in normal form. Is the result a rotation or a reflection?
\wrec This is a product of two reflections (two factors each containing one $s$): an \emph{even} number of $s$'s, so the answer must be a rotation $r^m$. Use the method: push the inner $s$ left past $r^3$.
\wsol
\[
(sr^3)(sr^5)=s\,(r^3 s)\,r^5
= s\,(s r^{-3})\,r^5
= s^2 r^{-3} r^5
= r^{2}.
\]
Here $r^3 s = s r^{-3}$ (sign flip), then $s^2=1$, then add exponents $-3+5=2$. Reduce mod $n=6$: $2$ is already in $\{0,\dots,5\}$, so the normal form is $\boxed{r^2}$, a rotation.
\textit{Check.} $\ord{r^2}=6/\gcd(6,2)=3$. Two reflections compose to a rotation (orientation-reversing twice $=$ orientation-preserving), consistent with getting $r^2$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{The conjugate $r^k s r^{-k}$}
In $D_{2n}$, simplify $r^k s r^{-k}$ to normal form. Interpret the result.
\wrec One $s$ in the middle: odd number of $s$'s, so expect a reflection $sr^m$. Slide the $s$ to the far left by pushing it past $r^k$ on its left (or equivalently push $r^k$ to the right of $s$).
\wsol
Use $r^k s = s r^{-k}$ on the leftmost pair:
\[
r^k s r^{-k}=(r^k s)r^{-k}=(s r^{-k})r^{-k}=s r^{-k-k}=s r^{-2k}.
\]
Reduce the exponent mod $n$: $sr^{-2k}=s r^{\,n-2k\bmod n}$. Normal form $\boxed{sr^{-2k}}$ (a reflection).
\textit{Check.} As a reflection it should square to $1$: $(sr^{-2k})^2=1$ by Proposition~\ref{p:orders@c1}. Geometrically, conjugating the axis of $s$ by the rotation $r^k$ rotates that axis through the angle $2\pi k/n$ (onto the axis through vertex $k$), i.e.\ by $2k$ steps of $\pi/n$ (the angle between neighboring reflection axes), matching the index $-2k$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{All elements of order $2$ in $D_8$}
List every element of $D_8$ ($n=4$) of order exactly $2$.
\wrec Order-2 elements are the self-inverse non-identity elements. Split into rotations $r^k$ (use $\ord{r^k}=4/\gcd(4,k)$) and reflections $sr^i$ (all have order $2$).
\wsol
\emph{Rotations.} $\ord{r^0}=1$; $\ord{r}=4/\gcd(4,1)=4$; $\ord{r^2}=4/\gcd(4,2)=2$; $\ord{r^3}=4/\gcd(4,3)=4$. So the only rotation of order $2$ is $r^2$.
\emph{Reflections.} By Proposition~\ref{p:orders@c1}, $s, sr, sr^2, sr^3$ each have order $2$.
Thus the order-$2$ elements are
\[
\boxed{\,r^2,\ s,\ sr,\ sr^2,\ sr^3\,}\qquad(5\text{ elements}).
\]
\textit{Check.} $|D_8|=8$; removing $1$ (order $1$) and $r,r^3$ (order $4$) leaves exactly these $5$, all of order $2$. $(r^2)^2=r^4=1$ confirms $r^2$; e.g.\ $(sr)^2=sr\,sr=s(rs)r=s(sr^{-1})r=s^2r^0=1$.

\begin{wex}{A longer word: $r^2 s r^3 s r$ in $D_{14}$}
Simplify $r^2 s r^3 s r$ in $D_{14}$ ($n=7$) to normal form and give its order.
\wrec Two $s$'s (even) $\Rightarrow$ rotation. Push each $s$ leftward; each jump over a power of $r$ flips that power's sign.
\wsol
Start by sliding the left $s$ past $r^3$, then the resulting $s$'s cancel:
\[
r^2 s r^3 s r
= r^2 (s r^3) s r
= r^2 (r^{-3} s) s r
= r^{2-3} s^2 r
= r^{-1} r
= r^{0}=1.
\]
(I used $s r^3=r^{-3}s$, i.e.\ $sr^k=r^{-k}s$ for all $k$.) Normal form: $\boxed{1}$.
\textit{Check (push both $s$'s the other way).} $r^2 s r^3 s r$; pair the inner block $sr^3 s=(sr^3)s=(r^{-3}s)s=r^{-3}$, so the word is $r^2\cdot r^{-3}\cdot r=r^{2-3+1}=r^0=1$. Same answer, $\ord{1}=1$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Solve for $x$: $r^3 x = sr$ in $D_8$}
In $D_8$ ($n=4$) find the unique $x$ with $r^3 x=sr$, in normal form.
\wrec Left-multiply by $(r^3)^{-1}=r^{-3}=r^{1}$ (since $r^4=1$). The right side is a reflection, so $x$ will be a reflection.
\wsol
\[
x=r^{-3}(sr)=r^{1}(sr)=(r s)r=(s r^{-1})r=s r^{0}=s.
\]
Here $rs=sr^{-1}$ (one sign flip). So $\boxed{x=s}$.
\textit{Check.} $r^3 x=r^3 s$. And $r^3 s=s r^{-3}=s r^{1}=sr$ (since $-3\equiv1\bmod4$). Indeed $r^3 s=sr$, matching the right-hand side.
\end{wex}

latex:
The relation $srs=r^{-1}$ says exactly that conjugation by $s$ inverts $r$; equivalently the map $r\mapsto r^{-1}$, $s\mapsto s$ extends to an automorphism. This is encoded by the commuting square (left) and the fact that $s$ conjugates $\langle r\rangle$ by inversion (right):
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
\langle r\rangle \arrow[r, "x\,\mapsto\,sxs"] \arrow[d, hook, "\iota"'] & \langle r\rangle \arrow[d, hook, "\iota"] \\
D_{2n} \arrow[r, "x\,\mapsto\,sxs"'] & D_{2n}
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad\qquad
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=huge]
r \arrow[r, mapsto, "\text{conj.\ by }s"] & r^{-1}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The square uses two copies each of two groups: the cyclic rotation subgroup $\langle r\rangle \cong \mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ (upper row) and the full dihedral group $D_{2n}$ (lower row), each appearing twice (once as domain, once as codomain). The right diagram has a single element-level arrow tracking what conjugation does to the generator $r$.

\dgi{Arrows:} The top horizontal arrow is the map $\langle r\rangle \to \langle r\rangle$, $x \mapsto sxs$ (conjugation by $s$, restricted to $\langle r\rangle$). The bottom horizontal arrow is the same conjugation formula on all of $D_{2n}$. The two vertical arrows are the inclusion $\iota\colon\langle r\rangle \hookrightarrow D_{2n}$ (the canonical inclusion homomorphism). The right mini-diagram records the single value $r \mapsto r^{-1}$, confirming that conjugation by $s$ inverts the generator.

\dgi{What commutes:} The square says that inclusion then conjugation equals conjugation then inclusion: for every $x \in \langle r\rangle$, applying the top map and then the right inclusion gives $sxs \in D_{2n}$; applying the left inclusion first and then the bottom map also gives $sxs \in D_{2n}$. These are the same element, so the square commutes: $\iota \circ (x \mapsto sxs) = (x \mapsto sxs) \circ \iota$, where $\iota: \langle r\rangle \hookrightarrow D_{2n}$.

\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase $x \in \langle r\rangle$, say $x = r^k$. Top then right: $r^k \mapsto sr^k s \mapsto sr^k s \in D_{2n}$. Left then bottom: $r^k \mapsto r^k \in D_{2n} \mapsto sr^k s$. Both give $sr^k s$. The two paths agree because both just compute $sxs$ and include the result; the square is recording compatibility of a formula with an inclusion, not a non-trivial constraint.

\dgi{Why this matters here:} The prose just established $srs = r^{-1}$, which says conjugation by $s$ is not merely a set-map but an automorphism of $\langle r\rangle$ that happens to extend to all of $D_{2n}$. The square makes that extension visible: the automorphism of $\langle r\rangle$ is the restriction of the conjugation automorphism of $D_{2n}$. This is the structural content behind the relation $srs = r^{-1}$ and it will recur when proving $\langle r\rangle \nor D_{2n}$.

\dgi{Concrete example:} In $D_8$ ($n=4$), take $x = r^2 \in \langle r\rangle$. Top path: $r^2 \mapsto sr^2 s = r^{-2} = r^2$. Bottom path: include $r^2 \in D_8$, then $r^2 \mapsto sr^2 s = r^2$. The element-level diagram gives $r \mapsto r^{-1} = r^3$, so conjugation inverts: $sr^2 s = (r^{-1})^2 = r^2$ (consistent since $r^2 = r^{-2}$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$).

\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the commuting square as saying the two horizontal maps are the \emph{same} arrow or that the inclusions are isomorphisms. They are not: the inclusions are proper embeddings ($\langle r\rangle \subsetneq D_{2n}$ for $n \ge 3$), and the commutativity just records that the conjugation formula $x \mapsto sxs$ is consistent across the two group levels.

\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the relation $srs = r^{-1}$ is not merely an algebraic identity but says that conjugation by $s$ is an automorphism of $\langle r\rangle$ that extends compatibly to all of $D_{2n}$, making $\langle r\rangle$ a normal subgroup.
\end{dgx}

The universal property of $D_{2n}$ (it is the largest group on generators $a,b$ with $a^n=b^2=1$, $bab=a^{-1}$) gives, for any group $G$ containing elements $\rho,\sigma$ with $\rho^n=\sigma^2=1$ and $\sigma\rho\sigma=\rho^{-1}$, a unique homomorphism filling the dashed arrow:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large,column sep=large]
\{a,b\} \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[dr, "{a\mapsto\rho,\ b\mapsto\sigma}"'] & D_{2n} \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\varphi"] \\
& G
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three objects appear. The generating set $\{a,b\}$ is not a group but the source data: two abstract symbols satisfying $a^n = b^2 = 1$ and $bab = a^{-1}$. The group $D_{2n}$ is the dihedral group presented by those generators and relations. The group $G$ is any group containing elements $\rho, \sigma$ with $\rho^n = \sigma^2 = 1$ and $\sigma\rho\sigma = \rho^{-1}$.

\dgi{Arrows:} The top horizontal arrow $\{a,b\} \hookrightarrow D_{2n}$ is the inclusion of the generators into $D_{2n}$ (the canonical embedding sending $a \mapsto r$, $b \mapsto s$). The diagonal arrow $\{a,b\} \to G$ is the assignment $a \mapsto \rho$, $b \mapsto \sigma$, recording the hypothesized relations in $G$. The dashed vertical arrow $\varphi: D_{2n} \to G$ is the unique group homomorphism extending the diagonal assignment; it is dashed because its existence and uniqueness are what the diagram asserts.

\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: the composition $\{a,b\} \hookrightarrow D_{2n} \xrightarrow{\varphi} G$ equals the direct assignment $a \mapsto \rho$, $b \mapsto \sigma$. Concretely: $\varphi(r) = \rho$ and $\varphi(s) = \sigma$, and for every word $r^i$ or $sr^i$ in $D_{2n}$, $\varphi(r^i) = \rho^i$ and $\varphi(sr^i) = \sigma\rho^i$.

\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness is the key point. Every element of $D_{2n}$ has a unique normal form $r^i$ or $sr^i$, so defining $\varphi(r^i) = \rho^i$ and $\varphi(sr^i) = \sigma\rho^i$ is unambiguous. The relations $\rho^n = 1$, $\sigma^2 = 1$, $\sigma\rho\sigma = \rho^{-1}$ in $G$ guarantee that $\varphi$ respects the group operation: e.g.\ $\varphi(sr \cdot r^{i}) = \sigma\rho^{i+1} = \varphi(sr)\varphi(r^i)$. The assignment on $\{a,b\}$ forced $\varphi$ uniquely because $a,b$ generate $D_{2n}$.

\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the universal property of $D_{2n}$ as a group presented by generators and relations. It converts the geometric fact ``$D_{2n}$ is the symmetry group'' into the algebraic fact ``any group satisfying those relations receives a homomorphism from $D_{2n}$.'' Every time one constructs a homomorphism out of $D_{2n}$ in the chapter, this triangle is the silent justification: just verify $\rho^n = \sigma^2 = 1$ and $\sigma\rho\sigma = \rho^{-1}$ in the target.

\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $G = \mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ (written additively, so $\rho^n$ means $n\rho$), $\rho = \overline{0}$, $\sigma = \overline{1}$. Then $\rho^n = \overline{0}$, $\sigma^2 = \overline{1}+\overline{1} = \overline{0}$, and $\sigma\rho\sigma = \overline{1}+\overline{0}+\overline{1} = \overline{0} = -\rho = \rho^{-1}$, so $\varphi$ exists: it sends every rotation $r^i$ to $\overline{0}$ and every reflection $sr^i$ to $\overline{1}$. (By contrast, $G = \mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ with $\rho = \overline{1}$, $\sigma = \overline{0}$ does not work for $n\ge 3$: there $\sigma\rho\sigma = \overline{1} \ne \overline{n-1} = \rho^{-1}$.) Another example: $G = D_{2n}$ itself, $\rho = r$, $\sigma = s$; then $\varphi = \id_{D_{2n}}$ fills the dashed arrow, confirming that $D_{2n}$ maps to itself via the identity.

\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think the dashed arrow exists for any $\rho, \sigma \in G$. It does not: the three relations $\rho^n = 1$, $\sigma^2 = 1$, $\sigma\rho\sigma = \rho^{-1}$ must hold in $G$ first. Without them, there is no well-defined $\varphi$: for instance $srs$ and $r^{-1}$ are the same element of $D_{2n}$, so $\varphi$ would have to send it both to $\sigma\rho\sigma$ and to $\rho^{-1}$, which is impossible if $\sigma\rho\sigma \ne \rho^{-1}$. The relations are the kernel condition that makes the induced map well-defined.

\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that $D_{2n}$ is the universal group on two generators satisfying the dihedral relations, meaning any concrete realization of those relations in a group $G$ yields a unique homomorphism $D_{2n} \to G$ extending the generator assignment.
\end{dgx}

\begin{remark}[How D\&F fixes notation]\label{r:dnf-notation-mrg@c1}
Once the count is known, D\&F names two specific symmetries and uses them as a working alphabet. Let $r$ be the rotation through $2\pi/n$ (one vertex step, in the direction of increasing labels) and let $s$ be the reflection fixing vertex $1$. The text then verifies, directly from the geometry, that
\[
1,r,r^2,\dots,r^{n-1}\ \text{are distinct with }r^n=1;\qquad s^2=1;\qquad s\ne r^i\ \text{for any }i,
\]
and the single mixing relation, obtained by tracking what each side does to the vertices,
\[
rs=sr^{-1}\qquad(\text{equivalently } srs^{-1}=r^{-1},\ \ s^{-1} rs=r^{-1}).
\]
Every element is then named in the form $r^i$ or $sr^i$ with $0\le i<n$; this naming, not an abstract presentation, is what the book computes with.
\end{remark}
title: How D\&F fixes notation

\begin{wex}{The smallest case: $D_6$, symmetries of the triangle}
Take the equilateral triangle with vertices $1,2,3$. List all $6=2\cdot 3$ symmetries of $D_6$ both as words in $r,s$ and as permutations of $\{1,2,3\}$, where $r$ rotates $1\to2\to3\to1$ and $s$ fixes vertex $1$.
\wrec Proposition~\ref{p:count-2n-mrg@c1} guarantees exactly $2n=6$ symmetries. List the three rotations $1,r,r^2$ and the three reflections $s,sr,sr^2$, then read off each one's action on the vertices to confirm they are distinct.
\wsol
The rotation $r$ sends $1\mapsto2,\ 2\mapsto3,\ 3\mapsto1$, i.e.\ the $3$-cycle $(1\,2\,3)$; the reflection $s$ fixes vertex $1$ and swaps the other two, i.e.\ $(2\,3)$. Compute the rest (permutations compose right-to-left):
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
1\ &=\ \text{identity} & \text{fixes }1,2,3,\\
r\ &=\ (1\,2\,3) & 1\mapsto2\mapsto3\mapsto1,\\
r^2\ &=\ (1\,3\,2) & 1\mapsto3\mapsto2\mapsto1,\\
s\ &=\ (2\,3) & \text{fixes }1,\\
sr\ &=\ (2\,3)(1\,2\,3)=(1\,3) & \text{fixes }2,\\
sr^2\ &=\ (2\,3)(1\,3\,2)=(1\,2) & \text{fixes }3.
\end{array}
\]
So $D_6=\{1,r,r^2,s,sr,sr^2\}$, and as permutations these are exactly the six elements of $\operatorname{Sym}\{1,2,3\}$.
\textit{Check.} The three reflections $s=(2\,3)$, $sr=(1\,3)$, $sr^2=(1\,2)$ are the three transpositions, each fixing one vertex; the three rotations are the identity and the two $3$-cycles. All six permutations are distinct, confirming $|D_6|=6$. Here $D_6\cong\operatorname{Sym}\{1,2,3\}$ because both have order $6$ and every permutation of the three vertices is a symmetry of the triangle.
\end{wex}
title: The smallest case: $D_6$, symmetries of the triangle

\begin{wex}{$D_8$ as permutations of the square's vertices}
For the square with vertices $1,2,3,4$ in cyclic order, write each of the $8$ elements of $D_8$ as a permutation of $\{1,2,3,4\}$, with $r=(1\,2\,3\,4)$ and $s$ the reflection fixing vertices $1$ and $3$ (the diagonal axis).
\wrec There are $2n=8$ symmetries by Proposition~\ref{p:count-2n-mrg@c1}. The four rotations are powers of $r=(1\,2\,3\,4)$; the four reflections are $s,sr,sr^2,sr^3$. Multiply out each reflection as a permutation, composing right-to-left.
\wsol
The reflection across the diagonal through vertices $1$ and $3$ fixes those and swaps $2,4$, so $s=(2\,4)$. Composing right-to-left ($sr$ means ``apply $r$, then $s$''):
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
1=\text{id}, & s=(2\,4),\\
r=(1\,2\,3\,4), & sr=(2\,4)(1\,2\,3\,4)=(1\,4)(2\,3),\\
r^2=(1\,3)(2\,4), & sr^2=(2\,4)(1\,3)(2\,4)=(1\,3),\\
r^3=(1\,4\,3\,2), & sr^3=(2\,4)(1\,4\,3\,2)=(1\,2)(3\,4).
\end{array}
\]
\textit{Check.} The reflections split into the two diagonal flips $s=(2\,4)$, $sr^2=(1\,3)$ (each fixing two opposite vertices) and the two edge-midpoint flips $sr=(1\,4)(2\,3)$, $sr^3=(1\,2)(3\,4)$ (fixing no vertex), as expected for even $n$. Each squares to the identity, e.g.\ $(1\,4)(2\,3)$ has order $2$, matching $\ord{sr^i}=2$. The eight permutations are distinct, so $|D_8|=8$, and $D_8$ sits as a subgroup of $\operatorname{Sym}\{1,2,3,4\}$ of index $3$ (since $|\operatorname{Sym}\{1,2,3,4\}|=24$).
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Verifying the relation $rs=sr^{-1}$ on vertices}
Confirm D\&F's mixing relation $rs=sr^{-1}$ directly on the square ($n=4$) by evaluating both sides on every vertex, using $r=(1\,2\,3\,4)$ and $s=(2\,4)$.
\wrec The relation $rs=sr^{-1}$ is the one non-obvious defining fact; D\&F establishes it geometrically. To verify it concretely, compute the permutation on each side and compare images vertex by vertex (right-to-left composition).
\wsol
Left side $rs$: apply $s=(2\,4)$ first, then $r=(1\,2\,3\,4)$.
\[
1\xrightarrow{s}1\xrightarrow{r}2,\quad
2\xrightarrow{s}4\xrightarrow{r}1,\quad
3\xrightarrow{s}3\xrightarrow{r}4,\quad
4\xrightarrow{s}2\xrightarrow{r}3,
\]
so $rs=(1\,2)(3\,4)$.
Right side $sr^{-1}$ with $r^{-1}=r^3=(1\,4\,3\,2)$: apply $r^{-1}$ first, then $s$.
\[
1\xrightarrow{r^{-1}}4\xrightarrow{s}2,\quad
2\xrightarrow{r^{-1}}1\xrightarrow{s}1,\quad
3\xrightarrow{r^{-1}}2\xrightarrow{s}4,\quad
4\xrightarrow{r^{-1}}3\xrightarrow{s}3,
\]
so $sr^{-1}=(1\,2)(3\,4)$.
The two permutations agree, so $rs=sr^{-1}$ holds.
\textit{Check.} Both sides equal $sr^3=(1\,2)(3\,4)$ from the previous example, as they must, since $rs=sr^{-1}$ and $r^{-1}=r^3$ give $sr^{-1}=sr^3$; but here we verified $rs=sr^{-1}$ as permutations without assuming the relation. This is the geometric content D\&F extracts: reflecting, then rotating, equals rotating backward, then reflecting.
\end{wex}

\begin{proof}
A bijection $f$ is determined by choosing $f(1),f(2),\dots,f(n)$ in turn. There are $n$
choices for $f(1)$; once chosen, $n-1$ remaining values for $f(2)$ (it must differ from
$f(1)$); then $n-2$ for $f(3)$, and so on down to $1$ choice for $f(n)$. By the
multiplication principle the count is $n(n-1)\cdots 2\cdot 1=n!$, and every such choice
gives a genuine bijection.
\end{proof}

section_path.title: The symmetric group $S_n$: cycle notation, products, and inverses

title: Cycle notation

latex:
A single permutation pictured as a two-row map; the arrows are exactly the rule
$\sigma=(1\,3\,5)(2\,4)$ on $\{1,\dots,6\}$ (so $6$ is fixed):
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=small]
1 \arrow[drr] & 2 \arrow[drr] & 3 \arrow[drr] & 4 \arrow[dll] & 5 \arrow[dllll] & 6 \arrow[d] \\
1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Reading the targets off the bottom row: $1\mapsto3,\ 2\mapsto4,\ 3\mapsto5,\ 4\mapsto2,\
5\mapsto1,\ 6\mapsto6$.

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Two copies of the set $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$: the top row is the \emph{domain}
  and the bottom row is the \emph{codomain}, both just the same finite set viewed as
  inputs vs.\ outputs of the bijection $\sigma=(1\,3\,5)(2\,4)$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each arrow runs from a point $i$ in the top row to the point $\sigma(i)$ in
  the bottom row.  Specifically: $1\to3$ (start of the $3$-cycle), $3\to5$ (second step),
  $5\to1$ (closing the $3$-cycle), $2\to4$ (start of the transposition), $4\to2$ (closing
  it), and $6\to6$ (a vertical arrow, indicating $6$ is a fixed point).  Every arrow is
  the application of the permutation to one element; no arrow is a group homomorphism.
\dgi{What commutes:} This is a function diagram, not a square or triangle, so there is no
  composition identity to verify.  The single constraint is that the arrow out of each
  top-row node lands on exactly one bottom-row node and every bottom-row node is hit exactly
  once -- i.e.\ the arrows encode a bijection, which the cycle structure guarantees.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Because $\sigma$ is a well-defined function: each of the six inputs
  has a unique output determined by the cycles $(1\,3\,5)$ and $(2\,4)$, and the outputs
  are all distinct (no two arrows share a target), confirming $\sigma$ is a bijection.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This picture sits immediately after the formal definition of
  a $k$-cycle and is the \emph{transition bridge} from the abstract cycle notation to the
  concrete function-values picture.  It makes the definition checkable at a glance: every
  orbit forms a path of arrows, and a fixed point is the special case of a trivial
  self-loop.  It also anticipates the two-row (matrix) notation introduced later.
\dgi{Concrete example:} For $\sigma=(1\,2)$ in $S_3$, the diagram has $1\to2$, $2\to1$
  (the transposition), and $3\to3$ (fixed point vertical arrow), illustrating the same
  pattern with the simplest nontrivial case.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read a multi-step path (e.g.\ $1\to3\to5\to1$)
  as a single arrow labelled by the composition $\sigma^3$, but each arrow in the diagram
  represents \emph{one application} of $\sigma$.  Reading the path as composition conflates
  the picture with the orbit diagram, which is a different object.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that cycle notation is just a compressed
  description of the arrow-map: each cycle lists one closed path of arrows, and fixed
  points are the trivial vertical arrows.
\end{dgx}

title: Disjoint-cycle decomposition

latex:
\begin{proof}
Define a relation on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ by $x\sim y$ iff $y=\sigma^m(x)$ for some
$m\in\mathbb{Z}$. This is an equivalence relation (reflexive via $m=0$, symmetric via $-m$,
transitive by adding exponents), so $\{1,\dots,n\}$ splits into disjoint orbits. On the
orbit of $x$, the points $x,\sigma(x),\sigma^2(x),\dots$ recur with least period $k$
(finiteness forces $\sigma^k(x)=x$ for some least $k\ge1$), giving the cycle
$(x\,\sigma(x)\,\cdots\,\sigma^{k-1}(x))$. Distinct orbits are disjoint, and $\sigma$
agrees with the product of these cycles on every point, hence equals it. Uniqueness: the
orbits are intrinsic to $\sigma$, and within an orbit the cyclic order
$x\to\sigma(x)\to\cdots$ is forced, so the only freedom is the listing order of the cycles
and the starting point of each.
\end{proof}

title: Inverse reverses each cycle

latex:
\begin{proof}
A $k$-cycle sends $a_i\mapsto a_{i+1}$ (indices mod $k$); its inverse must send
$a_{i+1}\mapsto a_i$, i.e. run the same wheel backwards, which is precisely
$(a_k\,\cdots\,a_1)$. For a product, $(\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_r)^{-1}=\gamma_r^{-1}\cdots
\gamma_1^{-1}$ in general; disjointness lets us reorder the factors freely
by Proposition~\ref{p:comm@c1}.
\end{proof}

latex:
\begin{method}{How to multiply two permutations $\sigma\tau$}
Trigger: you must compose two permutations (given in cycle form or two-row form), and you
want the answer back in disjoint cycles.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Fix the convention: $(\sigma\tau)(x)=\sigma(\tau(x))$ -- apply the
\emph{right} factor $\tau$ first, then feed the result to $\sigma$.
\item Start at $1$. Track it through the cycles \emph{right to left}: find where the
rightmost cycle sends it, carry that number leftward through each remaining cycle.
\item Write $1\mapsto(\text{final image})$. Continue from that image; when you return to
$1$, close the cycle.
\item Pick the smallest unused point and repeat until all of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ is placed.
Drop fixed points.
\end{enumerate}
\end{method}

latex:
\begin{wex}{Multiply two permutations of $\{1,\dots,6\}$}
Let $\sigma=(1\,3\,5)(2\,4)$ and $\tau=(1\,2\,6)(3\,5)$ in $S_6$. Compute $\sigma\tau$.
\wrec Two permutations, product wanted: this is the multiply-method. The trigger is the
juxtaposition $\sigma\tau$; resolve it by tracking each point with $\tau$ first
(rightmost), then $\sigma$.
\wsol First record both maps. From $\sigma=(1\,3\,5)(2\,4)$:
$1\mapsto3,\,2\mapsto4,\,3\mapsto5,\,4\mapsto2,\,5\mapsto1,\,6\mapsto6$. From
$\tau=(1\,2\,6)(3\,5)$: $1\mapsto2,\,2\mapsto6,\,3\mapsto5,\,4\mapsto4,\,5\mapsto3,\,
6\mapsto1$. Now $(\sigma\tau)(x)=\sigma(\tau(x))$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1 &\xrightarrow{\tau} 2 \xrightarrow{\sigma} 4, &
2 &\xrightarrow{\tau} 6 \xrightarrow{\sigma} 6, &
3 &\xrightarrow{\tau} 5 \xrightarrow{\sigma} 1,\\
4 &\xrightarrow{\tau} 4 \xrightarrow{\sigma} 2, &
5 &\xrightarrow{\tau} 3 \xrightarrow{\sigma} 5, &
6 &\xrightarrow{\tau} 1 \xrightarrow{\sigma} 3.
\end{aligned}
\]
So $1\mapsto4\mapsto2\mapsto6\mapsto3\mapsto1$ (closing), and $5\mapsto5$ is fixed. Hence
\[
\sigma\tau=(1\,4\,2\,6\,3).
\]
Check: a $5$-cycle moves exactly $\{1,2,3,4,6\}$ and fixes $5$, matching the table; and
$5$ is the unique fixed point, consistent with $\tau(5)=3,\ \sigma(3)=5$.
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Order matters: same factors, other product}
With $\sigma,\tau$ as above, compute $\tau\sigma$ and compare with $\sigma\tau$.
\wrec Same two permutations but the product is reversed. The recognition cue is that we
swapped the order, so now apply $\sigma$ first, then $\tau$. Expect a different answer
because $S_6$ is nonabelian.
\wsol $(\tau\sigma)(x)=\tau(\sigma(x))$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1 &\xrightarrow{\sigma} 3 \xrightarrow{\tau} 5, &
2 &\xrightarrow{\sigma} 4 \xrightarrow{\tau} 4, &
3 &\xrightarrow{\sigma} 5 \xrightarrow{\tau} 3,\\
4 &\xrightarrow{\sigma} 2 \xrightarrow{\tau} 6, &
5 &\xrightarrow{\sigma} 1 \xrightarrow{\tau} 2, &
6 &\xrightarrow{\sigma} 6 \xrightarrow{\tau} 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Following $1\mapsto5\mapsto2\mapsto4\mapsto6\mapsto1$ and $3\mapsto3$ fixed:
\[
\tau\sigma=(1\,5\,2\,4\,6)\neq(1\,4\,2\,6\,3)=\sigma\tau.
\]
Check: both are $5$-cycles (same cycle type, as they must be since $\tau\sigma$ and
$\sigma\tau$ are conjugate via $\tau\sigma=\tau(\sigma\tau)\tau^{-1}$), but they fix
different points ($3$ versus $5$), confirming $\sigma\tau\ne\tau\sigma$.
\end{wex}

In $S_5$ compute $(1\,2\,4\,3)(1\,3\,5)$.
\wrec Two cycles sharing the points $1$ and $3$: overlapping, so we cannot just

\begin{aligned}

4 &\to 4 \to 3, & 5 &\to 1 \to 2.
\end{aligned}
\]
So $1\mapsto1$ (fixed); then $2\mapsto4\mapsto3\mapsto5\mapsto2$ closes:
\[
(1\,2\,4\,3)(1\,3\,5)=(2\,4\,3\,5).
\]
Check: $1$ is fixed, and the other four points form one $4$-cycle moving
$\{2,3,4,5\}$; total support size $4$ matches the four nonfixed images.
\end{wex}

title: How to decompose a messy product into disjoint cycles

latex:
\begin{wex}{Decompose a four-factor mess}
Write $(1\,2\,3)(2\,4)(1\,5\,3)(4\,2)$ as a product of disjoint cycles in $S_5$.
\wrec A long chain of overlapping cycles: pure decomposition. Build the full map by the
multiply-method, then read orbits.
\wsol Maps (rightmost first): $(4\,2)$ swaps $2,4$; $(1\,5\,3)$: $1\to5,5\to3,3\to1$;
$(2\,4)$ swaps $2,4$; $(1\,2\,3)$: $1\to2,2\to3,3\to1$. Carry each $x$ through all four,
right to left:
\[
\begin{aligned}
1 &\xrightarrow{(42)}1\xrightarrow{(153)}5\xrightarrow{(24)}5\xrightarrow{(123)}5,\\
2 &\xrightarrow{(42)}4\xrightarrow{(153)}4\xrightarrow{(24)}2\xrightarrow{(123)}3,\\
3 &\xrightarrow{(42)}3\xrightarrow{(153)}1\xrightarrow{(24)}1\xrightarrow{(123)}2,\\
4 &\xrightarrow{(42)}2\xrightarrow{(153)}2\xrightarrow{(24)}4\xrightarrow{(123)}4,\\
5 &\xrightarrow{(42)}5\xrightarrow{(153)}3\xrightarrow{(24)}3\xrightarrow{(123)}1.
\end{aligned}
\]
So the net map is $1\mapsto5,\,2\mapsto3,\,3\mapsto2,\,4\mapsto4,\,5\mapsto1$. Follow
orbits: $1\mapsto5\mapsto1$ gives $(1\,5)$; $2\mapsto3\mapsto2$ gives $(2\,3)$; $4$ fixed.
\[
(1\,2\,3)(2\,4)(1\,5\,3)(4\,2)=(1\,5)(2\,3).
\]
Check: cycle lengths $2+2=4=5-1$ (one fixed point $4$), consistent; and the order is
$\lcm(2,2)=2$, so squaring should give $\id$, which it does since each factor is its own
inverse.
\end{wex}

Find $\sigma^{-1}$ for $\sigma=(1\,5\,2\,6\,3)(4\,7)$ in $S_7$.
\wrec Inverse requested and $\sigma$ is already in disjoint cycles: apply the reverse-each-

\wsol Reverse the $5$-cycle: $(1\,5\,2\,6\,3)^{-1}=(3\,6\,2\,5\,1)=(1\,3\,6\,2\,5)$

\[

consistent. Composing $\sigma\sigma^{-1}$ fixes all of $\{1,\dots,7\}$.
\end{wex}

Let $\sigma=(1\,2\,3\,4)(5\,6\,7\,8)$ in $S_8$. Compute $\sigma^2$ and $\sigma^3$.

\wsol $\sigma^2$: each $4$-cycle steps $+2$. $(1\,2\,3\,4)^2=(1\,3)(2\,4)$ and

\[

\[
\sigma^3=(1\,4\,3\,2)(5\,8\,7\,6)=\sigma^{-1}.
\]
Check: $\ord{\sigma}=\lcm(4,4)=4$, so $\sigma^3=\sigma^{-1}$ exactly as found; and
$\sigma^2$ has order $\lcm(2,2,2,2)=2$, while $(\sigma^2)^2=\sigma^4=\id$, consistent.
