  the proposition \emph{is} the implication diagram. The diagram is a schematic summary;
  the proposition is the actual proof that every ideal of an ED has a minimal-norm
  generator. The diagram does not prove the result---it just records where it lives.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the two-step implication
  $\text{ED}\xRightarrow{\text{Prop.\ 8.1}}\text{PID}\xRightarrow{\text{8.3}}\text{UFD}$
  maps each class to its proof reference, so the reader knows exactly which theorems
  establish the refinement hierarchy.
\end{dgx}
\end{remark}

\begin{wex}{Reading off the generator from minimal norm in $\mathbb{Z}$}
Use the proposition to find a generator of $I=\langle 12,30\rangle\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$.
\wrec $\mathbb{Z}$ is Euclidean; the generator is the nonzero element of $I$ of least absolute
value, which the Euclidean algorithm produces as $\gcd$.
\wsol
$I=\langle 12,30\rangle=\{12s+30t:s,t\in\mathbb{Z}\}$. The smallest positive element is $\gcd(12,30)$:
$30=2\cdot 12+6$, $12=2\cdot 6+0$, so $\gcd=6$ and $6=30-2\cdot 12\in I$. By the
proposition $I=\langle 6\rangle$. \textit{Check.} $12=6\cdot 2$, $30=6\cdot 5\in\langle 6\rangle$, and
$6\in I$, so $\langle 12,30\rangle=\langle 6\rangle$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{definition}[Universal side divisor]
Let $R$ be an integral domain and $\tilde R=\units R\cup\{0\}$. A nonzero nonunit
$u\in R$ is a \emph{universal side divisor} if for every $x\in R$ there is some
$z\in\tilde R$ with $u\mid (x-z)$ in $R$ -- i.e.\ $u$ divides $x$ ``up to a unit or
zero.'' Equivalently, $u$ divides $x-z$ for some $z$ that is $0$ or a unit.
\end{definition}

\begin{proposition}[Existence of a universal side divisor in any ED]
Let $R$ be a Euclidean domain that is not a field. Then $R$ possesses a universal side
divisor.
\end{proposition}

title: Existence of a universal side divisor in any ED

latex:
\begin{proof}
Choose $u$ a nonzero nonunit of \emph{minimal norm} among all nonzero nonunits (such $u$
exists by well-ordering of norms; the set is nonempty as $R$ is not a field). For any
$x\in R$ divide: $x=qu+r$ with $r=0$ or $\Nm(r)<\Nm(u)$. If $r=0$ then $u\mid x$, take
$z=0$. If $r\neq0$ then $\Nm(r)<\Nm(u)$ forces $r$ to be a unit (by minimality of $\Nm(u)$
among nonzero nonunits, anything of strictly smaller positive norm is a unit). Then
$u\mid (x-r)$ with $r\in\units R$, so $z=r$ works. Hence $u$ is a universal side
divisor.
\end{proof}

latex:
\begin{proof}[Sketch]
One shows $\units R=\{\pm1\}$, so $\tilde R=\{0,\pm1\}$. If $R$ were Euclidean it would have a
universal side divisor $u$. Taking $x=2$ in the definition, $u$ divides $2$, $1$ or $3$, and
$u\nmid 1$ since $u$ is not a unit. The field norm $\Nm(a+b\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}2)=a^2+ab+5b^2$
never equals $2$ or $3$, so $2$ and $3$ are irreducible in $R$ and $u\in\{\pm2,\pm3\}$. But
neither $\pm2$ nor $\pm3$ is a universal side divisor: taking $x=\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}2$, one checks $u\nmid(x-z)$ for
$z\in\{0,1,-1\}$ in each case (the relevant norm equations have no solution in $R$). With no
universal side divisor, the Proposition forces $R$ non-Euclidean. That $R$ is nonetheless a
PID is shown by a Dedekind--Hasse style norm argument; the details are in Section 8.2.
\end{proof}

\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}$ has a universal side divisor}
Exhibit a universal side divisor in $\mathbb{Z}$.
\wrec $\mathbb{Z}$ is a non-field ED, so one must exist; the Proposition says to take a nonzero
nonunit of minimal norm.
\wsol
Units are $\pm1$, so $\tilde\mathbb{Z}=\{0,1,-1\}$. The nonzero nonunits of least $|\cdot|$ are

\textit{Check.} Every residue mod $2$ is $0$ or a unit ($1$), exactly as the Proposition
predicts. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{A universal side divisor in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$}
Find a universal side divisor in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.
\wrec Non-field ED; minimal-norm nonzero nonunit means least positive degree, i.e.\
degree $1$.
\wsol
$\units{\mathbb{Q}[x]}=\mathbb{Q}^\times$ (nonzero constants), so $\tilde R=\mathbb{Q}^\times\cup\{0\}=\mathbb{Q}$. Take
$u=x$. For any $f\in\mathbb{Q}[x]$, divide by $x$: $f=x\,g + f(0)$ with remainder the constant
$f(0)\in\mathbb{Q}=\tilde R$. Thus $x\mid(f-f(0))$, so $u=x$ is a universal side divisor.
\textit{Check.} The remainder $f(0)$ is always $0$ or a unit (a nonzero constant), matching
the definition. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Recall (8.1) that a \emph{Euclidean domain} (ED) is an integral domain $R$ equipped with a norm $N\colon R\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ (with $N(0)=0$) such that for all $a,b\in R$ with $b\neq 0$ there exist $q,r\in R$ with
\[
a = qb + r,\qquad r=0 \ \text{ or }\ N(r)<N(b).
\]
The division algorithm is exactly what lets us run the Euclidean algorithm to compute gcds. We now isolate the purely ideal-theoretic consequence that makes the machinery work, and find that it is strictly weaker than possessing a division algorithm.

\begin{wex}{Generator of $(f,g)$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$}
In $R=\mathbb{Q}[x]$ find a generator of $I=\langle f,g\rangle$ with $f=x^3-1$, $g=x^2-1$.

\[
x^3-1 = x\,(x^2-1) + (x-1),\qquad r_1=x-1.

Divide $g$ by $r_1$:
\[
x^2-1 = (x+1)(x-1) + 0,\qquad r_2=0.
\]
The last nonzero remainder is $x-1$, so $\gcd(f,g)=x-1$ (already monic) and $I=\langle x-1\rangle$. \textit{Check.} $x-1\mid x^3-1$ since $x=1$ is a root of $x^3-1$, and $x-1\mid x^2-1=(x-1)(x+1)$. \end{wex}

\begin{theorem}[PID $\Longrightarrow$ Noetherian]
Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain. Then $R$ satisfies the \emph{ascending chain condition} (ACC) on ideals: every chain
\[
I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq I_3\subseteq\cdots
\]
of ideals stabilizes, i.e. there is $n$ with $I_n=I_{n+1}=\cdots$. Equivalently, every nonempty collection of ideals has a maximal element. (Such a ring is called \emph{Noetherian}.)
\end{theorem}
title: PID $\Longrightarrow$ Noetherian

latex:
\begin{proof}
Let $I_1\subseteq I_2\subseteq\cdots$ be an ascending chain. Put $I=\bigcup_{k\ge 1} I_k$. This is an ideal: if $a,b\in I$ then $a\in I_j,\ b\in I_k$ for some $j,k$, so both lie in $I_{\max(j,k)}$ (the chain is nested), hence $a-b\in I$ and $ra\in I$ for all $r\in R$. Since $R$ is a PID, $I=\langle d\rangle$ for some $d$. Now $d\in I=\bigcup_k I_k$, so $d\in I_n$ for some $n$. Then
\[
\langle d\rangle\subseteq I_n\subseteq I_{n+1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq I=\langle d\rangle,
\]
forcing $I_n=I_{n+1}=\cdots=\langle d\rangle$. The chain stabilizes at stage $n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Indication]
\textbf{Not Euclidean.} The key is the notion of a \emph{universal side divisor}: in any Euclidean domain that is not a field, there exists a nonzero nonunit $u$ such that for every $x\in R$ there is $z\in\{0\}\cup\units{R}$ with $u\mid (x-z)$ --- equivalently every residue class of $R/\langle u\rangle$ is represented by $\{0\}\cup\units{R}$. For $R=\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ one checks $\units{R}=\{\pm 1\}$ (the norm form $a^2+ab+5b^2$ equals $1$ only at $(\pm 1,0)$). Taking $x=2$, a universal side divisor $u$ divides $2-0$, $2-1$ or $2+1$, i.e.\ $2$, $1$ or $3$, and $u\nmid 1$ since $u$ is not a unit. For $b\neq 0$ the norm form equals $(a+\tfrac b2)^2+\tfrac{19}{4}b^2\ge 5$, and for $b=0$ it is $a^2$, so it never takes the values $2$ or $3$; hence $2$ and $3$ are irreducible in $R$ and the only candidates are $u=\pm 2$ and $u=\pm 3$. Testing them shows neither is a universal side divisor: $R/\langle 2\rangle$ and $R/\langle 3\rangle$ have order $\Nm(2)=4$ and $\Nm(3)=9$ respectively, too large to be covered by the three residues $\{0,\pm 1\}$. Hence $R$ has no universal side divisor, so $R$ is not Euclidean for \emph{any} norm.

\textbf{Is a PID.} One uses the \emph{Dedekind--Hasse} criterion: an integral domain $R$ is a PID iff there is a function $N\colon R\to\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$ (a Dedekind--Hasse norm) with $N(a)>0$ for $a\neq 0$ such that for all nonzero $a,b\in R$, either $a\in\langle b\rangle$ or there is a nonzero $r\in\langle a,b\rangle$ with $N(r)<N(b)$. The field norm $\Nm$ is shown to be a Dedekind--Hasse norm on $\mathbb{Z}[\omega]$ by a direct (case) verification: given $a,b$, the quotient $a/b\in\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-19})$ can be approximated by an element of $R$ closely enough (or, when it cannot, one multiplies by a small element) to produce such an $r$. This makes every ideal principal, so $R$ is a PID. Full details are in Dummit \& Foote, $\S$8.1--8.2.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[The strict hierarchy]
We have proper containments
\[
\{\text{fields}\}\subsetneq\{\text{Euclidean domains}\}\subsetneq\{\text{PIDs}\}\subsetneq\{\text{UFDs}\}\subsetneq\{\text{integral domains}\}.
\]
Witnesses for strictness: $\mathbb{Z}$ is a non-field ED; $\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$ is a non-Euclidean PID; $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a non-PID UFD; $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a non-UFD domain (e.g. $6=2\cdot 3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ are two essentially different factorizations into irreducibles).
\end{corollary}
title: The strict hierarchy

latex:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\text{fields} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{ED} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{PID} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{UFD} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{domain}
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Each node is a class of commutative rings (or integral domains): fields, Euclidean domains (ED), principal ideal domains (PID), unique factorization domains (UFD), and general integral domains. The arrow direction runs from more structured to less structured.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each double arrow ($\Rightarrow$) is a logical implication between ring classes: fields $\Rightarrow$ ED means every field is a Euclidean domain (the trivial norm $N(a)=0$ for all $a\neq 0$ works, or simply every nonzero ideal is $R$ so division is trivial); ED $\Rightarrow$ PID is the theorem proved in this section; PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD is stated in the remark and proved in the next section; UFD $\Rightarrow$ domain is definitional (UFDs are defined to be integral domains).
\dgi{What commutes:} The chain is a transitive sequence: fields $\Rightarrow$ ED $\Rightarrow$ PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD $\Rightarrow$ domain. By transitivity, fields $\Rightarrow$ domain (every field is an integral domain), and every ED is a UFD, etc. All six composite implications hold (ten implications in all, counting the four arrows).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Each implication is strict one-way. The chain is linear, not a square, so ``commutativity'' here means transitivity: if $A\Rightarrow B$ and $B\Rightarrow C$ then $A\Rightarrow C$ by chaining. No nontrivial reverse implication holds, as the witnesses in the corollary show.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram crystallizes the cumulative work of Section 8.2: every theorem in this section either proves one of the forward arrows (ED $\Rightarrow$ PID was the first theorem) or exhibits a witness showing the arrow cannot be reversed. It is the organizing spine of the section.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $\mathbb{Z}$ is an ED (norm $|\cdot|$) but not a field ($2$ is not invertible). $\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$ is a PID but not an ED (no universal side divisor). $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a UFD but not a PID ($\langle 2,x\rangle$ is non-principal). $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a domain but not a UFD ($6=2\cdot 3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$).
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read $\Rightarrow$ as $\Leftrightarrow$, concluding, e.g., that every PID must be Euclidean. The corollary's list of witnesses is precisely to block this: each arrow is strict, so the reverse implication fails for an explicit ring.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the five standard classes of integral domains form a strict linear hierarchy of inclusions, with each arrow forward proved and each reversal blocked by a concrete example.
\end{dgx}

The next diagram records, inside a PID, the coincidence of nonzero primes with maximal ideals and the gcd computation $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$:

\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=normal, column sep=0pt]
\langle a\rangle \arrow[dr, phantom, "\subseteq"] & & \langle b\rangle \arrow[dl, phantom, "\supseteq"] \\
& \langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle=\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle \arrow[d, "{\text{if }d\text{ prime}}"] & \\
& \langle d\rangle\ \text{maximal} &
\end{tikzcd}\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four ideal-nodes inside a fixed PID $R$. Top row: $\langle a\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle$, the principal ideals generated by individual elements $a,b\in R$. Middle: $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle=\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle$, the sum of those two ideals, which collapses to a single principal ideal because $R$ is a PID; $d$ is the gcd, well-defined up to a unit. Bottom: $\langle d\rangle$ labeled maximal, active only when $d$ is a prime element.
\dgi{Arrows:} The phantom arrows from $\langle a\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle$, labeled $\subseteq$ and $\supseteq$ (each symbol opens toward the larger ideal), record containments: $\langle a\rangle\subseteq\langle a,b\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle\subseteq\langle a,b\rangle$ (each generator belongs to the larger ideal). The vertical arrow from $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ to $\langle d\rangle\ \text{maximal}$ is a conditional logical step: when $d$ is a prime element, the theorem ``nonzero prime ideals are maximal in a PID'' promotes $\langle d\rangle$ from merely principal to maximal.
\dgi{What commutes:} No closed square, so the relevant equalities are: (1) $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ as ideals (PID gives every two-generator ideal a single generator, namely the gcd); (2) $\langle d\rangle=\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle$ names that generator as the gcd; (3) when $d$ is prime, $\langle d\rangle$ is maximal (the nonzero-prime-is-maximal theorem).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $d$: different choices of gcd are associates ($d'=ud$, $u\in\units{R}$), so $\langle d'\rangle=\langle d\rangle$; the ideal is independent of the choice of associate. The equality $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ follows because $d\mid a$ and $d\mid b$ give $\langle a\rangle\subseteq\langle d\rangle$ and $\langle b\rangle\subseteq\langle d\rangle$, hence $\langle a,b\rangle\subseteq\langle d\rangle$; and $d=ax+by\in\langle a,b\rangle$ gives the reverse.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The diagram is a visual summary of two payoffs of the PID axiom proved in this section: ideal-sums compress to a gcd generator, and prime generators produce maximal ideals (hence fields as quotients). It shows the student what ``every ideal is principal'' buys in one picture.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $\mathbb{Z}$: $a=12$, $b=8$, $d=\gcd(12,8)=4$, so $\langle 12,8\rangle=\langle 4\rangle$. If $d=5$ (prime), $\langle 5\rangle$ is maximal and $\mathbb{Z}/\langle 5\rangle=\F_5$ is a field. In $\mathbb{Q}[x]$: $a=x^3-1$, $b=x^2-1$, $d=x-1$, $\langle x^3-1,x^2-1\rangle=\langle x-1\rangle$; since $x-1$ is irreducible (prime in a PID), $\langle x-1\rangle$ is maximal and $\mathbb{Q}[x]/\langle x-1\rangle\cong\mathbb{Q}$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the middle equality $\langle a,b\rangle=\langle d\rangle$ as saying $a=d$ or $b=d$; in fact $d$ is a new element (the gcd), generally different from $a$ and $b$, and the equality is of ideals, not elements. Also, the bottom node $\langle d\rangle\ \text{maximal}$ applies only when $d$ is prime; if $d=4$ in $\mathbb{Z}$, $\langle 4\rangle$ is not maximal ($\langle 4\rangle\subsetneq\langle 2\rangle\subsetneq\mathbb{Z}$).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that in a PID the two-generator ideal $\langle a,b\rangle$ automatically collapses to the principal ideal $\langle \gcd(a,b)\rangle$, and if that gcd happens to be prime the ideal is moreover maximal, linking the gcd computation directly to the prime-equals-maximal theorem.
\end{dgx}

\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Show directly that every ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ is principal: given a nonzero ideal $I\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$, prove that $I=\langle d\rangle$, where $d$ is the least positive element of $I$. (Hint: well-ordering produces $d$; for $a\in I$ divide $a=qd+r$ with $0\le r<d$ and rule out $r>0$.)

\item In a PID, prove that a nonzero element $p$ is prime if and only if it is irreducible. (You may use: every proper ideal lies in a maximal ideal, and in a PID nonzero primes are maximal.)

\item In a PID $R$, suppose $\langle a\rangle+\langle b\rangle=R$ (so $a,b$ are comaximal). Prove the Chinese Remainder Theorem in this setting: the natural map
\[
R/\langle ab\rangle\longrightarrow R/\langle a\rangle\times R/\langle b\rangle,\qquad x+\langle ab\rangle\mapsto\bigl(x+\langle a\rangle,\,x+\langle b\rangle\bigr),
\]
is a ring isomorphism. (Hint: surjectivity uses $1=ax+by$; for injectivity show $\langle a\rangle\cap\langle b\rangle=\langle ab\rangle$ when $a,b$ are comaximal.)

\item Use the ascending chain condition in a PID to prove existence of factorizations: every nonzero nonunit of a PID is a finite product of irreducible elements. title: Prime implies irreducible, by hand in $\mathbb{Z}$

\begin{wex}{An irreducible that is not prime in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$}
\wrec We want a domain where unique factorization fails; the norm $\Nm(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2$ flags two genuinely different factorizations of the same element.
\wsol In $R = \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ the norm $\Nm(a+b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2$ is multiplicative, and $\units{R} = \{\pm 1\}$ since $\Nm(\alpha) = 1 \Longrightarrow a^2 + 5b^2 = 1 \Longrightarrow b = 0,\ a = \pm 1$. Consider
\[
6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}).
\]
\textbf{$2$ is irreducible:} $\Nm(2) = 4$. If $2 = \alpha\beta$ with both nonunits then $\Nm(\alpha) = \Nm(\beta) = 2$, but $a^2 + 5b^2 = 2$ has no integer solution. So no such factorization exists; $2$ is irreducible. (Same argument: $3$ has $\Nm = 9$, and $a^2 + 5b^2 = 3$ is unsolvable, so $3$ is irreducible; $1 \pm \sqrt{-5}$ each have $\Nm = 6$, and $\Nm = 2$ or $3$ are both unsolvable, so they are irreducible too.)
\textbf{$2$ is not prime:} $2 \mid 6 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$. But $2 \nmid (1 \pm \sqrt{-5})$: if $1 + \sqrt{-5} = 2(a + b\sqrt{-5})$ then $2b = 1$, impossible in $\mathbb{Z}$. So $2$ divides the product but neither factor: $2$ is irreducible but not prime.
\textit{Check.} The two factorizations of $6$ use irreducibles $\{2, 3\}$ versus $\{1+\sqrt{-5}, 1-\sqrt{-5}\}$, and $2 \not\sim 1 \pm \sqrt{-5}$ (different norms $4$ vs $6$), so factorization into irreducibles is \emph{not} unique. Hence $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD.
\end{wex}

title: Irreducibility via prime norm in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$

\begin{wex}{Factoring rational primes in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$}
\wrec $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ is a UFD (it is Euclidean), so each integer prime $p$ either stays irreducible or splits; the splitting is governed by $p \bmod 4$ and read off the norm.
\wsol \emph{(a) $5$ splits.} $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$. Check: $(2+i)(2-i) = 4 - i^2 = 4 + 1 = 5$. Both factors have norm $5$ (prime), hence irreducible; $5$ is a product of two nonassociate irreducibles.
\emph{(b) $2$ ramifies.} $2 = -i(1+i)^2$. Check: $(1+i)^2 = 1 + 2i + i^2 = 2i$, and $-i \cdot 2i = -2i^2 = 2$. Here $1 + i$ is irreducible ($\Nm = 2$) and $-i$ is a unit, so $2$ is (a unit times) the square of one irreducible.
\emph{(c) $3$ is inert.} $\Nm(3) = 9$; a proper factor would need norm $3$, but $a^2 + b^2 = 3$ has no integer solution, so $3$ remains irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$.
\textit{Check.} Norms multiply correctly: (a) $5 \cdot 5 = 25 = \Nm(5)$; (b) $\Nm((1+i)^2) = 2^2 = 4 = \Nm(2)$ and the unit $-i$ has norm $1$; (c) $9$ has no factorization $9 = 3 \cdot 3$ realized by norm-$3$ Gaussian integers. All consistent with $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ being a UFD.
\end{wex}

\begin{proof}
Prime $\Longrightarrow$ irreducible holds in any domain. For the converse, let $p$ be irreducible and suppose $p \mid ab$, say $ab = pc$. If $a$ is a unit then $b = a^{-1} p c$, so $p \mid b$; symmetrically if $b$ is a unit then $p \mid a$. So assume $a$ and $b$ are nonzero nonunits (if $a = 0$ then $p \mid a$ trivially, similarly for $b$). Factor $a = \prod_i p_i$ and $b = \prod_j q_j$ into irreducibles, and factor $c$ into irreducibles (absorbing any unit). Then
\[
\Big(\prod_i p_i\Big)\Big(\prod_j q_j\Big) = p \cdot \prod_k r_k
\]
are two factorizations of $ab$ into irreducibles. By uniqueness, the irreducible $p$ on the right is an associate of some factor on the left, i.e.\ $p \sim p_i$ for some $i$ (so $p \mid a$) or $p \sim q_j$ for some $j$ (so $p \mid b$). Hence $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$, and $p$ is prime.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[gcds exist in a UFD]
Let $R$ be a UFD. Write the distinct irreducibles (up to associates) appearing in $a$ and $b$ as $p_1, \dots, p_k$, so
\[
a = u \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{\,e_i}, \qquad b = v \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{\,f_i} \qquad (u, v \in \units{R},\ e_i, f_i \geq 0).
\]
Then $d = \prod_{i=1}^k p_i^{\,\min(e_i, f_i)}$ is a greatest common divisor of $a$ and $b$ (unique up to associates), and $\ell = \prod_i p_i^{\,\max(e_i,f_i)}$ is a least common multiple.
\end{theorem}

title: Proof sketch

latex:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\text{ED} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{PID} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{UFD} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{domain}
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Four classes of integral domains, listed left to right in strictly increasing generality:
  Euclidean domains (ED), principal ideal domains (PID), unique factorization domains (UFD),
  and arbitrary integral domains (domain).  Each node represents a class of rings, not a single ring.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each double arrow $\Rightarrow$ is a class inclusion: every ED is a PID,
  every PID is a UFD, every UFD is an integral domain.  There are no arrows going right to left,
  signalling that each inclusion is strict.
\dgi{What commutes:} The chain is a linear sequence, not a square, so commutativity is trivial:
  the unique path from ED to domain passes through PID and UFD.  What matters is the direction
  and the absence of reverse arrows.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} ED $\Rightarrow$ PID: in a nonzero ideal $I$ a nonzero element $d$ of minimal norm
  generates $I$ (dividing $a\in I$ by $d$ leaves a remainder in $I$ of smaller norm, hence $0$).  PID $\Rightarrow$ UFD: in a PID, ACC on principal ideals gives existence of
  irreducible factorizations, and every irreducible is prime (because $\langle p\rangle$ is maximal hence
  prime), giving uniqueness.  UFD $\Rightarrow$ domain: a UFD is by definition a domain.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the structural punchline of the section.  After
  proving prime $\Rightarrow$ irreducible (always), irreducible $\Rightarrow$ prime (in a UFD), and
  every PID is a UFD, the diagram collects those implications into a single memorable hierarchy,
  and the proof-sketch above has just verified each implication.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ (Gaussian integers) is Euclidean via the norm, hence a PID,
  hence a UFD.  $\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}]$ is a PID but not Euclidean (no Euclidean function).
  $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a UFD (since $\mathbb{Z}$ is) but not a PID ($\langle 2,x\rangle$ is not principal).
  $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is a domain but not a UFD (the element $6$ has two genuinely different
  irreducible factorizations).
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read the implication chain as ``every UFD has a
  Euclidean algorithm'' or conflate PID and UFD.  Neither reverse arrow exists: each class
  is genuinely more restrictive than the one to its right.  In particular, having unique factorization does
  not by itself guarantee that every ideal is principal.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the standard classes of ``nice'' domains form a
  strict linear hierarchy, and each step genuinely loses structure, as witnessed by concrete
  examples sitting in each gap.
\end{dgx}

Inside the world of elements, the dual picture is the relation between prime and irreducible:

\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=small, column sep=huge]
\{\text{prime}\} \arrow[r, hook, "{\text{always}}"] & \{\text{irreducible}\} \arrow[l, bend left=25, dashed, "{\text{in a UFD}}"]
\end{tikzcd}
\]

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Two subsets of the nonzero nonunits of an integral domain $R$: the set of prime
  elements $\{\text{prime}\}$ and the set of irreducible elements $\{\text{irreducible}\}$.
  Both live inside the same domain; the diagram compares them as subsets.
\dgi{Arrows:} The solid hooked arrow $\hookrightarrow$ labelled ``always'' is a set inclusion:
  every prime element is irreducible, in any integral domain, with no extra hypotheses.  The
  dashed arrow going back, labelled ``in a UFD,'' is a conditional inclusion: in a UFD (and only
  in a UFD, among the named classes) every irreducible is also prime, so the two sets coincide.
  The dashed style signals that this reverse arrow does not exist in general.
\dgi{What commutes:} There is no square to commute; the diagram expresses set-containment.
  The solid arrow means $\{\text{prime}\} \subseteq \{\text{irreducible}\}$ in every domain.
  Together with the dashed arrow in a UFD, the conclusion is
  $\{\text{prime}\} = \{\text{irreducible}\}$ inside any UFD.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Solid arrow: if $p$ is prime and $p = ab$, then $p \mid ab$, so
  $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$; say $p \mid a$, write $a = px$; then $p(1-xb) = 0$ and
  $p \neq 0$ forces $xb = 1$, so $b$ is a unit.  Dashed arrow (in a UFD only): if $p$ is
  irreducible and $p \mid ab$, factor $a$ and $b$ into irreducibles; unique factorization
  forces $p$ to be an associate of some factor in $a$ or in $b$, giving $p \mid a$ or
  $p \mid b$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The two diagrams together (the domain-class chain and this
  element-level diagram) explain \emph{why} UFDs are the right setting for unique factorization:
  uniqueness requires cancellation, which requires that irreducibles generate prime ideals, which
  is exactly the dashed arrow.  The failure of the dashed arrow in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ (where $2$ is
  irreducible but not prime) is what breaks unique factorization there.
\dgi{Concrete example:} In $\mathbb{Z}$ (a UFD) every irreducible is $\pm p$ for a rational prime $p$,
  and every such $p$ is prime: both arrows hold and the sets are equal.  In $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ (not
  a UFD) the element $2$ is irreducible but $2 \mid (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5}) = 6$ while
  $2$ divides neither factor, so $2$ is not prime: the dashed reverse arrow fails.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students often assume the dashed arrow is ``obvious'' and apply it outside
  UFDs.  Checking that an element is irreducible (no factorization into nonunits) does not
  automatically make it prime (divides a product implies divides a factor); the extra hypothesis
  of unique factorization is essential and cannot be dropped.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that prime and irreducible coincide in every UFD,
  and that in a domain where factorizations into irreducibles exist (such as $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$) the
  failure of this coincidence is exactly what makes it not a UFD: it is the mechanism by which
  unique factorization breaks down.
\end{dgx}

\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Factor $85$ into irreducibles in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, using the norm $\Nm(a+bi) = a^2 + b^2$. (Hint: $85 = 5 \cdot 17$.)

\textit{Answer.} Both $5$ and $17$ are $\equiv 1 \bmod 4$, hence split: $5 = (2+i)(2-i)$ and $17 = (4+i)(4-i)$. Each factor has prime norm ($\Nm(2 \pm i) = 5$, $\Nm(4 \pm i) = 17$), so each is irreducible. Thus, up to units,
\[
85 = (2+i)(2-i)(4+i)(4-i).
\]
\textit{Check.} $\Nm(2+i)\Nm(2-i)\Nm(4+i)\Nm(4-i) = 5 \cdot 5 \cdot 17 \cdot 17 = 25 \cdot 289 = 7225 = 85^2 = \Nm(85)$. Consistent.

\item Determine whether $1 + 3i$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, using the norm $\Nm(a+bi) = a^2 + b^2$.

\textit{Answer.} $\Nm(1+3i) = 1 + 9 = 10 = 2 \cdot 5$, which is \emph{not} a rational prime, so the prime-norm shortcut does not apply and $1+3i$ may well be reducible. Seek a factor of norm $2$ or $5$: the norm-$2$ element $1+i$ divides $1+3i$, since
\[
(1+i)(2+i) = 2 + i + 2i + i^2 = 1 + 3i.
\]
Both $1+i$ ($\Nm = 2$) and $2+i$ ($\Nm = 5$) have prime norm, hence are irreducible nonunits. So $1 + 3i = (1+i)(2+i)$ is reducible. \textit{Check.} $\Nm(1+i)\Nm(2+i) = 2 \cdot 5 = 10 = \Nm(1+3i)$. Consistent. (Contrast: a Gaussian integer of \emph{prime} norm is forced to be irreducible; composite norm leaves the question open until you exhibit a proper factor.)

\item Prove that in any integral domain every prime element is irreducible. (Reproduce the one-line argument.)

\textit{Answer.} Let $p$ be prime and write $p = ab$. Then $p \mid ab$, so $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$; say $p \mid a$, $a = px$. Then $p = pxb$, so $p(1 - xb) = 0$. Since $R$ is a domain and $p \neq 0$, $xb = 1$, so $b$ is a unit. Thus in any factorization one factor is a unit, and $p$ is irreducible.

\item Show that $3$ is irreducible but not prime in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ by exhibiting two factorizations of $9$. (Use $\Nm(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2 + 5b^2$.)

\textit{Answer.} Two factorizations:
\[
9 = 3 \cdot 3 = (2+\sqrt{-5})(2-\sqrt{-5}), \qquad \Nm(2 \pm \sqrt{-5}) = 4 + 5 = 9.
\]
\textit{$3$ irreducible:} $\Nm(3) = 9$, so a proper factor would have norm $3$, but $a^2 + 5b^2 = 3$ has no integer solution; hence $3$ is irreducible. \textit{$3$ not prime:} $3 \mid 9 = (2+\sqrt{-5})(2-\sqrt{-5})$, but $3 \nmid 2 + \sqrt{-5}$ (would force $3 \mid 2$ in $\mathbb{Z}$) and $3 \nmid 2 - \sqrt{-5}$. So $3$ is irreducible but not prime, and $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD.

\item In $\F_3[x]$, decide whether $x^2 + 1$ is irreducible; if reducible, factor it.

\textit{Answer.} Test for roots in $\F_3$: $0^2 + 1 = 1$, $1^2 + 1 = 2$, $2^2 + 1 = 5 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$. No root, and a degree-$2$ polynomial over a field with no root is irreducible. So $x^2 + 1$ is irreducible in $\F_3[x]$. (Contrast: over $\F_2$, $x^2 + 1 = (x+1)^2$; over $\F_5$, $x^2 + 1 = (x+2)(x-2)$. The $\F_3$ case is inert.)

\item In $\mathbb{Z}$, factor $a = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5^2$ and $b = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5 \cdot 7$, and read off $\gcd$ and $\lcm$ by taking $\min/\max$ exponents.

\textit{Answer.} Here $a = 600$, $b = 630$.
\[
\gcd(a,b) = 2^{\min(3,1)} 3^{\min(1,2)} 5^{\min(2,1)} 7^{\min(0,1)} = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 = 30,
\]
\[
\lcm(a,b) = 2^{3} 3^{2} 5^{2} 7^{1} = 8 \cdot 9 \cdot 25 \cdot 7 = 12600.
\]
\textit{Check.} $\gcd \cdot \lcm = 30 \cdot 12600 = 378000 = 600 \cdot 630 = ab$. Consistent.

\item Suppose $R$ is a UFD and $p$ is irreducible. Prove $p$ is prime, appealing to uniqueness of factorization.

\textit{Answer.} Suppose $p \mid ab$, say $ab = pc$. If $a$ or $b$ is $0$ or a unit, then $p$ divides $a$ or $b$ directly (e.g.\ $b = a^{-1} pc$ if $a$ is a unit). Otherwise factor $a$, $b$, and $c$ into irreducibles, absorbing $c$ into $p$ if $c$ is a unit. Then
\[
\Big(\prod_i p_i\Big)\Big(\prod_j q_j\Big) = p \cdot \prod_k r_k
\]
are two irreducible factorizations of $ab$. By uniqueness the irreducible $p$ on the right is an associate of some factor on the left, so $p \sim p_i$ for some $i$ (whence $p \mid a$) or $p \sim q_j$ for some $j$ (whence $p \mid b$). Hence $p$ is prime.

\item In $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, list the associates of $1 + i$, show $1 - i$ is among them, and deduce $2 = -i(1+i)^2$.

\textit{Answer.} $\units{\mathbb{Z}[i]} = \{1, -1, i, -i\}$, so the associates of $1+i$ are
\[
1+i,\quad -(1+i) = -1-i,\quad i(1+i) = -1+i,\quad -i(1+i) = 1-i.
\]
Thus $1 - i = -i(1+i)$ is an associate of $1+i$. Then
\[
2 = (1+i)(1-i) = (1+i)\big(-i(1+i)\big) = -i(1+i)^2,
\]
with $1+i$ irreducible ($\Nm(1+i) = 2$), so $2$ ramifies. \textit{Check.} $(1+i)^2 = 2i$ and $-i \cdot 2i = 2$. Consistent.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}
\item Prove that an integral domain $R$ is a UFD if and only if every nonzero nonunit is a product of irreducibles \emph{and} every irreducible element of $R$ is prime.

\textit{Answer.} $(\Rightarrow)$ In a UFD factorizations exist by definition, and irreducible $\Longrightarrow$ prime holds (the uniqueness axiom forces it). $(\Leftarrow)$ Existence is the first hypothesis. For uniqueness, suppose $p_1 \cdots p_n = q_1 \cdots q_m$ with all factors irreducible, hence prime. Then $p_1 \mid q_1 \cdots q_m$, so $p_1 \mid q_j$ for some $j$; since $q_j$ is irreducible, $q_j \sim p_1$. Cancel (valid in a domain) and induct on $n$. Thus $n = m$ and the factors match up to associates and order, so $R$ is a UFD.

\item Show $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD by exhibiting an element with two essentially different irreducible factorizations, proving each factor irreducible by the norm.

\textit{Answer.} Take
\[
21 = 3 \cdot 7 = (1+2\sqrt{-5})(1-2\sqrt{-5}),
\]
with $\Nm(3) = 9$, $\Nm(7) = 49$, $\Nm(1 \pm 2\sqrt{-5}) = 1 + 20 = 21$. Each factor is irreducible: $a^2 + 5b^2 = 3$ and $a^2 + 5b^2 = 7$ are unsolvable in $\mathbb{Z}$, so $3$ and $7$ are irreducible; a proper factor of $1 \pm 2\sqrt{-5}$ would have norm $3$ or $7$, impossible, so $1 \pm 2\sqrt{-5}$ are irreducible. No factor on the left is an associate of one on the right: the units are only $\pm 1$, and the norms $9, 49$ on the left differ from $21, 21$ on the right. Hence the two factorizations of $21$ are essentially different, and $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD.

\item Prove Gauss's Lemma: with $R$ a UFD, the product of two primitive polynomials in $R[x]$ is primitive (so $\cont(fg) \sim \cont(f)\cont(g)$). State where content is used.

\textit{Answer.} Let $f, g \in R[x]$ be primitive. If $fg$ were not primitive, some irreducible $p$ (hence prime, since $R$ is a UFD) would divide every coefficient of $fg$. Reduce mod $p$: in $(R/\langle p\rangle)[x]$, an integral domain, $\bar f \, \bar g = 0$, so $\bar f = 0$ or $\bar g = 0$, i.e.\ $p \mid \cont(f)$ or $p \mid \cont(g)$, contradicting primitivity. For the general formula, write $f = \cont(f) f_0$, $g = \cont(g) g_0$ with $f_0, g_0$ primitive; then $fg = \cont(f)\cont(g)\, f_0 g_0$ with $f_0 g_0$ primitive by the first part, so $\cont(fg) \sim \cont(f)\cont(g)$. Content enters twice: to reduce the general claim to the primitive case, and to make $R/\langle p\rangle$ a domain by invoking the primality of the irreducible $p$.

\item Let $p$ be a rational prime with $p \equiv 1 \bmod 4$. Using that $p$ is a sum of two squares, show $p$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ and describe its factorization up to units.

\textit{Answer.} Since $p \equiv 1 \bmod 4$, $p = a^2 + b^2 = (a+bi)(a-bi)$. Now $\Nm(a+bi) = p$ is prime, so $a+bi$ and $a-bi$ are irreducible; they are non-associate, since their ratio is not a unit (a unit multiple would force $a = \pm b$ or $ab = 0$, making $p = a^2 + b^2$ degenerate, not an odd prime). Thus $p$ splits into two non-associate irreducibles, hence is reducible in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, with $p = \pi \overline{\pi}$ up to units. \textbf{Example:} $13 = 3^2 + 2^2 = (3+2i)(3-2i)$.

\item Give a domain with a nonzero nonunit having \emph{no} factorization into irreducibles, showing existence can fail without an ascending-chain hypothesis. Use $R = \mathbb{Z} + x\mathbb{Q}[x]$.

\textit{Answer.} Let $R = \mathbb{Z} + x\mathbb{Q}[x]$ (polynomials with integer constant term and rational higher coefficients). The element $x$ is a nonzero nonunit. But $x = 2 \cdot \tfrac{x}{2}$ with $\tfrac{x}{2} \in R$, and $\tfrac{x}{2} = 2 \cdot \tfrac{x}{4}$, etc., giving an infinite chain of proper divisors $x, \tfrac{x}{2}, \tfrac{x}{4}, \dots$. Equivalently the principal ideals ascend without stabilizing,
\[
\langle x\rangle \subsetneq \langle \tfrac{x}{2}\rangle \subsetneq \langle \tfrac{x}{4}\rangle \subsetneq \cdots,
\]
so ACC on principal ideals fails. This chain alone does not rule out a factorization of $x$, so argue directly: the units of $R$ are $\pm 1$, and a nonzero $f \in R$ with constant term $0$ is never irreducible, since $f = 2 \cdot \tfrac{f}{2}$ with $2$ and $\tfrac{f}{2}$ nonunits of $R$. So every irreducible of $R$ has nonzero constant term, hence so does every product of irreducibles, while $x$ has constant term $0$. Hence $x$ admits no finite factorization into irreducibles, and existence of irreducible factorizations is not automatic in a domain; UFDs must assume it.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item Draw the strict implication chain $\text{ED} \Longrightarrow \text{PID} \Longrightarrow \text{UFD} \Longrightarrow \text{domain}$ and give a one-line witness ring for the failure of each reverse arrow.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\text{ED} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{PID} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{UFD} \arrow[r, Rightarrow] & \text{domain}
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\textit{Answer (reverse arrows all fail).}
\begin{itemize}
\item $\text{PID} \not\Longrightarrow \text{ED}$: witness $\mathbb{Z}\!\left[\tfrac{1+\sqrt{-19}}{2}\right]$, a PID with no Euclidean function.
\item $\text{UFD} \not\Longrightarrow \text{PID}$: witness $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, a UFD where $\langle 2, x\rangle$ is not principal.
\item $\text{domain} \not\Longrightarrow \text{UFD}$: witness $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, a domain with $6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$.
\end{itemize}

\item For a UFD $R$ and a prime $p$, draw the quotient map $R \twoheadrightarrow R/\langle p\rangle$ and explain, via primeness (not mere irreducibility), why the target is an integral domain.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, two heads, "\pi"] & R/\langle p\rangle
\end{tikzcd}
\qquad \ker\pi = \langle p\rangle,\quad R/\langle p\rangle\ \text{a domain}
\]
\textit{Answer.} $p$ prime $\Longleftrightarrow \langle p\rangle$ a prime ideal $\Longleftrightarrow R/\langle p\rangle$ an integral domain. The map $\pi$ is surjective with kernel $\langle p\rangle$; the target is a domain precisely because $p$ is \emph{prime}. Irreducibility alone would not suffice in a non-UFD: in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$, $2$ is irreducible but $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]/\langle 2\rangle$ has zero divisors (the image of $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ is a nonzero nilpotent). In a UFD irreducible $=$ prime, so for irreducible $p$ the quotient is a domain. (Contrast the PID case, where $\langle p\rangle$ is maximal and $R/\langle p\rangle$ is a \emph{field}.)

\item Draw the relationship $\{\text{prime}\} \hookrightarrow \{\text{irreducible}\}$ (always), with a dashed reverse arrow labeled ``in a UFD,'' and instantiate the failure of the reverse arrow in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=small, column sep=huge]
\{\text{prime}\} \arrow[r, hook, "{\text{always}}"] & \{\text{irreducible}\} \arrow[l, bend left=25, dashed, "{\text{in a UFD}}"]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\textit{Answer.} The solid hook is the body's ``prime $\Longrightarrow$ irreducible,'' valid in any domain. The dashed back-arrow ``irreducible $\Longrightarrow$ prime'' holds in every UFD, but not in every domain. Failure in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$: $2$ is irreducible but not prime, since $2 \mid 6 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ while $2 \nmid 1+\sqrt{-5}$ and $2 \nmid 1-\sqrt{-5}$. So the dashed arrow is absent there, which is exactly why $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD.

\item For $R$ a UFD with $F = \Frac(R)$, draw the content factorization $f \mapsto \cont(f) \cdot f_0$ (with $f_0$ primitive) and relate irreducibility in $R[x]$ to $F[x]$ via Gauss's Lemma.
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
R[x] \ni f \arrow[r, mapsto, "\cont"] & \cont(f) \cdot f_0
& f_0\ \text{irred.\ in}\ R[x] \arrow[r, Leftrightarrow, "{\text{Gauss}}"] & f_0\ \text{irred.\ in}\ F[x]
\end{tikzcd}
\]
\textit{Answer.} Every nonzero $f \in R[x]$ factors as $f = \cont(f) f_0$ with $f_0$ primitive. The irreducibles of $R[x]$ are (a) the irreducibles of $R$ (constants) and (b) primitive polynomials irreducible in $F[x]$. Gauss's Lemma is the bridge: a primitive $f_0$ is irreducible in $R[x]$ iff it is irreducible in $F[x]$. \textbf{Instantiate:} $x^2 - 2 \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ is primitive and irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, hence irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$; whereas $2x + 4 = 2(x+2)$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ (content $2$ a nonunit) but a unit times an irreducible in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$, where $2$ is a unit.
\end{exers}

We have seen that the ring of Gauss integers $\mathbb{Z}[i]=\{\,a+bi\st a,b\in\mathbb{Z}\,\}$ is a Euclidean domain, hence a PID and a UFD: every nonzero nonunit is a product of prime elements, called \emph{Gauss primes}, unique up to units and order. The units are $\{\pm 1,\pm i\}$. Our goal is to \emph{classify} the Gauss primes by relating them to the rational primes $2,3,5,7,\dots$ of $\mathbb{Z}$, and to harvest from that classification Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares.

The whole story is governed by the multiplicative \emph{norm}
\[
\Nm(a+bi)=(a+bi)(a-bi)=a^2+b^2=\abs{a+bi}^2\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0},
\]
which satisfies $\Nm(\alpha\beta)=\Nm(\alpha)\Nm(\beta)$. A Gauss integer $\alpha$ is a unit iff $\Nm(\alpha)=1$. We write $\overline{\alpha}=a-bi$ for the complex conjugate, so $\Nm(\alpha)=\alpha\overline{\alpha}$.

This same equation $\pi\overline{\pi}=p_1\cdots p_k$ holds in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, but the right side need not be a prime factorization there. Continue factoring each $p_j$ in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ to reach a Gauss-prime factorization. By unique factorization in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, the Gauss primes obtained must be associates of the two factors $\pi$ and $\overline{\pi}$. Hence at most two prime factors occur, so $\Nm(\pi)$ is either a rational prime or a product of two rational primes; in the latter case matching $\pi,\overline{\pi}$ against the factors forces the two to be equal, so $\Nm(\pi)=p^2$.

\textbf{(b)} A rational prime $p$ is not a unit of $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, so some Gauss prime $\pi$ divides $p$. Then $\overline{\pi}$ divides $\overline{p}=p$ as well, so $\Nm(\pi)=\pi\overline{\pi}$ divides $p^2$ in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ and (being a positive integer) in $\mathbb{Z}$. Thus $\Nm(\pi)\in\{p,p^2\}$. If $\Nm(\pi)=p^2$ then $\pi$ and $p$ are associates and $p$ is itself a Gauss prime; if $\Nm(\pi)=p$ then $p=\pi\overline{\pi}$ splits.

\textbf{(d)} We show (i)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iii), (i)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iv), and (ii)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iv); part (c) then follows since the inert primes are precisely those that are \emph{not} of the split type.

\emph{(i)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iii).} If $p=\pi\overline{\pi}$ with $\pi=a+bi$ a Gauss prime, then $p=a^2+b^2$ is a sum of two squares. Conversely if $p=a^2+b^2$, then $p=(a-bi)(a+bi)$ factors in $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, and by (a) each factor has norm $p$, hence is a Gauss prime; so $p$ is a product of conjugate Gauss primes.

\emph{(i)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iv).} The quotient $R=\mathbb{Z}[i]/(p)$ may be built in two steps from $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Killing $x^2+1$ first yields $\mathbb{Z}[i]$, then killing $p$ yields $R$; killing $p$ first yields $\F_p[x]$, then killing $x^2+1$ yields $R$ again. So $R\cong\F_p[x]/(x^2+1)$. Now $(p)$ is a maximal ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[i]$ iff $p$ is a Gauss prime; equivalently $R$ is a field iff $x^2+1$ is irreducible in $\F_p[x]$. Thus $p$ is \emph{inert} iff $x^2+1$ is irreducible mod $p$, i.e. iff $-1$ is \emph{not} a square mod $p$. Negating, $p$ splits iff $-1$ is a square mod $p$, which is (iv). (For $p=2$, $x^2+1=(x+1)^2$ in $\F_2[x]$ and $-1\equiv 1$ is a square; $2=-i(1+i)^2$ is ramified.)

\emph{(ii)$\Longleftrightarrow$(iv).} It is clear that $-1$ is a square modulo $2$. For odd $p$, the multiplicative group $\F_p^\times$ is cyclic of order $p-1$. An element $\overline a$ solves $x^2\equiv -1$ iff $\overline a$ has order $4$ (its square then has order $2$, and $-1$ is the unique element of order $2$). And $\F_p^\times$ contains an element of order $4$ iff $4\mid p-1$, i.e. iff $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$. Hence $-1$ is a square mod $p$ iff $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ (or $p=2$), which is (ii).
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[The polynomial ring in one variable]
Let $R$ be a commutative ring. The \emph{polynomial ring} $R[x]$ is the set of all formal
finite sums
\[
f(x)=a_n x^n + a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots+a_1 x + a_0,\qquad a_i\in R,
\]
where the \emph{coefficient} $a_i$ lies in $R$ for each $i$ and only finitely many are
nonzero. If $a_n\neq 0$ we call $n=\deg f$ the \emph{degree} of $f$, $a_n$ the
\emph{leading coefficient} $\LC(f)$, and $a_n x^n$ the \emph{leading term}. A polynomial
is \emph{monic} if $\LC(f)=1$. The zero polynomial has, by convention, $\deg 0=-\infty$
(equivalently, undefined); it has no leading term. Polynomials of degree $0$ together with
$0$ are the \emph{constants} $R\subseteq R[x]$.

Addition and multiplication are: with $f=\sum_i a_i x^i$ and $g=\sum_j b_j x^j$,
\[
f+g=\sum_k (a_k+b_k)\,x^k,\qquad
fg=\sum_k\Big(\textstyle\sum_{i+j=k} a_i b_j\Big)x^k .
\]
\end{definition}
title: The polynomial ring in one variable
Computing $f+g$ and $fg$ by hand

latex:
\begin{wex}{Multiplying in $\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}[x]$}
Compute $(2x^2+x+1)(x+2)$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\wrec Convolution multiplication with coefficient arithmetic done mod $3$.
\wsol
Expand, then reduce each coefficient mod $3$:
\[
(2x^2+x+1)(x+2)=2x^3+4x^2+x^2+2x+x+2=2x^3+5x^2+3x+2 .
\]
Reduce mod $3$: $5\equiv 2$, $3\equiv 0$, so
\[
(2x^2+x+1)(x+2)=2x^3+2x^2+2 \in \mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}[x].
\]
\textit{Check (convolution by slots).} $a=(1,1,2)$ for $(a_0,a_1,a_2)$, $b=(2,1)$.
$c_0=1\cdot2=2$; $c_1=1\cdot2+1\cdot1=3\equiv0$; $c_2=2\cdot2+1\cdot1=5\equiv2$;
$c_3=2\cdot1=2$. Coefficients $(2,0,2,2)$ match. $\deg=3=2+1$, as expected since
$\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}$ is a field (a domain), so no degree drop. \checkmark
\end{wex}
title: Multiplying in $\mathbb{Z}/(3)\mathbb{Z}[x]$

latex:
\begin{wex}{Degree can drop in $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]$}
In $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]$ compute $(2x+1)^2$ and report its degree.
\wrec $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ has the zero divisor $2$ ($2\cdot2=4\equiv0$); the top coefficient of a
product may vanish.
\wsol
\[
(2x+1)^2=4x^2+4x+1 .
\]
Reduce mod $4$: $4\equiv0$, $4\equiv0$, so $(2x+1)^2=1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\textit{Check.} The leading coefficients multiply to $2\cdot2=4\equiv0$, so the $x^2$ term
dies and the $x$ term dies too. Result is the constant $1$, of degree $0$, while
$\deg(2x+1)+\deg(2x+1)=1+1=2$. Hence $\deg(fg)<\deg f+\deg g$. This is impossible over an
integral domain, but $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ is not a domain. As a bonus, $2x+1$ is a \emph{unit} of
$\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]$ with inverse itself. \checkmark
\end{wex}
title: Degree can drop in $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]$

latex:
\begin{wex}{Adding and multiplying in $\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}[x]$}
In $\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}[x]$, let $f=3x^2+4$ and $g=2x+3$. Compute $f+g$ and $fg$.
\wrec Slot addition and convolution, all coefficients mod $5$.
\wsol
$f=3x^2+0\cdot x+4$, $g=0\cdot x^2+2x+3$.
\[
f+g=3x^2+2x+7\equiv 3x^2+2x+2 .
\]
For $fg$: $c_0=4\cdot3=12\equiv2$; $c_1=4\cdot2=8\equiv3$; $c_2=3\cdot3=9\equiv4$;
$c_3=3\cdot2=6\equiv1$. So
\[
fg=x^3+4x^2+3x+2 \in\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}[x].
\]
\textit{Check.} $\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$ is a field, so $\deg(fg)=2+1=3$ and $\LC(fg)=3\cdot2=6\equiv1$,
matching the $x^3$ coefficient. \checkmark
\end{wex}
title: Adding and multiplying in $\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}[x]$

latex:
\begin{wex}{A product over $\mathbb{Z}$ with telescoping middle terms}
Compute $(x^2+x+1)(x-1)$ in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\wrec Ordinary convolution over the domain $\mathbb{Z}$; watch cancellation in the interior
coefficients.
\wsol
\[
(x^2+x+1)(x-1)=x^3+x^2+x-x^2-x-1=x^3-1 .
\]
\textit{Check.} $c_0=1\cdot(-1)=-1$; $c_1=1\cdot(-1)+1\cdot1=0$;
$c_2=1\cdot(-1)+1\cdot1=0$; $c_3=1\cdot1=1$. So $x^3-1$. Interior cancellation does
\emph{not} lower the degree because the top coefficient $1\cdot1=1\neq0$. \checkmark
\end{wex}
title: A product over $\mathbb{Z}$ with telescoping middle terms

\begin{definition}[Polynomials in several variables, by iteration]
Define $R[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ recursively by
\[
R[x_1,\dots,x_n]:=\big(R[x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}]\big)[x_n].
\]
Concretely an element is a finite sum of \emph{monomials}
$a\,x_1^{d_1}x_2^{d_2}\cdots x_n^{d_n}$ with $a\in R$. The (total) \emph{degree} of such a
monomial is $d_1+\dots+d_n$, and the \emph{total degree} of $f\neq 0$ is the maximum total
degree of a monomial appearing with nonzero coefficient. A polynomial is \emph{homogeneous}
of degree $d$ if every monomial has total degree $d$.
\end{definition}
title: Polynomials in several variables, by iteration

latex:
\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$ and its total degree}
Let $f=x^2y+3xy^2+y+5\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$. Find the total degree of $f$, view $f$ in
$(\mathbb{Z}[x])[y]$, and compute $f\cdot y$.
\wrec Total degree counts the largest $d_x+d_y$; iteration groups by powers of $y$.
\wsol
Monomial total degrees: $x^2y\!:2{+}1{=}3$; $3xy^2\!:1{+}2{=}3$; $y\!:1$; $5\!:0$. So
$\deg f=3$. As an element of $(\mathbb{Z}[x])[y]$:
\[
f=(3x)\,y^2+(x^2+1)\,y+5,\qquad \deg_y f=2,\ \LC_y(f)=3x .
\]
Multiplying by $y$ shifts every $y$-power up by one:
\[
f\cdot y=x^2y^2+3xy^3+y^2+5y,\qquad \deg(f\cdot y)=4 .
\]
\textit{Check.} $3x\cdot y^2\cdot y=3xy^3$ has total degree $1+3=4$, the new maximum;
since $\mathbb{Z}$ is a domain, $\deg(f\cdot y)=\deg f+\deg y=3+1=4$. \checkmark
\end{wex}
title: $\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$ and its total degree

\begin{proof}
Write $f=a_mx^m+\cdots$, $g=b_nx^n+\cdots$ with $a_m=\LC(f)\neq0$, $b_n=\LC(g)\neq0$.
The coefficient of $x^{m+n}$ in $fg$ is $a_mb_n$. Since $R$ is a domain and
$a_m,b_n\neq0$, we have $a_mb_n\neq0$. No monomial of higher degree can occur, so $fg\neq0$,
$\deg(fg)=m+n$, and $\LC(fg)=a_mb_n$. This proves (1) and shows $R[x]$ has no zero divisors,
i.e.\ (3).

For (2): if $u\in\units{R}$ then $u$ is a unit in $R[x]$, so $\units{R}\subseteq\units{R[x]}$.
Conversely, suppose $fg=1$ in $R[x]$. Taking degrees and using (1),
$\deg f+\deg g=\deg 1=0$, and since degrees are nonnegative integers, $\deg f=\deg g=0$.
Thus $f,g\in R$ and $fg=1$ in $R$, so $f\in\units{R}$. Hence
$\units{R[x]}\subseteq\units{R}$.
\end{proof}

latex:
\begin{wex}{Units of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ versus $\mathbb{Q}[x]$}
Determine $\units{\mathbb{Z}[x]}$ and $\units{\mathbb{Q}[x]}$.
\wrec $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ are integral domains, so $\units{R[x]}=\units{R}$.
\wsol
$\mathbb{Z}$ is a domain with $\units{\mathbb{Z}}=\{\pm1\}$, so by Prop.\ 4(2),
$\units{\mathbb{Z}[x]}=\{\,1,\,-1\,\}$. In particular $x$, $2$, and $x+1$ are non-units in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
$\mathbb{Q}$ is a field, so $\units{\mathbb{Q}}=\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$ and
$\units{\mathbb{Q}[x]}=\mathbb{Q}\setminus\{0\}$, the nonzero constants; e.g.\ $\tfrac12$ is a unit but $x$
is not.
\textit{Check (degree argument).} If $fg=1$ in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ then $\deg f=\deg g=0$, so $f,g\in\mathbb{Z}$
with $fg=1$, forcing $f=\pm1$. The same argument over $\mathbb{Q}$ gives nonzero rationals.
\checkmark
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{$2x+1$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]$ but the proposition does not apply}
Show $2x+1\in\units{\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]}$, and explain why this does not contradict Prop.\ 4(2).
\wrec A degree-$1$ unit can only exist when the base ring is \emph{not} a domain.
\wsol
$(2x+1)(2x+1)=4x^2+4x+1=1$ in $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]$ (computed earlier), so $2x+1$ is its own inverse,
hence a unit of degree $1$.
\textit{Check.} Prop.\ 4 requires $R$ to be an integral domain; $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$ is not
($2\cdot2=0$), so $\units{\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}[x]}\neq(\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z})^{\times}$. Indeed the nilpotent $2$ produces
the non-constant unit $1+2x$ (a unit because $2$ is nilpotent: $(1+2x)(1-2x)=1-4x^2=1$).
\checkmark
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{No nontrivial factorization of a linear polynomial over a domain}
Over the domain $\mathbb{Z}$, show $x$ cannot be written as a product of two non-units of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\wrec Pure degree count plus $\units{\mathbb{Z}[x]}=\{\pm1\}$.
\wsol
Suppose $x=fg$ with $f,g\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$. By additivity $\deg f+\deg g=\deg x=1$, so one factor,
say $g$, has degree $0$: $g=c\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then $f=ax+b$ and $cf=x$ forces $ca=1$, $cb=0$, so
$c\in\{\pm1\}$, i.e.\ $c$ is a unit. Hence any factorization of $x$ has a unit factor; $x$ is
irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\textit{Check.} The leading coefficient equation $\LC(f)\LC(g)=1$ in $\mathbb{Z}$ forces a unit
leading coefficient. \checkmark
\end{wex}

Decide whether $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a domain and whether $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a domain.
\wrec $R$ a domain $\Rightarrow R[x]$ a domain; $R$ with zero divisors $\Rightarrow R[x]$
has them too.
\wsol
$\mathbb{Z}$ is a domain, so $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a domain by Prop.\ 4(3). $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$ is \emph{not} a domain
($2\cdot3=0$), and these zero divisors persist as constants in $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}[x]$:
$\bar2\cdot\bar3=\bar0$ with $\bar2,\bar3\neq0$. So $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is not a domain.
\textit{Check.} $\deg$ additivity fails in $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}[x]$, e.g.\ $(3x+1)(2x)=6x^2+2x=2x$ drops
from degree $2$ to degree $1$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{proof}
Consider the \emph{reduction-of-coefficients} map. Reducing each coefficient mod $I$ via
$R\twoheadrightarrow R/I$, $a\mapsto\bar a$, induces a ring homomorphism
\[
\varphi: R[x]\longrightarrow (R/I)[x],\qquad
\varphi\Big(\textstyle\sum_i a_i x^i\Big)=\textstyle\sum_i \bar a_i\, x^i .
\]
It is a homomorphism because reduction mod $I$ respects the coefficient formulas for sums
($\overline{a_k+b_k}=\bar a_k+\bar b_k$) and products
($\overline{\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j}=\sum_{i+j=k}\bar a_i\bar b_j$). It is surjective since any
$\sum \bar c_i x^i$ is hit by $\sum c_i x^i$. Its kernel is exactly the polynomials all of
whose coefficients reduce to $0$, i.e.\ all of whose coefficients lie in $I$:
$\ker\varphi=I[x]$. In particular $I[x]$ is an ideal (a kernel), proving (1), and the
First Isomorphism Theorem gives
\[
R[x]/I[x]\;\cong\;(R/I)[x],
\]
proving (2). For (3): if $I$ is prime then $R/I$ is an integral domain, so by Prop.\ 4(3)
$(R/I)[x]$ is an integral domain; hence $R[x]/I[x]\cong(R/I)[x]$ is a domain, which says
exactly that $I[x]$ is a prime ideal of $R[x]$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[{The reduction map $\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\F_p[x]$}]
The most important instance is $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $I=(p)$ for a prime $p$. Then $\mathbb{Z}/(p)=\F_p$ and
Prop.\ 2 gives the surjective \emph{reduction mod $p$} homomorphism with kernel $(p)[x]=(p)$
(the polynomials with all coefficients divisible by $p$):
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\mathbb{Z}[x] \arrow[r, two heads, "\bmod p"] & \F_p[x]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is the polynomial ring over the integers, a commutative domain. $\F_p[x]$ is the polynomial ring over the prime field $\F_p = \mathbb{Z}/(p)$, also a commutative domain (in fact a Euclidean domain, since $\F_p$ is a field).
\dgi{Arrows:} The single arrow is the \emph{reduction-mod-$p$} ring homomorphism $\varphi: \mathbb{Z}[x] \to \F_p[x]$ defined by $\varphi(\sum_i a_i x^i) = \sum_i \bar{a}_i x^i$, where $\bar{a}_i = a_i \bmod p$. It is surjective (every polynomial in $\F_p[x]$ is hit by any lift of its coefficients to $\mathbb{Z}$), hence the double-head arrow.
\dgi{What commutes:} This is a single arrow, so there is no path equality to verify. The key identity is $\ker \varphi = (p)[x] = (p)$, the set of polynomials all of whose coefficients are divisible by $p$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} $\varphi$ is a ring homomorphism because coefficient-reduction mod $p$ is itself a ring homomorphism $\mathbb{Z} \to \F_p$, and polynomial arithmetic (sum and convolution formulas) is defined coefficient-by-coefficient, so $\varphi(f+g) = \varphi(f)+\varphi(g)$ and $\varphi(fg) = \varphi(f)\varphi(g)$ follow termwise.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The surjectivity and kernel computation give, by the First Isomorphism Theorem, $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p) \cong \F_p[x]$. Since $\F_p[x]$ is a domain, $(p)$ is prime in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. This single arrow \emph{is} the engine of the reduction-mod-$p$ irreducibility test: if $f$ is monic and $\varphi(f)$ is irreducible in $\F_p[x]$, then $f$ is irreducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. (Monic cannot be dropped: $f=3x+3=3(x+1)$ is reducible in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, yet $\varphi(f)=x+1$ is irreducible in $\F_2[x]$.)
\dgi{Concrete example:} With $p=3$: $\varphi(2x^2 + 3x + 7) = 2x^2 + 0\cdot x + 1 = 2x^2 + 1 \in \F_3[x]$. The polynomial $3x \in \ker\varphi$ since all coefficients are divisible by $3$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think $\varphi$ sends $x \mapsto p$ or changes the variable; it does not. Only the \emph{coefficients} are reduced; the indeterminate $x$ is unchanged. Also, surjectivity does not mean $\varphi$ has a ring-homomorphism section: the map $\F_p[x] \to \mathbb{Z}[x]$ sending $\bar{a}_i \mapsto a_i$ (any lift) is a set map but not a ring map.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that reducing coefficients mod a prime $p$ gives a surjective ring homomorphism from $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ onto the simpler Euclidean domain $\F_p[x]$, whose kernel is exactly the ideal $(p)$, proving $(p)$ prime and enabling the reduction-mod-$p$ irreducibility criterion.
\end{dgx}
so $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p)\cong\F_p[x]$. Because $(p)$ is prime in $\mathbb{Z}$, $(p)$ is prime in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ and
$\F_p[x]$ is an integral domain. This is the engine behind the reduction-mod-$p$
irreducibility test of \S9.4.
\end{remark}

latex:
\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p,x)\cong\F_p$ via a two-step reduction}
Show $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p,x)\cong\F_p$ for a prime $p$, identifying the maps.
\wrec The ideal $(p,x)$ kills coefficients mod $p$ and then evaluates at $x=0$; compose
reduction with evaluation.
\wsol
Use the evaluation-at-$0$ homomorphism composed with reduction mod $p$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
\mathbb{Z}[x] \arrow[r, two heads, "\bmod p"] & \F_p[x] \arrow[r, two heads, "x\,\mapsto\,0"] & \F_p
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is the polynomial ring over $\mathbb{Z}$. $\F_p[x]$ is the Euclidean domain of polynomials over the prime field $\F_p = \mathbb{Z}/(p)$. $\F_p$ is the prime field itself, viewed here as the codomain of evaluation at $0$.
\dgi{Arrows:} The left arrow is the surjective reduction-mod-$p$ homomorphism $\varphi: \mathbb{Z}[x] \twoheadrightarrow \F_p[x]$, $\sum a_i x^i \mapsto \sum \bar{a}_i x^i$. The right arrow is the surjective evaluation-at-$0$ homomorphism $\mathrm{ev}_0: \F_p[x] \twoheadrightarrow \F_p$, $\sum \bar{a}_i x^i \mapsto \bar{a}_0$. Both are surjective ring homomorphisms.
\dgi{What commutes:} The composite $\Phi = \mathrm{ev}_0 \circ \varphi: \mathbb{Z}[x] \to \F_p$ satisfies $\Phi(\sum a_i x^i) = \bar{a}_0$, the constant term of $f$ reduced mod $p$. The kernel of the composite is $\ker \Phi = (p, x)$, the ideal generated by $p$ and $x$ in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} A generic $f = \sum a_i x^i$ travels along the top: first reduce coefficients to get $\sum \bar{a}_i x^i$, then evaluate at $0$ to get $\bar{a}_0$. The composite sends $f \mapsto \bar{a}_0 \in \F_p$. This is the constant term of $f$ reduced mod $p$; any $f$ with $p \mid a_0$ or with $a_0 = 0$ lies in $\ker \Phi$, confirming $\ker \Phi = (p) + (x) = (p, x)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram decomposes the maximal ideal $(p, x) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}[x]$ into two successive quotients, making clear why $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p,x) \cong \F_p$: first kill the prime $p$ from coefficients, then kill the variable $x$ by evaluation. The result is a field, so $(p, x)$ is maximal in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} With $p = 3$ and $f = 6x^2 + 4x + 7$: after reduction mod $3$, $\varphi(f) = 0 \cdot x^2 + x + 1 = x + 1 \in \F_3[x]$; then $\mathrm{ev}_0(x+1) = 1 \in \F_3$. So $\Phi(f) = \bar{7} = 1$, which equals $\overline{a_0} = \bar{7} = 1$. \checkmark
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes think $(p, x)$ consists only of multiples of $p$ and multiples of $x$, forgetting that their \emph{sum} $ap + bx$ (with $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$) is the general element. In particular $f = 7 \in (p, x)$ only when $p \mid 7$; otherwise $7 \notin (3, x)$ even though $7$ has no $x$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the two-step surjection -- reduce mod $p$, then evaluate at $x = 0$ -- decomposes the maximal ideal $(p, x) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}[x]$ into two successive kernels and proves $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p, x) \cong \F_p$ without needing a separate generator-by-generator argument.
\end{dgx}
The composite $\Phi:\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\F_p$ sends $f=\sum a_i x^i\mapsto \overline{a_0}$ (the constant
term mod $p$). It is surjective. Its kernel consists of all $f$ with $\overline{a_0}=0$,
i.e.\ $p\mid a_0$, equivalently $f\in(p)+(x)=(p,x)$:
\[
\ker\Phi=(p,x).
\]
By the First Isomorphism Theorem,
\[
\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p,x)\;\cong\;\F_p .
\]
\textit{Check.} $|\F_p|=p$, finite, and $\F_p$ is a field, so $(p,x)$ is a maximal ideal of
$\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Concretely $\bar f=\overline{f(0)}=\overline{a_0}\in\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$. With $p=3$,
$f=6x^2+4x+7$ maps to $7\bmod 3=1$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p)\cong\F_p[x]$ explicitly}
Identify the quotient $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p)$ and show $(p)$ is prime in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\wrec Prop.\ 2 with $R=\mathbb{Z}$, $I=(p)$: $(p)[x]=(p)$ and the quotient is $(\mathbb{Z}/(p))[x]$.
\wsol
Every coefficient is reduced mod $p$; the reduction map $\varphi:\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\F_p[x]$ has kernel
$(p)$, so
\[
\mathbb{Z}[x]/(p)\;\cong\;\F_p[x].
\]
Since $\F_p$ is a field (hence a domain) and a domain's polynomial ring is a domain,
$\F_p[x]$ is a domain; therefore $(p)$ is a \emph{prime} ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ by Prop.\ 2(3).
\textit{Check.} $(p)$ is not maximal in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$: $\F_p[x]$ is not a field (e.g.\ $x$ has no
inverse), and indeed $(p)\subsetneq(p,x)\subsetneq\mathbb{Z}[x]$ shows a strictly larger proper
ideal. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Factoring across the reduction map $\mathbb{Z}[x]\to\F_5[x]$}
Reduce $f=x^2+6x+10\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$ mod $5$ and use the quotient $\F_5[x]$ to factor the image.

factorizations; work in the smaller ring $\F_5[x]$.
\wsol
Reduce coefficients mod $5$: $6\equiv1$, $10\equiv0$, so $\bar f=x^2+x=x(x+1)$ in $\F_5[x]$.
Thus the image factors. (Over $\mathbb{Z}$ itself $f=x^2+6x+10$ is irreducible by the quadratic
formula: discriminant $36-40=-4<0$.)
\textit{Check.} Evaluate the factorization in $\F_5$ at, say, $x=2$: $\bar f(2)=4+2=6\equiv1$,
and $x(x+1)\big|_{2}=2\cdot3=6\equiv1$; they agree. Reduction is the homomorphism
$\varphi$ of Prop.\ 2 with $I=(5)$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{$I$ prime $\Rightarrow I[x]$ prime, and $I$ not prime $\Rightarrow I[x]$ not prime}
In $R=\mathbb{Z}$ compare $I=(7)$ (prime) with $I=(6)$ (not prime), and decide whether $I[x]$ is
prime in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
\wrec Prop.\ 2(3): primeness of $I[x]$ is controlled by whether $R/I$ is a domain.
\wsol
For $I=(7)$: $\mathbb{Z}/(7)=\F_7$ is a domain, so $(7)[x]=(7)$ is a prime ideal of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, and
$\mathbb{Z}[x]/(7)\cong\F_7[x]$, a domain.
For $I=(6)$: $\mathbb{Z}/(6)=\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$ is \emph{not} a domain ($\bar2\cdot\bar3=\bar0$). Hence
$(6)[x]=(6)$ is \emph{not} prime in $\mathbb{Z}[x]$: the constants $\bar2,\bar3$ multiply to $\bar0$
in $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(6)\cong\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}[x]$, i.e.\ $2\cdot3=6\in(6)$ while $2,3\notin(6)$.
\textit{Check.} The witness $2\cdot3=6\in(6)[x]$ with $2\notin(6)[x]$, $3\notin(6)[x]$ is
exactly a failure of the prime-ideal property. For $(7)$, no such constant witness exists
because $7$ is prime. \checkmark
\end{wex}

\begin{wex}{Quotient by $(x)$: evaluation at $0$}
Identify $R[x]/(x)$ for any commutative ring $R$, and apply it to $R=\mathbb{Z}[y]$.

\begin{remark}[{Summary diagram: extend an ideal vs.\ reduce coefficients}]
The two viewpoints of Prop.\ 2 are the two legs of one commutative square. Reducing
coefficients of $R[x]$ by $I[x]$ is the same as forming polynomials over the reduced ring
$R/I$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=large, column sep=large]
R \arrow[r, hook] \arrow[d, two heads, "\bmod I"'] & R[x] \arrow[d, two heads, "{\bmod\,I[x]}"] \\
R/I \arrow[r, hook] & (R/I)[x]
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Top-left: $R$, a commutative ring. Top-right: $R[x]$, the polynomial ring over $R$. Bottom-left: $R/I$, the quotient ring of $R$ by an ideal $I$. Bottom-right: $(R/I)[x]$, the polynomial ring over the quotient ring $R/I$.
\dgi{Arrows:} Top horizontal: the canonical inclusion $R \hookrightarrow R[x]$, sending a constant $r \mapsto r$ (the degree-$0$ polynomial). Left vertical: the surjection $R \twoheadrightarrow R/I$, $r \mapsto r + I = \bar{r}$, the standard quotient map. Right vertical: the surjection $R[x] \twoheadrightarrow (R/I)[x]$, $\sum a_i x^i \mapsto \sum \bar{a}_i x^i$, reducing each coefficient mod $I$; its kernel is $I[x]$. Bottom horizontal: the canonical inclusion $R/I \hookrightarrow (R/I)[x]$, $\bar{r} \mapsto \bar{r}$ as constant polynomials.
\dgi{What commutes:} Going right-then-down equals going down-then-right: for $r \in R$, the path $r \xrightarrow{\text{incl}} r \xrightarrow{\bmod I[x]} \bar{r}$ equals $r \xrightarrow{\bmod I} \bar{r} \xrightarrow{\text{incl}} \bar{r}$. Both composites send $r \in R$ to the constant polynomial $\bar{r} \in (R/I)[x]$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Chase $r \in R$: right-then-down gives $r \mapsto r \in R[x] \mapsto \bar{r} \in (R/I)[x]$. Down-then-right gives $r \mapsto \bar{r} \in R/I \mapsto \bar{r} \in (R/I)[x]$. Both land at the same constant polynomial $\bar{r}$. The right vertical map is well-defined on $R[x]$ coefficientwise; each coefficient's image $a_i + I$ does not depend on the representative $a_i$ chosen from its coset because all representatives differ by an element of $I$, which maps to $0$ in $R/I$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The square encodes the isomorphism $R[x]/I[x] \cong (R/I)[x]$ (Proposition 2(2)) in diagrammatic form. It shows that two operations -- extend first then reduce, vs.\ reduce first then extend -- commute: you can reduce coefficients before or after forming the polynomial ring and get the same ring.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $R = \mathbb{Z}$, $I = (p)$. The square becomes $\mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Z}[x]$, $\mathbb{Z} \twoheadrightarrow \F_p$, $\mathbb{Z}[x] \twoheadrightarrow \F_p[x]$, $\F_p \hookrightarrow \F_p[x]$. For the constant $3 \in \mathbb{Z}$: right-then-down sends $3 \mapsto 3 \in \mathbb{Z}[x] \mapsto \bar{3} \in \F_p[x]$; down-then-right sends $3 \mapsto \bar{3} \in \F_p \mapsto \bar{3} \in \F_p[x]$. Both give the constant polynomial $\bar{3}$. \checkmark
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes confuse the inclusion $R \hookrightarrow R[x]$ with an isomorphism; $R$ is a proper subring of $R[x]$. Also, the right vertical arrow $R[x] \twoheadrightarrow (R/I)[x]$ requires checking well-definedness: different lifts $a_i$ vs.\ $a_i + c_i$ (with $c_i \in I$) give the same image $\bar{a}_i$ in $R/I$, so the map on polynomials is indeed independent of coefficient representatives.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that forming a polynomial ring and quotienting by a coefficient ideal are interchangeable operations -- the square commutes -- which is precisely the content of $R[x]/I[x] \cong (R/I)[x]$.
\end{dgx}
Going right-then-down equals going down-then-right; the right vertical map has kernel
$I[x]$, which is why $R[x]/I[x]\cong(R/I)[x]$.
\end{remark}

\begin{exers}{Exercises (from the text).}
\item Let $p(x,y,z) = 2x^2y - 3xy^3z + 4y^2z^5$ and $q(x,y,z) = 7x^2 + 5x^2y^3z^4 - 3x^2z^3$ be polynomials in $\mathbb{Z}[x,y,z]$.
\begin{enumerate}

\item[(b)] Find the degree of each of $p$ and $q$.
\item[(c)] Find the degree of $p$ and $q$ in each of the three variables $x$, $y$ and $z$.
\item[(d)] Compute $pq$ and find the degree of $pq$ in each of the three variables $x$, $y$ and $z$.
\item[(e)] Write $pq$ as a polynomial in the variable $z$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{Z}[x,y]$.
\end{enumerate}

\item Repeat the preceding exercise under the assumption that the coefficients of $p$ and $q$ are in $\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$.

\item If $R$ is a commutative ring and $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$ are independent variables over $R$, prove that $R[x_{\pi(1)}, x_{\pi(2)}, \dots, x_{\pi(n)}]$ is isomorphic to $R[x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n]$ for any permutation $\pi$ of $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$.

\item Prove that the ideals $(x)$ and $(x, y)$ are prime ideals in $\mathbb{Q}[x, y]$ but only the latter ideal is a maximal ideal.

\item Prove that $(x, y)$ and $(2, x, y)$ are prime ideals in $\mathbb{Z}[x, y]$ but only the latter ideal is a maximal ideal.

\item Prove that $(x, y)$ is not a principal ideal in $\mathbb{Q}[x, y]$.

\item Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. Prove that a polynomial ring in more than one variable over $R$ is never a Principal Ideal Domain.

\item Let $F$ be a field and let $R = F[x, x^2y, x^3y^2, \dots, x^ny^{n-1}, \dots]$ be a subring of the polynomial ring $F[x, y]$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that the fields of fractions of $R$ and $F[x, y]$ are the same.
\item[(b)] Prove that $R$ contains an ideal that is not finitely generated.
\end{enumerate}

\item Prove that a polynomial ring in infinitely many variables with coefficients in any commutative ring contains ideals that are not finitely generated.

\item Prove that the ring $\mathbb{Z}[x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots]/(x_1x_2, x_3x_4, x_5x_6, \dots)$ contains infinitely many minimal prime ideals (cf.\ Exercise 36 of Section 7.4).

\item Show that the radical of the ideal $I = (x, y^2)$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x, y]$ is $(x, y)$ (cf.\ Exercise 30, Section 7.4). Deduce that $I$ is a primary ideal that is not a power of a prime ideal (cf.\ Exercise 41, Section 7.4).

\item Let $R = \mathbb{Q}[x, y, z]$ and let bars denote passage to $\mathbb{Q}[x, y, z]/(xy - z^2)$. Prove that $\overline{P} = (\overline{x}, \overline{z})$ is a prime ideal. Show that $\overline{xy} \in \overline{P}^2$ but no power of $\overline{y}$ lies in $\overline{P}^2$. (This shows $\overline{P}$ is a prime ideal whose square is not a primary ideal -- cf.\ Exercise 41, Section 7.4.)

\item Prove that the rings $F[x, y]/(y^2 - x)$ and $F[x, y]/(y^2 - x^2)$ are not isomorphic for any field $F$.

\item Let $R$ be an integral domain and let $i, j$ be relatively prime integers. Prove that the ideal $(x^i - y^j)$ is a prime ideal in $R[x, y]$. [Consider the ring homomorphism $\varphi$ from $R[x, y]$ to $R[t]$ defined by mapping $x$ to $t^j$ and mapping $y$ to $t^i$. Show that an element of $R[x, y]$ differs from an element in $(x^i - y^j)$ by a polynomial $f(x,y)$ of degree at most $j - 1$ in $y$ and observe that the exponents of $\varphi(x^r y^s)$ are distinct for $0 \le s < j$.]

\item Let $p(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)$ be a homogeneous polynomial of degree $k$ in $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$. Prove that for all $\lambda \in R$ we have $p(\lambda x_1, \lambda x_2, \dots, \lambda x_n) = \lambda^k p(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)$.

\item Prove that the product of two homogeneous polynomials is again homogeneous.

\item An ideal $I$ in $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is called a \emph{homogeneous ideal} if whenever $p \in I$ then each homogeneous component of $p$ is also in $I$. Prove that an ideal is a homogeneous ideal if and only if it may be generated by homogeneous polynomials. [Use induction on degrees to show the ``if'' implication.]

\item Let $R$ be an arbitrary ring and let $\Func(R)$ be the ring of all functions from $R$ to itself. If $p(x) \in R[x]$ is a polynomial, let $f_p \in \Func(R)$ be the function on $R$ defined by $f_p(r) = p(r)$ (the usual way of viewing a polynomial in $R[x]$ as defining a function on $R$ by ``evaluating at $r$'').

\item[(a)] For fixed $a \in R$, prove that ``evaluation at $a$'' is a ring homomorphism from $\Func(R)$ to $R$ (cf.\ Example 4 following Theorem 7 in Section 7.3).
\item[(b)] Prove that the map $\varphi : R[x] \to \Func(R)$ defined by $\varphi(p(x)) = f_p$ is not a ring homomorphism in general. Deduce that polynomial identities need not give corresponding identities when the polynomials are viewed as functions. [If $R = \mathbb{H}$ is the ring of real Hamilton Quaternions show that $p(x) = x^2 + 1$ factors as $(x + i)(x - i)$, but that $p(j) = 0$ while $(j + i)(j - i) \ne 0$.]
\item[(c)] For fixed $a \in R$, prove that the composite ``evaluation at $a$'' of the maps in (a) and (b) mapping $R[x]$ to $R$ is a ring homomorphism if and only if $a$ is in the center of $R$.
\end{enumerate}

Throughout this section $F$ denotes a \emph{field}. The single fact that drives
everything is that we can divide one polynomial by another and control the size of the
remainder by its \emph{degree}. This makes $F[x]$ a Euclidean domain, and Euclidean
domains are automatically PIDs and UFDs. We develop the consequences concretely: every
ideal is principal (generated by a monic gcd), the Euclidean algorithm computes gcds and
B\'ezout coefficients, roots correspond to linear factors, and a polynomial of degree $n$
has at most $n$ roots in a field.

latex:
\begin{theorem}[{Division Algorithm in $F[x]$}]
Let $F$ be a field and let $f,g \in F[x]$ with $g \neq 0$. Then there exist
\emph{unique} polynomials $q,r \in F[x]$ such that
\[
  f = qg + r, \qquad \text{with } r = 0 \text{ or } \deg r < \deg g .
\]
\end{theorem}

section_path.title: $F[x]$ is a Euclidean domain: division, GCDs, and roots

title: {Division Algorithm in $F[x]$}

latex:
\begin{proof}
\emph{Existence.} If $f = 0$ or $\deg f < \deg g$ take $q=0,\ r=f$. Otherwise induct on
$\deg f$. Write $\LT(f) = a x^{m}$ and $\LT(g) = b x^{n}$ with $m \ge n$. Because $F$ is a
field, $b$ is a unit, so we may form
\[
  f_1 \;=\; f - \frac{a}{b}\,x^{m-n} g .
\]
The leading terms cancel by construction, so $f_1 = 0$ or $\deg f_1 < \deg f$. By
induction $f_1 = q_1 g + r$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r < \deg g$, whence
$f = \bigl(\frac{a}{b}x^{m-n} + q_1\bigr) g + r$.

\emph{Uniqueness.} If $qg + r = q'g + r'$ with both remainders of degree $<\deg g$ (or
zero), then $(q-q')g = r'-r$. If $q \neq q'$ the left side has degree
$\ge \deg g$ while the right side has degree $<\deg g$ (or is $0$), a contradiction. Hence
$q=q'$ and then $r=r'$.
\end{proof}

title: Polynomial long division in $F[x]$

latex:
\begin{wex}{Long division in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$}
Divide $f = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x - 5$ by $g = x^2 - x + 2$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.
\wrec Division Algorithm: $g \neq 0$ and $\LC(g)=1$ is a unit, so a unique $(q,r)$ with
$\deg r < 2$ exists. Run the long-division loop.
\wsol
Start $r = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + 0x^2 + x - 5$.

\emph{Step 1.} $\LT(r)=2x^4$, $\LT(g)=x^2$, so $t_1 = 2x^2$.
\[
  r - 2x^2 g = (2x^4-3x^3+x-5) - (2x^4 - 2x^3 + 4x^2) = -x^3 - 4x^2 + x - 5 .
\]

\emph{Step 2.} $\LT(r) = -x^3$, so $t_2 = -x$.
\[
  r - (-x)g = (-x^3-4x^2+x-5) - (-x^3 + x^2 - 2x) = -5x^2 + 3x - 5 .
\]

\emph{Step 3.} $\LT(r) = -5x^2$, so $t_3 = -5$.
\[
  r - (-5)g = (-5x^2+3x-5) - (-5x^2 + 5x - 10) = -2x + 5 .
\]
Now $\deg(-2x+5) = 1 < 2$, stop. Thus
\[
  q = 2x^2 - x - 5, \qquad r = -2x + 5 .
\]
\textit{Check.} Compute $qg$ term by term:
$2x^2\cdot g = 2x^4-2x^3+4x^2$; $-x\cdot g = -x^3+x^2-2x$; $-5\cdot g = -5x^2+5x-10$.
Summing,
\[
  qg = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + (4+1-5)x^2 + (-2+5)x - 10 = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + 3x - 10 .
\]
Then $qg + r = (2x^4-3x^3+3x-10) + (-2x+5) = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x - 5 = f$, and
$\deg r = 1 < 2$. \checkmark
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{Division forcing fractions}
Divide $f = x^3 + 2x + 1$ by $g = 3x - 1$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$.
\wrec $\LC(g)=3$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Q}$, so division is legal and the remainder is a constant.
\wsol
$t_1 = \frac{1}{3}x^2$: \quad $r = f - \frac13 x^2 (3x-1) = x^3+2x+1 - (x^3 - \tfrac13 x^2)
= \tfrac13 x^2 + 2x + 1$.

$t_2 = \frac{1}{9}x$: \quad $r = \tfrac13 x^2+2x+1 - \tfrac19 x(3x-1)
= \tfrac13 x^2 + 2x + 1 - (\tfrac13 x^2 - \tfrac19 x) = \tfrac{19}{9}x + 1$.

$t_3 = \frac{19}{27}$: \quad $r = \tfrac{19}{9}x+1 - \tfrac{19}{27}(3x-1)
= \tfrac{19}{9}x + 1 - (\tfrac{19}{9}x - \tfrac{19}{27}) = 1 + \tfrac{19}{27}
= \tfrac{46}{27}$.
So $q = \tfrac13 x^2 + \tfrac19 x + \tfrac{19}{27}$, $r = \tfrac{46}{27}$.
\textit{Check.} By the root form, $r = f(\tfrac13) = \tfrac{1}{27} + \tfrac23 + 1
= \tfrac{1 + 18 + 27}{27} = \tfrac{46}{27}$. \checkmark
This shows why we need a field: over $\mathbb{Z}[x]$, $3x-1$ would not divide with $\mathbb{Z}$
coefficients.
\end{wex}

\begin{theorem}[{GCD as ideal generator; B\'ezout}]
For $f,g \in F[x]$ not both $0$, the ideal $(f,g)$ equals $(d)$ where $d$ is the monic
$\gcd(f,g)$. Hence there exist $s,t \in F[x]$ with
\[
  d = s f + t g \qquad(\text{B\'ezout's identity}),
\]
and $d$ is characterized by: $d \mid f$, $d \mid g$, and every common divisor of
$f,g$ divides $d$.
\end{theorem}

title: Euclidean algorithm + back-substitution in $F[x]$

latex:
\begin{wex}{GCD and B\'ezout in $\F_5[x]$}
Compute $\gcd(f,g)$ with $f = x^3 + 2x + 1$, $g = x^2 + 1$ in $\F_5[x]$, and find $s,t$.
\wrec Euclidean algorithm in a Euclidean domain; track coefficients for B\'ezout.
\wsol
\emph{Step 1.} $x^3 + 2x + 1 = (x)(x^2+1) + (x+1)$, since $x(x^2+1)=x^3+x$ and
$(x^3+2x+1)-(x^3+x)=x+1$. So $q_1 = x$, $r_2 = x+1$.

\emph{Step 2.} Divide $r_1=x^2+1$ by $r_2=x+1$:
$x^2 + 1 = (x-1)(x+1) + 2$, since $(x-1)(x+1)=x^2-1$ and $(x^2+1)-(x^2-1)=2$. So
$q_2 = x-1$, $r_3 = 2$.

\emph{Step 3.} Divide $r_2 = x+1$ by $r_3 = 2$: $x+1 = (3x+3)\cdot 2 + 0$ (since
$2^{-1}=3$). Remainder $0$, so the last nonzero remainder is $r_3 = 2$, a nonzero constant.
Hence $\gcd = 2^{-1}\cdot 2 = 1$: \quad $f,g$ are coprime.

\emph{B\'ezout.} From Step 2, $2 = (x^2+1) - (x-1)(x+1)$. From Step 1,
$x+1 = (x^3+2x+1) - x(x^2+1)$. Substitute:
\[
  2 = (x^2+1) - (x-1)\bigl[(x^3+2x+1) - x(x^2+1)\bigr]
    = -(x-1)f + \bigl[1 + x(x-1)\bigr]g .
\]
So $2 = -(x-1)f + (x^2 - x + 1)g$. Multiply by $2^{-1}=3$:
\[
  1 = 3(1-x)\,f + 3(x^2 - x + 1)\,g = (3 - 3x)f + (3x^2 + 2x + 3)g
    = (2x+3)f + (3x^2+2x+3)g
\]
(using $-3 \equiv 2 \pmod 5$).
\textit{Check.} In $(2x+3)f$ the top term is $2x\cdot x^3 = 2x^4$; in $(3x^2)g$ it is
$3x^2\cdot x^2 = 3x^4$, and $2+3 = 5 \equiv 0$, so $x^4$ cancels. Continuing term by term
mod $5$, all lower-degree terms cancel except the constant $3\cdot1 + 3\cdot1 = 6 \equiv
1$, giving $1$. \checkmark So $s = 2x+3$, $t = 3x^2+2x+3$, $d=1$.
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{A nontrivial gcd in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$}
Find $\gcd(x^4 - 1,\ x^3 - x^2 + x - 1)$ in $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ and write it as a B\'ezout combination.
\wrec Repeated division. Both polynomials vanish at $x=1$, so $x-1$ is a common factor.
\wsol
\emph{Step 1.} $r_0 = x^4-1$, $r_1 = x^3 - x^2 + x - 1$.
Try $x^4 - 1 = (x+1)\,r_1 + r_2$. Compute $(x+1)r_1 = x^4 - x^3 + x^2 - x + x^3 - x^2 +
x - 1 = x^4 - 1$. So $r_2 = 0$: the division terminates at once and $r_1 \mid r_0$.

Hence $\gcd$ is the monic scaling of $r_1$, and $r_1$ is already monic. Factoring,
$r_1 = x^2(x-1) + (x-1) = (x-1)(x^2+1)$, while $x^4 - 1 = (x-1)(x+1)(x^2+1)$, confirming
$r_1 \mid r_0$. Thus
\[
  \gcd(x^4-1,\ x^3-x^2+x-1) = x^3 - x^2 + x - 1 .
\]
\textit{Check.} $r_1 \mid r_0$ since $x^4-1 = (x+1)r_1$, and $r_1 \mid r_1$; any
common divisor divides $r_1$, so $r_1$ is the gcd. \checkmark Here B\'ezout is trivial:
$r_1 = 0\cdot r_0 + 1\cdot r_1$.
\end{wex}

latex:
\begin{wex}{Ideal $(f,g)=(\gcd)$ explicitly in $\F_2[x]$}
In $\F_2[x]$ let $f = x^3 + x + 1$, $g = x^2 + x$. Identify $(f,g)$ as a principal ideal.
\wrec $(f,g) = (\gcd(f,g))$; compute the gcd by the Euclidean algorithm over $\F_2$.
\wsol
\emph{Step 1.} $x^3 + x + 1 = (x+1)(x^2 + x) + r_2$. Compute $(x+1)(x^2+x) = x^3 + x^2 +
x^2 + x = x^3 + x$ (since $2x^2 = 0$). So $r_2 = (x^3+x+1)-(x^3+x) = 1$.

\emph{Step 2.} Divide $g = x^2 + x$ by $r_2 = 1$: remainder $0$. Last nonzero remainder is
$1$. Hence $\gcd = 1$ and
\[
  (f,g) = (1) = \F_2[x] .
\]
\textit{Check.} $1 = (x^3+x+1) - (x+1)(x^2+x) = 1\cdot f + (x+1)g \in (f,g)$, so the ideal
contains a unit and is everything. \checkmark Geometrically, $g = x(x+1)$ vanishes at
$0,1$ but $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=1$, so $f,g$ share no root and are coprime.
\end{wex}
