\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}


\item Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and let $M$ be a left $R$-module. Show that the
subset $N$ of $M$ consisting of all $R$-linear combinations of a fixed set
$A\subseteq M$ equals the intersection of all submodules of $M$ containing $A$.
Conclude that $RA=\langle A\rangle$.

\item In the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\mathbb{Z}$, find a generating set of size $1$. Show that the
single element $2$ does \emph{not} generate $\mathbb{Z}$ as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module (since
$\mathbb{Z}\cdot 2=2\mathbb{Z}\ne\mathbb{Z}$), but that $\{2,3\}$ \emph{does} generate $\mathbb{Z}$ as a
$\mathbb{Z}$-module because $\gcd(2,3)=1$. Identify a minimal generating set of the
$\mathbb{Z}$-module $\mathbb{Z}$.

\item Let $M=\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$ as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module. List all submodules, and for each give a
single generator. Which elements of $M$ generate $M$?

\item Show that $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a finitely generated $\mathbb{Z}$-module. (Hint: a finite
generating set has a common denominator.)

\item Let $R$ be a ring and let $M_1,\dots,M_k$ be submodules of a module $M$.
Prove that the sum $M_1+\cdots+M_k=\{m_1+\cdots+m_k \st m_i\in M_i\}$ is a
submodule, and that it is the smallest submodule containing every $M_i$.

\item Give an explicit isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}\cong \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\mathbb{Z}$ of
$\mathbb{Z}$-modules, and verify it is a bijective $R$-homomorphism. Explain why
$\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}\not\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$.

\item Let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules. Show that the external direct sum
$M\oplus N$ together with the maps $\iota_M\colon m\mapsto(m,0)$ and
$\pi_M\colon(m,n)\mapsto m$ satisfies $\pi_M\iota_M=\id_M$, $\pi_N\iota_N=\id_N$,
and $\iota_M\pi_M+\iota_N\pi_N=\id_{M\oplus N}$.

\item Prove that for $R$-modules $A,B,C$ there is a natural isomorphism
$\Hom_R(A\oplus B,\,C)\cong \Hom_R(A,C)\oplus\Hom_R(B,C)$.

\item Let $F$ be the free $\mathbb{Z}$-module on the set $A=\{x,y,z\}$. Write down the
element $3x-2y+5z$ as a function $A\to\mathbb{Z}$ with finite support, and compute the
image of this element under the unique homomorphism $F\to\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ sending
$x\mapsto 1,\ y\mapsto 1,\ z\mapsto 2$.

\item Suppose $R$ is a nonzero commutative ring and $R^m\cong R^n$ as
$R$-modules. Use the fact that $R$ has a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and reduce
modulo $\mathfrak m$ to prove $m=n$ (so free rank is well defined over a nonzero
commutative ring).

\item Let $V$ be the $\F[x]$-module given by $V=\F^2$ with $x$ acting as the
matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ over $\F=\mathbb{R}$. Determine whether
$V$ is generated by a single element as an $\F[x]$-module, and if so exhibit a
generator.

\item Let $N\sgr M$ be $R$-modules. Prove that if $M/N$ and $N$ are both finitely
generated, then $M$ is finitely generated. Give generators of $M$ explicitly in
terms of generators of $N$ and lifts of generators of $M/N$.

\item Show that a finitely generated module over a field $\F$ (i.e.\ a finite
dimensional vector space) is free, and that its rank equals its dimension.

\item Let $R=\mathbb{Z}$ and consider the submodule $N=\langle (2,0),(0,3)\rangle\sgr \mathbb{Z}^2$.
Compute the quotient $\mathbb{Z}^2/N$ as an explicit direct sum of cyclic groups.

\item Prove that an $R$-module $M$ is generated by a single element if and only
if $M\cong R/I$ for some left ideal $I$ of $R$. Identify $I$ as an annihilator.


\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Additional exercises.}


\item Let $R$ be a ring with $1$ and suppose the left $R$-module $R$ has a
proper submodule that is also a direct summand, say $R=I\oplus J$ with $I,J$
nonzero left ideals. Prove that $1=e+f$ with $e\in I$, $f\in J$, that $e,f$ are
orthogonal idempotents, and that $I=Re$, $J=Rf$.

\item Show that $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a projective $\mathbb{Z}$-module. (Hint: $\mathbb{Q}$ is not free
since it is not finitely generated and any free $\mathbb{Z}$-module of rank $\ge 2$ has
linearly independent elements, while any two elements of $\mathbb{Q}$ are $\mathbb{Z}$-linearly
dependent; then argue that a projective module is a direct summand of a free
module, and a nonzero divisible submodule of a free $\mathbb{Z}$-module must be $0$.)

\item Let $A$ be an infinite set and $R$ a nonzero ring. Prove that the free
module $R^{(A)}$ (finite support) is \emph{not} isomorphic to the direct product
$R^A$ when $R$ is a field and $A$ is countably infinite, by a cardinality /
dimension argument.

\item Let $M$ be an $R$-module with submodules $N_1,N_2$ such that $M=N_1+N_2$
and $N_1\cap N_2=0$. Prove $M\cong N_1\oplus N_2$ via $n_1+n_2\mapsto(n_1,n_2)$,
and show by example over $R=\mathbb{Z}$ that $M=N_1+N_2$ alone is insufficient.

\item Prove that a finitely generated module $M$ over a commutative ring $R$
cannot be generated by fewer than $n$ elements if $M/\mathfrak m M$ has dimension
$n$ over $R/\mathfrak m$ for some maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ (Nakayama-style
lower bound). State precisely the version of Nakayama's lemma you use.

\item Let $0\to A\to B\to C\to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules with
$C$ free. Prove the sequence splits, so $B\cong A\oplus C$.

\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}


\item (Universal property of free modules.) Let $A$ be a set, $R^{(A)}$ the free
module with basis map $\iota\colon A\to R^{(A)}$, $M$ any $R$-module, and
$f\colon A\to M$ any set map. State and prove the universal property by
constructing the unique $R$-homomorphism $\Phi$ making the triangle commute:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & R^{(A)} \arrow[d, dashed, "{\exists!\,\Phi}"] \\
 & M
\end{tikzcd}\]
Then prove that this universal property characterizes $R^{(A)}$ up to unique
isomorphism.

\item (Projectivity via lifting.) Call $P$ projective if for every surjection
$g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$ and every $f\colon P\to C$ there is
$\tilde f\colon P\to B$ with $g\tilde f=f$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}
 & P \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[dl, dashed, "{\exists\,\tilde f}"'] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C
\end{tikzcd}\]
Using the universal property of free modules from the previous exercise, prove
that every free module is projective.

\item (Splitting a short exact sequence.) Given
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, hook, "\psi"] & B \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] & C \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}\]
prove the equivalence of: (a) there is $s\colon C\to B$ with $\varphi s=\id_C$;
(b) there is $r\colon B\to A$ with $r\psi=\id_A$; (c) $B\cong A\oplus C$
compatibly with $\psi,\varphi$. Draw the maps $s$ and $r$ on the diagram and
verify each implication.

\item (Pullback of generators.) Let $\pi\colon R^{(A)}\twoheadrightarrow M$ be
the surjection induced by a generating set $\{m_a\}_{a\in A}$ of $M$, with kernel
$K$. Display the short exact sequence
$0\to K\to R^{(A)}\xrightarrow{\pi} M\to 0$ and prove that $M$ is finitely
generated iff $A$ may be chosen finite. Show $K$ is the module of relations among
the $m_a$.

\item (Hom is left exact.) Given an exact sequence
$0\to A\xrightarrow{\psi}B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C$ of $R$-modules and an
$R$-module $D$, prove the induced sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & \Hom_R(D,A) \arrow[r, "\psi_*"] & \Hom_R(D,B) \arrow[r, "\varphi_*"] & \Hom_R(D,C)
\end{tikzcd}\]
is exact, and give an example with $D=\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ over $R=\mathbb{Z}$ showing $\varphi_*$
need not be surjective even when $\varphi$ is.


\end{exers}

title: Commutative-diagram exercises.

latex: Throughout, $R$ is a ring with $1$. The tensor product mixes a \emph{right} $R$-module with a \emph{left} $R$-module to produce an \emph{abelian group}. Let $M$ be a right $R$-module and $N$ a left $R$-module.

\begin{definition}[$R$-balanced map]
A map $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$ into an abelian group $L$ is \textbf{$R$-balanced} (or \emph{middle linear}) if for all $m,m'\in M$, $n,n'\in N$, $r\in R$:
\[
\varphi(m+m',\,n)=\varphi(m,n)+\varphi(m',n),\quad
\varphi(m,\,n+n')=\varphi(m,n)+\varphi(m,n'),\quad
\varphi(mr,\,n)=\varphi(m,\,rn).
\]
The first two say $\varphi$ is biadditive; the third lets scalars ``slide across'' the $\times$.
\end{definition}
title: $R$-balanced map

latex:
\begin{definition}[Tensor product $M\otimes_R N$]
The \textbf{tensor product} of $M$ and $N$ over $R$ is the abelian group
\[
M\otimes_R N \;=\; F\big/H,
\]
where $F$ is the free abelian group $\mathbb{Z}^{(M\times N)}$ on the set $M\times N$, and $H$ is the subgroup generated by all elements
\[
(m+m',n)-(m,n)-(m',n),\quad (m,n+n')-(m,n)-(m,n'),\quad (mr,n)-(m,rn),
\]
for $m,m'\in M$, $n,n'\in N$, $r\in R$. The image of $(m,n)$ in $M\otimes_R N$ is the \textbf{simple tensor} $m\otimes n$. Every element of $M\otimes_R N$ is a \emph{finite sum} $\sum_i m_i\otimes n_i$.
\end{definition}
title: Tensor product $M\otimes_R N$

latex:
By construction the relations defining $H$ become, in $M\otimes_R N$, exactly the bilinearity identities:
\[
(m+m')\otimes n = m\otimes n + m'\otimes n,\qquad
m\otimes(n+n') = m\otimes n + m\otimes n',\qquad
mr\otimes n = m\otimes rn.
\]
Useful consequences: $0\otimes n = m\otimes 0 = 0$ and $(-m)\otimes n = -(m\otimes n) = m\otimes(-n)$, since $0\otimes n=(0+0)\otimes n=0\otimes n+0\otimes n$.

\begin{theorem}[Universal property of $\otimes$]
The canonical map $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$, $\iota(m,n)=m\otimes n$, is $R$-balanced, and it is universal: for every $R$-balanced map $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$ there is a \emph{unique} group homomorphism $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$ with $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$, i.e. $\varphi=\Phi\circ\iota$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M\times N \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"'] & M\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]
Thus $\{R\text{-balanced maps }M\times N\to L\}\;\longleftrightarrow\;\{\text{group homs }M\otimes_R N\to L\}$, naturally in $L$.
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Three objects. Top-left: the \emph{Cartesian product} $M\times N$, a set (not a module), where $M$ is a right $R$-module and $N$ is a left $R$-module. Top-right: the \emph{tensor product} $M\otimes_R N$, an abelian group, constructed as the free abelian group on $M\times N$ modulo the balanced relations. Bottom: an arbitrary abelian group $L$, the target of any $R$-balanced map.
\dgi{Arrows:} (1) $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$, $\iota(m,n)=m\otimes n$, is the canonical $R$-balanced map whose existence is the whole point of the construction. (2) $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$ is an arbitrary $R$-balanced map. (3) The dashed $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$ is the \emph{unique} group homomorphism induced by $\varphi$ via the universal property; it satisfies $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\Phi\circ\iota=\varphi$, i.e., for every $(m,n)\in M\times N$, $\Phi(\iota(m,n))=\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Start with $(m,n)\in M\times N$. Along the top-then-down path: $\iota$ sends $(m,n)$ to $m\otimes n$, then $\Phi$ sends $m\otimes n$ to $\varphi(m,n)$---that is exactly how $\Phi$ is defined on simple tensors. Along the diagonal: $\varphi$ sends $(m,n)$ directly to $\varphi(m,n)$. Both paths produce $\varphi(m,n)$. Well-definedness: $\Phi$ is defined first on the free group $F$ by $\tilde\varphi(m,n)=\varphi(m,n)$, then one checks $\tilde\varphi$ kills the subgroup $H$ of balanced relations (possible exactly because $\varphi$ is balanced), so $\Phi$ descends to $F/H=M\otimes_R N$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the \emph{raison d'etre} of the tensor product: it converts the non-additive data of a balanced map into a clean group homomorphism. The theorem is placed here immediately after defining $M\otimes_R N$ to show that the messy quotient construction is the \emph{right} object: one never has to return to the quotient; one just works with balanced maps.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $M=\mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z}$, $N=\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$, $L=\mathbb{Z}/(d)\mathbb{Z}$ ($d=\gcd(m,n)$), and $\varphi(\bar a,\bar b)=\overline{ab}$. This is $\mathbb{Z}$-balanced and well defined on cosets; the induced $\Phi\colon\mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(d)\mathbb{Z}$ is an isomorphism, recovering $\mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(d)\mathbb{Z}$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students try to define $\Phi$ directly by ``$\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$'' without first verifying $\varphi$ is balanced. This is circular: the universal property only hands you $\Phi$ \emph{after} the balanced-axiom check. Skipping that check means $\Phi$ may not be well defined on the tensor product (different representatives of a simple tensor could give different outputs).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the tensor product $M\otimes_R N$ is precisely the abelian group that linearizes balanced maps---every balanced map out of $M\times N$ corresponds uniquely to a group homomorphism out of $M\otimes_R N$.
\end{dgx}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Extension of scalars / induced module]
Let $R\subseteq S$ be a subring (with $1_R=1_S$) and $N$ a left $R$-module. Regard $S$ as an $(S,R)$-bimodule (left $S$-action by multiplication, right $R$-action by multiplication). Then
\[
S\otimes_R N
\]
is a \emph{left $S$-module} via $s'\cdot(s\otimes n)=(s's)\otimes n$, extended additively. Moreover $\iota\colon N\to S\otimes_R N$, $\iota(n)=1\otimes n$, is an $R$-module homomorphism, and the pair $(S\otimes_R N,\iota)$ is universal for $R$-maps into $S$-modules:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
N \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & S\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,F"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]
i.e. for every $S$-module $L$ and $R$-module hom $f\colon N\to L$ there is a unique $S$-module hom $F\colon S\otimes_R N\to L$ with $F\circ\iota=f$ (so $F(s\otimes n)=s\,f(n)$).
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Top-left: $N$, a left $R$-module (living at the smaller scalar level). Top-right: $S\otimes_R N$, the \emph{extended} module, a left $S$-module formed by tensoring over $R$ with the $(S,R)$-bimodule $S$; simple tensors $s\otimes n$ span it, with $S$-action $s'(s\otimes n)=(s's)\otimes n$. Bottom: $L$, an arbitrary left $S$-module serving as target.
\dgi{Arrows:} (1) $\iota\colon N\to S\otimes_R N$, $\iota(n)=1\otimes n$, is the canonical $R$-module map from $N$ into the extended module, given by tensoring with the identity $1\in S$; it need not be injective (e.g.\ for $\mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}$, $\iota\colon\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}=0$). (2) $f\colon N\to L$, any $R$-module homomorphism (the map to be ``extended'' to $S$-linearity). (3) The dashed $F\colon S\otimes_R N\to L$, the unique $S$-module homomorphism with $F(s\otimes n)=s\,f(n)$, is induced by the UP.
\dgi{What commutes:} $F\circ\iota=f$: for every $n\in N$, $F(\iota(n))=F(1\otimes n)=1\cdot f(n)=f(n)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Start with $n\in N$. Top-then-down: $\iota$ sends $n$ to $1\otimes n$; then $F$ sends $1\otimes n$ to $1\cdot f(n)=f(n)$. Diagonal: $f$ sends $n$ directly to $f(n)$. They agree. Well-definedness of $F$: the assignment $(s,n)\mapsto s\,f(n)$ must be checked $R$-balanced into $L$; the key relation is $(sr)\otimes n\mapsto (sr)f(n)=s(rf(n))=s\,f(rn)$, which holds because $f$ is $R$-linear. So the balanced map induces $F$ as a group hom; $F$ is $S$-linear because $F(s'(s\otimes n))=F((s's)\otimes n)=(s's)f(n)=s'(sF(1\otimes n))$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The theorem justifies why $S\otimes_R N$ is the \emph{correct} way to promote an $R$-module to an $S$-module: the diagram encodes that any $R$-linear information about $N$ can be uniquely lifted to $S$-linear information about $S\otimes_R N$. This is the adjunction between restriction and induction (extension of scalars $\dashv$ restriction of scalars).
\dgi{Concrete example:} $R=\mathbb{R}$, $S=\mathbb{C}$, $N=\mathbb{R}^n$, $L=\mathbb{C}^n$, $f(v)=v$ (view real vectors in $\mathbb{C}^n$). The induced $F\colon\mathbb{C}\otimes_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{C}^n$ sends $z\otimes v\mapsto zv$; this is the complexification isomorphism $\mathbb{C}^n\cong\mathbb{C}\otimes_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}^n$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Confusing $\iota\colon N\to S\otimes_R N$ with an $S$-module map. It is only $R$-linear: $\iota(rn)=1\otimes rn=r\otimes n=r\cdot(1\otimes n)$ for $r\in R$, but $N$ carries no $S$-action, so $S$-linearity of $\iota$ is not even meaningful. The induced $F$ is the $S$-linear one, not $\iota$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that $S\otimes_R N$ is the universal $S$-module receiving $N$, meaning every $R$-linear map from $N$ into any $S$-module extends uniquely to an $S$-linear map out of $S\otimes_R N$.
\end{dgx}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proposition}[$\otimes$ over a commutative ring]
Let $R$ be commutative and $M,N$ be $R$-modules (a right module \emph{is} a left module via $mr:=rm$). Then $M\otimes_R N$ is an $R$-module via
\[
r\cdot(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn),
\]
extended additively, and this action is well defined. The canonical map $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$ is $R$-bilinear, and $M\otimes_R N$ is universal among $R$-modules receiving an $R$-bilinear map: every $R$-bilinear $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$ into an $R$-module $L$ factors uniquely through an $R$-module hom $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M\times N \arrow[r, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi\ (R\text{-bilinear})"'] & M\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi\ (R\text{-linear})"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Top-left: the Cartesian product $M\times N$ of two $R$-modules (here $R$ is commutative, so left and right actions coincide). Top-right: $M\otimes_R N$, now an $R$-\emph{module} (not just an abelian group), via $r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$. Bottom: $L$, an arbitrary $R$-module serving as target.
\dgi{Arrows:} (1) $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$, $\iota(m,n)=m\otimes n$, the canonical map, now $R$-bilinear (not merely balanced) because $r(m\otimes n)=(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$ in the $R$-module $M\otimes_R N$. (2) $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$, any $R$-bilinear map. (3) The dashed $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$, the unique $R$-\emph{module} homomorphism with $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$; this upgrades the abelian-group UP to the $R$-module level.
\dgi{What commutes:} $\Phi\circ\iota=\varphi$: for every $(m,n)$, $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The abelian-group universal property already gives a unique group hom $\Phi$ with $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$. One then checks $\Phi$ is $R$-linear: $\Phi(r(m\otimes n))=\Phi((rm)\otimes n)=\varphi(rm,n)=r\varphi(m,n)=r\Phi(m\otimes n)$, using $R$-linearity of $\varphi$ in the first argument. Commutativity of $R$ is used to make $(rm)\otimes n=m\otimes(rn)$ a single well-posed relation rather than two separate axioms.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This proposition is placed here to show that, over a commutative ring, the tensor product is the universal \emph{$R$-module} for bilinear maps---it lives in the category of $R$-modules, not just abelian groups. This is the natural setting for all subsequent applications (direct-sum decompositions, rank computation, symmetry $M\otimes_R N\cong N\otimes_R M$).
\dgi{Concrete example:} $R=\mathbb{R}$, $M=N=\mathbb{R}^2$, $L=\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi=\det$ (the determinant, which is $\mathbb{R}$-bilinear). The unique $\Phi\colon\mathbb{R}^2\otimes_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ sends $e_i\otimes e_j\mapsto\det(e_i,e_j)$. Here $\Phi$ is an $\mathbb{R}$-linear map between $\mathbb{R}$-modules (not just an abelian-group hom).
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Over a non-commutative ring $R$, $M\otimes_R N$ is only an abelian group, not an $R$-module (there is no canonical way to make the scalar action well defined without commutativity). Students sometimes write $r(m\otimes n)$ for general $R$ without checking; this is only valid when $R$ is commutative (or $M$/$N$ are bimodules).
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that over a commutative ring the universal property of the tensor product holds in the richer category of $R$-modules, so $R$-bilinear maps correspond bijectively to $R$-linear maps out of $M\otimes_R N$---not just group homomorphisms.
\end{dgx}
\end{proposition}

\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Left diagram --- same three objects as the original tensor UP: $M\times N$ (Cartesian product, not a module), $M\otimes_R N$ (abelian group, or $R$-module when $R$ is commutative), and $L$ (an abelian group). This is the balanced-map / tensor-product universal property.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colon M\times N\to M\otimes_R N$, $\iota(m,n)=m\otimes n$, canonical balanced map (top). $\varphi\colon M\times N\to L$, any balanced map (diagonal). Dashed $\Phi\colon M\otimes_R N\to L$, unique group hom with $\Phi\circ\iota=\varphi$ (vertical, induced).
\dgi{What commutes:} $\Phi\circ\iota=\varphi$: both paths $(m,n)\to L$ agree.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} $\Phi$ is defined on generators $m\otimes n$ by $\Phi(m\otimes n)=\varphi(m,n)$; well-defined because $\varphi$ is balanced and therefore kills all relations in $H$. The summary presents this schematically to contrast it with the right-hand diagram.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The remark is placed after all three UP results to make visible that the \emph{same categorical pattern} governs ordinary tensor products, extension of scalars, and the commutative-ring case. The left diagram encodes: to get a map out of $M\otimes_R N$, supply a balanced map and the UP does the rest.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $M=\mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z}$, $N=\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$, $L=\mathbb{Z}/(\gcd(m,n))\mathbb{Z}$, $\varphi(\bar a,\bar b)=\overline{ab}$; the induced $\Phi$ is the isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Z}/(\gcd(m,n))\mathbb{Z}$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students reading the summary in isolation may think the two diagrams describe different objects. They describe the same \emph{shape} (a universal triangle) applied to two different situations; the objects and arrow-types differ in each.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the tensor-product UP and the extension-of-scalars UP share the same universal-triangle shape, so mastering the pattern in one context immediately transfers to the other.
\end{dgx}
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Right diagram --- $N$ (a left $R$-module, the module before extension), $S\otimes_R N$ (the extended left $S$-module), and $L$ (an arbitrary left $S$-module).
\dgi{Arrows:} $1\otimes -\colon N\to S\otimes_R N$, $n\mapsto 1\otimes n$, the canonical $R$-module map (top; not injective in general). $f\colon N\to L$, any $R$-module homomorphism (diagonal). Dashed $F\colon S\otimes_R N\to L$, unique $S$-module homomorphism extending $f$ via $F(s\otimes n)=s\,f(n)$ (vertical).
\dgi{What commutes:} $F\circ(1\otimes -)=f$: $F(1\otimes n)=1\cdot f(n)=f(n)$ for every $n\in N$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Well-definedness of $F$ relies on the $R$-balanced check $(s,n)\mapsto s\,f(n)$: the relation $(sr)\otimes n\mapsto (sr)f(n)=s\,f(rn)$ holds because $f$ is $R$-linear. Thus the balanced map induces $F$ as a group hom; it is $S$-linear by the $S$-action on $S\otimes_R N$. The uniqueness in the ``induction $\dashv$ restriction'' adjunction means any $R$-map $N\to L$ extends to a unique $S$-map $S\otimes_R N\to L$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The right diagram records that extension of scalars is the \emph{left adjoint} to restriction of scalars: $\operatorname{Hom}_S(S\otimes_R N,L)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_R(N,L)$, a bijection natural in $L$. Placing it beside the tensor UP makes clear that both are instances of a single ``represent a functor by a universal object'' construction.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $R=\mathbb{R}$, $S=\mathbb{C}$, $N=\mathbb{R}^2$, $L=\mathbb{C}^3$, $f\colon\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{C}^3$ an $\mathbb{R}$-linear embedding. The unique $\mathbb{C}$-linear extension is $F\colon\mathbb{C}\otimes_\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}^2\cong\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^3$, $F(z\otimes v)=zf(v)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Thinking $F$ is the same map as $f$. They differ: $f$ is only $R$-linear into $L$, while $F$ is $S$-linear out of the larger module $S\otimes_R N$. The canonical map $\iota=1\otimes -$ is the bridge between them.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the extension-of-scalars construction $S\otimes_R N$ is the universal way to convert an $R$-linear map into an $S$-linear one, exhibiting the adjunction between induction and restriction of scalars.
\end{dgx}
\end{remark}

\begin{definition}[Exact sequence]
A pair of $R$-module homomorphisms $X\xrightarrow{\ \alpha\ }Y\xrightarrow{\ \beta\ }Z$ is
\emph{exact at $Y$} if $\im\alpha=\ker\beta$. A (finite or infinite) sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
\cdots \arrow[r] & X_{n+1} \arrow[r, "\alpha_{n+1}"] & X_n \arrow[r, "\alpha_n"] & X_{n-1} \arrow[r] & \cdots
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Each $X_n$ is an $R$-module (a term in the sequence). The dots indicate the sequence may extend infinitely in either direction. The subscript tracks position: $X_{n+1}$ feeds into $X_n$, which feeds into $X_{n-1}$.

\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that exactness at each node is the precise local condition image-equals-kernel, and the full sequence is exact when this holds simultaneously at every interior term.

\begin{definition}[Short exact sequence]
A \emph{short exact sequence (SES)} is an exact sequence of the form
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, hook, "\psi"] & B \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] & C \arrow[r] & 0.
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $0$ is the zero module (placed at both ends). $A$, $B$, $C$ are $R$-modules. The zero modules bookend the sequence to enforce injectivity at the left and surjectivity at the right.
\dgi{Arrows:} The map $0\to A$ is forced to be the zero map. $\psi\colon A\to B$ is an $R$-module homomorphism required to be injective (exactness at $A$). $\varphi\colon B\to C$ is an $R$-module homomorphism required to be surjective (exactness at $C$). The map $C\to 0$ is also forced.
\dgi{What commutes:} Three exactness conditions hold simultaneously: (i) $\operatorname{ker}\psi=0$ so $\psi$ is injective; (ii) $\operatorname{im}\varphi=C$ so $\varphi$ is surjective; (iii) $\operatorname{im}\psi=\operatorname{ker}\varphi$ in the middle.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Condition (i) follows from exactness at $A$: $\operatorname{im}(0\to A)=0=\operatorname{ker}\psi$. Condition (ii) follows from exactness at $C$: $\operatorname{ker}(C\to0)=C=\operatorname{im}\varphi$. Condition (iii) is exactness at $B$. Together they say $\psi$ identifies $A$ as a submodule of $B$ and $\varphi$ exhibits $C$ as the quotient $B/\operatorname{im}\psi$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} The SES is the standard package for encoding a submodule--quotient relationship. It unifies injectivity, surjectivity, and the image-kernel equation into a single compact object that is the building block for all splitting, projectivity, and injectivity arguments that follow.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $0\to n\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}\to0$, with $\psi$ the inclusion and $\varphi=\pi$ the quotient map. Then $\operatorname{im}\psi=n\mathbb{Z}=\operatorname{ker}\pi$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students sometimes read a SES as saying $B\cong A\oplus C$; this is the split case only. The sequence records the relationship $C\cong B/A$ but says nothing about a complementary copy of $C$ inside $B$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that a short exact sequence packages the three conditions -- $\psi$ injective, $\varphi$ surjective, $\operatorname{im}\psi=\operatorname{ker}\varphi$ -- into one object that describes $B$ as an extension of $C$ by $A$.
\end{dgx}
Exactness at all three interior spots means precisely: $\psi$ is injective, $\varphi$ is
surjective, and $\im\psi=\ker\varphi$. Thus $\psi$ embeds $A$ as a submodule of $B$ and
$\varphi$ induces an isomorphism $B/\im\psi\cong C$, i.e. $C\cong B/A$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Split SES; splitting and retraction]
A SES $0\to A\xrightarrow{\psi}B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C\to0$ is \emph{split} if there is an

\emph{retraction}) with $t\circ\psi=\id_A$.

\begin{proof}
$(1)\Rightarrow(3)$: Given $s$, set $K=\im s$. For $b\in B$, write
$b=(b-s\varphi(b))+s\varphi(b)$. Now $\varphi(b-s\varphi(b))=\varphi(b)-\varphi
s\varphi(b)=\varphi(b)-\varphi(b)=0$, so $b-s\varphi(b)\in\ker\varphi=\im\psi$. Thus
$B=\im\psi+K$. If $x\in\im\psi\cap K$, then $x=s(c)$ and $\varphi(x)=0$, but
$\varphi(x)=\varphi s(c)=c$, so $c=0$ and $x=0$; the sum is direct. The map
$\varphi|_K\colon K\to C$ has inverse $s$, so it is an isomorphism.
$(3)\Rightarrow(2)$: With $B=\im\psi\oplus K$, define $t\colon B\to A$ by
$t(\psi(a)+k)=a$ (well defined since $\psi$ is injective). Then $t\psi=\id_A$.
$(2)\Rightarrow(1)$: Given $t$, restrict $\varphi$ to $\ker t$; one checks
$\varphi|_{\ker t}$ is an isomorphism whose inverse is a splitting $s$. Concretely, for
$c\in C$ pick $b$ with $\varphi(b)=c$ and set $s(c)=b-\psi t(b)$; this is independent of the
choice of $b$ and satisfies $\varphi s=\id_C$. Finally, in every case the assignment
$a+c\mapsto\psi(a)+s(c)$ gives an isomorphism $A\oplus C\xrightarrow{\cong}B$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Projective module]
An $R$-module $P$ is \emph{projective} if for every surjection $g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow
C$ and every homomorphism $f\colon P\to C$ there is a (not necessarily unique) lift
$\tilde f\colon P\to B$ with $g\circ\tilde f=f$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}
 & P \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[dl, dashed, "\exists\,\tilde f"'] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C.
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $P$ is the module being tested for projectivity. $B$ and $C$ are $R$-modules. The diagram encodes a universal lifting problem: can every map out of $P$ be routed through $B$ instead of going directly to $C$?
\dgi{Arrows:} $g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$ is a surjective $R$-module homomorphism (the twoheads notation). $f\colon P\to C$ is an arbitrary $R$-homomorphism. The dashed arrow $\tilde f\colon P\to B$ is the asserted lift, with $\exists$ indicating it need not be unique.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $g\circ\tilde f = f$. That is, the two paths from $P$ to $C$ agree: going directly via $f$ equals going via $\tilde f$ and then $g$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} By definition, $P$ is projective precisely when such a $\tilde f$ always exists. The surjectivity of $g$ guarantees enough elements in $B$ to hit any $f(p)$; projectivity says a coherent (homomorphism) choice of preimages can always be made.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the definition of projectivity. It asserts that $P$ is ``free enough'' to lift maps through any surjection, and it is the precise condition that later characterizes free modules and direct summands of free modules, and makes $\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,-)$ exact.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $P=\mathbb{Z}$, $g\colon\mathbb{Z}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$ (reduction mod 5), $f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(5)\mathbb{Z}$ with $f(1)=\bar3$. Lift: $\tilde f(1)=3\in\mathbb{Z}$; then $g(\tilde f(1))=\bar3=f(1)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The dashed arrow is not unique in general; the definition asks only for existence. Also the diagram requires $g$ to be surjective: if $g$ is merely an arbitrary homomorphism, the lift need not exist even for free $P$.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that $P$ is projective when every map from $P$ into a quotient can be lifted to a map into the module above it, making $P$ ``resolution-proof'' against surjections.
\end{dgx}
\end{definition}

\begin{wex}{Free $\Rightarrow$ projective}
Problem. Show every free $R$-module $F=R^{(A)}$ is projective.
\wrec Lifting on a free module is determined freely by where the basis goes.
\wsol Let $\{e_a\}_{a\in A}$ be a basis, $g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$ surjective,
$f\colon F\to C$. For each $a$ pick $b_a\in B$ with $g(b_a)=f(e_a)$ (possible by
surjectivity). Define $\tilde f\colon F\to B$ on the basis by $\tilde f(e_a)=b_a$ and extend
$R$-linearly; this is well defined since $F$ is free. Then $g\tilde f(e_a)=g(b_a)=f(e_a)$
for all $a$, so $g\tilde f=f$. \textit{Check.} The diagram commutes on a generating set, hence
everywhere. Correct.
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
 & R^{(A)} \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[dl, dashed, "{\tilde f\,:\,e_a\mapsto b_a}"'] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $R^{(A)}$ is the free $R$-module on index set $A$ with basis $\{e_a\}_{a\in A}$. $B$ and $C$ are arbitrary $R$-modules. This is the same lifting triangle as in the definition of projective, now specialized to a free module.
\dgi{Arrows:} $f\colon R^{(A)}\to C$ is the map to be lifted. $g\colon B\twoheadrightarrow C$ is a surjection. The dashed $\tilde f\colon R^{(A)}\to B$ is the explicit lift constructed by sending $e_a\mapsto b_a$ where $g(b_a)=f(e_a)$.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $g\circ\tilde f = f$. Concretely $g(\tilde f(e_a))=g(b_a)=f(e_a)$ for all $a\in A$, and since $\{e_a\}$ is a basis this forces $g\tilde f=f$ everywhere.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} The key is that $R^{(A)}$ is \emph{free}: defining a homomorphism on a free module requires only a choice of images for each basis element with no relations to satisfy. Surjectivity of $g$ supplies the needed $b_a$, and freeness lets the formula $\tilde f(\sum r_ae_a)=\sum r_ab_a$ extend consistently.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram provides the base case (free $\Rightarrow$ projective) for the whole theory. All other projectivity proofs either cite this directly or use summand arguments that reduce to it.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $R^{(A)}=\mathbb{Z}$, $g\colon\mathbb{Z}\twoheadrightarrow\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$, $f\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}$ with $f(1)=\bar k$. Pick any $b_1\in\mathbb{Z}$ with $g(b_1)=\bar k$, e.g. $b_1=k$; then $\tilde f(n)=kn$ lifts $f$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The lift $\tilde f$ depends on the choice of preimages $b_a$ and is not unique. Students sometimes think the diagram forces a canonical lift; it does not. What freeness guarantees is only that some consistent choice always works.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that a free module lifts every map through every surjection because its basis elements can be sent independently to any chosen preimages, with no relations obstructing the construction.
\end{dgx}
\end{wex}

\begin{definition}[Injective module]
An $R$-module $Q$ is \emph{injective} if for every injection $\iota\colon A\hookrightarrow
B$ and every homomorphism $f\colon A\to Q$ there is an extension $\tilde f\colon B\to Q$
with $\tilde f\circ\iota=f$:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
0 \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[d, "f"'] & B \arrow[dl, dashed, "\exists\,\tilde f"] \\
 & Q &
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $A$ and $B$ are $R$-modules with $A$ a submodule of $B$ (witnessed by $\iota$). $Q$ is the module being tested for injectivity. The $0$ at the left signals that $\iota$ is injective (the sequence $0\to A\to B$ is exact at $A$).
\dgi{Arrows:} $\iota\colon A\hookrightarrow B$ is an injection. $f\colon A\to Q$ is an arbitrary $R$-homomorphism from the submodule. The dashed $\tilde f\colon B\to Q$ is the asserted extension of $f$ past the inclusion, with $\exists$ indicating it need not be unique.
\dgi{What commutes:} The triangle commutes: $\tilde f\circ\iota = f$. That is, the two paths from $A$ to $Q$ agree: the direct map $f$ equals the composition $\tilde f$ followed back along $\iota$, i.e. $\tilde f$ restricted to $A$ is $f$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} $Q$ is injective precisely when such a $\tilde f$ always exists. This is the dual of projectivity: instead of lifting through a surjection on the output side, we extend along an injection on the input side. Divisibility over $\mathbb{Z}$ supplies the solutions needed to make the extension a homomorphism.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the definition of injectivity. It is the categorical dual of the projective lifting diagram, and it encodes the precise condition that makes $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,Q)$ exact: every map into $Q$ from a submodule extends to the whole ambient module.
\dgi{Concrete example:} $A=2\mathbb{Z}\subset B=\mathbb{Z}$, $f\colon2\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$ with $f(2)=3$. Since $\mathbb{Q}$ is divisible, extend: $\tilde f(1)=3/2$ and $\tilde f(n)=3n/2$; then $\tilde f(2)=3=f(2)$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students confuse the direction of duality: in the projective diagram $P$ maps \emph{into} a surjection; in the injective diagram $Q$ is the \emph{target} and the extension goes \emph{from} $B$ \emph{to} $Q$. The arrows run opposite to each other.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that $Q$ is injective when any map into $Q$ defined on a submodule can always be extended to the entire ambient module, making $Q$ ``absorption-proof'' against injections.
\end{dgx}
\end{definition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Rightarrow$) is the extension property applied to $I\hookrightarrow R$. ($\Leftarrow$)
Given $f\colon A\to Q$ with $A\subseteq B$, use Zorn's Lemma on the poset of partial
extensions $(A',f')$ with $A\subseteq A'\subseteq B$ and $f'|_A=f$. A maximal element
$(A^*,f^*)$ must have $A^*=B$: if some $b\in B\smallsetminus A^*$, the set $I=\{r\in
R:rb\in A^*\}$ is a left ideal, $r\mapsto f^*(rb)$ defines $g\colon I\to Q$, and the
hypothesis extends $g$ to $R$, which lets us extend $f^*$ to $A^*+Rb$, contradicting
maximality. Hence $f^*\colon B\to Q$ extends $f$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Left exactness of $\Hom$]\label{thm:homexact@c10}
Let $0\to A\xrightarrow{\psi}B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C\to0$ be a SES of $R$-modules and $D$
any $R$-module. Then the induced sequences
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & \Hom_R(D,A) \arrow[r, hook, "\psi_*"] & \Hom_R(D,B) \arrow[r, "\varphi_*"] & \Hom_R(D,C)
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Each node is a Hom-set: $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,A)$ is the abelian group of all $R$-module homomorphisms from $D$ to $A$, and similarly for $B$ and $C$. The fixed module $D$ is the source; applying $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,-)$ to the SES $0\to A\to B\to C\to 0$ produces this three-term sequence.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\psi_*\colon\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,A)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,B)$ is post-composition with $\psi$: $\psi_*(h)=\psi\circ h$. $\varphi_*\colon\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,B)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,C)$ is post-composition with $\varphi$: $\varphi_*(h)=\varphi\circ h$. The leading $0$ forces $\psi_*$ to be injective.
\dgi{What commutes:} Exactness holds at $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,A)$: $\psi_*$ is injective (if $\psi h=0$ then $h=0$ since $\psi$ is mono). Exactness at $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,B)$: $\operatorname{im}\psi_*=\operatorname{ker}\varphi_*$, i.e. a map $h\colon D\to B$ satisfies $\varphi(h(d))=0$ for all $d$ iff $h$ factors through $\psi$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For $\operatorname{ker}\varphi_*\subseteq\operatorname{im}\psi_*$: if $\varphi\circ h=0$ then $\operatorname{im}h\subseteq\operatorname{ker}\varphi=\operatorname{im}\psi$, so $h$ factors as $h=\psi\circ h'$ for a unique $h'\colon D\to A$ (injectivity of $\psi$ makes $h'$ unique). The right end need not be exact: a map $D\to C$ need not lift to $D\to B$ unless $D$ is projective.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the covariant left-exactness theorem, the foundational algebraic fact that $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,-)$ does not destroy exactness at the left, but the right end may fail. The extent of that failure is measured by $\operatorname{Ext}^1$.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\times2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ and $D=\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$. Then $\operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{Z}(\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z})=0$ (no nonzero map), $\operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{Z}(\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z})=0$, $\operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{Z}(\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$. The right arrow cannot be surjective since there is no lift $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students forget the sequence is only three terms long and not right-exact. Writing $0\to\operatorname{Hom}(D,A)\to\operatorname{Hom}(D,B)\to\operatorname{Hom}(D,C)\to0$ is wrong in general; the terminal $0$ requires $D$ projective.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that applying $\operatorname{Hom}_R(D,-)$ to a SES preserves the left two exactness conditions but can fail to be surjective at the right, with projectivity of $D$ being exactly the condition that restores full exactness.
\end{dgx}
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & \Hom_R(C,D) \arrow[r, hook, "\varphi^*"] & \Hom_R(B,D) \arrow[r, "\psi^*"] & \Hom_R(A,D)
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} Each node is again a Hom-set, but now the fixed module $D$ is the \emph{target} and the source varies. $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,D)$, $\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,D)$, $\operatorname{Hom}_R(A,D)$ are abelian groups. Applying the contravariant $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,D)$ reverses the order of the original $A\to B\to C$.
\dgi{Arrows:} $\varphi^*\colon\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,D)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,D)$ is pre-composition with $\varphi$: $\varphi^*(h)=h\circ\varphi$. $\psi^*\colon\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,D)\to\operatorname{Hom}_R(A,D)$ is pre-composition with $\psi$: $\psi^*(h)=h\circ\psi$. Note the arrows in the Hom sequence run \emph{opposite} to the original SES.
\dgi{What commutes:} Exactness at $\operatorname{Hom}_R(C,D)$: $\varphi^*$ is injective (if $h\circ\varphi=0$ and $\varphi$ is surjective then $h=0$). Exactness at $\operatorname{Hom}_R(B,D)$: $\operatorname{im}\varphi^*=\operatorname{ker}\psi^*$, since $h\circ\psi=0$ iff $h$ kills $\operatorname{im}\psi=\operatorname{ker}\varphi$, iff $h$ factors through $C=B/\operatorname{ker}\varphi$.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} For $\operatorname{ker}\psi^*\subseteq\operatorname{im}\varphi^*$: if $h\circ\psi=0$ then $\operatorname{ker}\varphi=\operatorname{im}\psi\subseteq\operatorname{ker}h$, so $h$ factors through $B/\operatorname{im}\psi\cong C$ via the map induced by $\varphi$, i.e. $h=h'\circ\varphi=\varphi^*(h')$. The right end need not be surjective unless $D$ is injective.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This is the contravariant left-exactness result, the dual partner of the covariant sequence above. Together they establish that both Hom functors are left exact but generally not right exact, with the two possible failures governed by injectivity (contravariant) and projectivity (covariant).
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\times2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ and $D=\mathbb{Z}$. Then $\operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{Z}(\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z})=0$, $\operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{Z}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}$, and $\operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{Z}(\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Z})=\mathbb{Z}$. The map $\psi^*$ is $\times2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$, which is not surjective (the identity $\id\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ has no preimage), showing the right end can fail.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Contravariance flips the arrows: the sequence runs $C\to B\to A$ in the Hom-sequence even though the original ran $A\to B\to C$. Students sometimes write the Hom sequence in the same order as the original, which is wrong.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that the contravariant functor $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,D)$ reverses the direction of maps and is left-exact, with the failure at the right end measuring the obstruction to extending maps into $D$ -- cured precisely when $D$ is injective.
\end{dgx}

\begin{theorem}[Right exactness of $\otimes$]\label{thm:tensorexact@c10}
Let $A\xrightarrow{\psi}B\xrightarrow{\varphi}C\to0$ be exact (right exact) and $M$ a right
$R$-module. Then
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
M\otimes_R A \arrow[r, "1\otimes\psi"] & M\otimes_R B \arrow[r, two heads, "1\otimes\varphi"] & M\otimes_R C \arrow[r] & 0
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} $M\otimes_R A$, $M\otimes_R B$, $M\otimes_R C$ are tensor products of the right $R$-module $M$ with left $R$-modules $A$, $B$, $C$ respectively. The terminal $0$ signals right-exactness: the last map is surjective.
\dgi{Arrows:} $1\otimes\psi\colon M\otimes_R A\to M\otimes_R B$ is the map induced on simple tensors by $m\otimes a\mapsto m\otimes\psi(a)$. $1\otimes\varphi\colon M\otimes_R B\to M\otimes_R C$ is $m\otimes b\mapsto m\otimes\varphi(b)$. The trailing $0$ says $1\otimes\varphi$ is surjective.
\dgi{What commutes:} Three exactness conditions: (i) $1\otimes\varphi$ is surjective (exactness at $M\otimes_R C$); (ii) $\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)\subseteq\operatorname{ker}(1\otimes\varphi)$ since $\varphi\circ\psi=0$; (iii) $\operatorname{ker}(1\otimes\varphi)=\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)$ (exactness at $M\otimes_R B$). The left map $1\otimes\psi$ need \emph{not} be injective.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Surjectivity of $1\otimes\varphi$: every simple tensor $m\otimes c$ with $c=\varphi(b)$ equals $(1\otimes\varphi)(m\otimes b)$. For exactness at $M\otimes_R B$: the identification $M\otimes_R C\cong(M\otimes_R B)/\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)$ follows from the universal property of the tensor product applied to the composite $M\times C\to M\otimes_R B/\operatorname{im}(1\otimes\psi)$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This theorem draws the dividing line between flat and non-flat modules. Right-exactness is free; left-exactness (injectivity of $1\otimes\psi$) is the flatness condition on $M$. The diagram organizes what tensor always preserves versus what it can destroy.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Take $M=\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$, $A\xrightarrow{\times2}B=\mathbb{Z}$ (injective). Then $1\otimes(\times2)\colon\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ sends $\bar a\mapsto\overline{2a}=\bar0$, the zero map; left-exactness fails. But the surjection $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ is preserved: $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ remains exact.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students assume tensor preserves injectivity as well as surjectivity, writing $0\to M\otimes A\to M\otimes B\to\cdots$ without checking flatness. The left $0$ is wrong unless $M$ is flat.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that tensoring with $M$ always preserves the right end of an exact sequence (surjections become surjections) but can destroy the left end (injections may become non-injective), with flatness of $M$ being the exact condition that restores full exactness.
\end{dgx}

\begin{wex}{$\mathbb{Q}$ is flat over $\mathbb{Z}$ (torsion-free) and restores exactness}
Problem. Tensor $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\times2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ with $\mathbb{Q}$ and identify the result.
\wrec $\mathbb{Q}$ is torsion-free over $\mathbb{Z}$, hence flat; tensoring should keep the left injection
injective.
\wsol Using $\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\cong0$ (since $q\otimes\bar
a=\tfrac{q}{2}\cdot2\otimes\bar a=\tfrac q2\otimes 2\bar a=\tfrac q2\otimes\bar0=0$), the
sequence becomes
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
0 \arrow[r] & \mathbb{Q} \arrow[r, "\times2", "\cong"'] & \mathbb{Q} \arrow[r] & 0 \arrow[r] & 0.
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The four nodes after the initial $0$ arise from tensoring $0\to\mathbb{Z}\xrightarrow{\times2}\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}\to0$ with $\mathbb{Q}$. The left two nodes are $\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}\cong\mathbb{Q}$; the third is $\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}=0$; the final $0$ is $\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}0=0$.
\dgi{Arrows:} The map $\times2\colon\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}$ is $1\otimes(\times2)$, i.e. $q\mapsto2q$. The subsequent arrow $\mathbb{Q}\to0$ is the zero map. The initial $0\to\mathbb{Q}$ says the left map is injective.
\dgi{What commutes:} The sequence is exact at all spots: $0\to\mathbb{Q}\xrightarrow{\times2}\mathbb{Q}\to0\to0$. Exactness at the left $\mathbb{Q}$: $\times2$ is injective (kernel is $\{q\in\mathbb{Q}:2q=0\}=0$). Exactness at the right $\mathbb{Q}$: $\times2$ is surjective (bijection on $\mathbb{Q}$). The middle term $0$ causes no issue.
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Flatness of $\mathbb{Q}$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ (it is torsion-free, hence flat by the PID criterion) means $1\otimes(\times2)$ inherits the injectivity of $\times2\colon\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$. The collapse $\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}=0$ occurs because $q\otimes\bar a=\tfrac{q}{2}\otimes2\bar a=\tfrac{q}{2}\otimes\bar0=0$ for all $q,\bar a$.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the worked demonstration of flatness at work: tensoring the non-split SES with a flat module produces a fully exact (even split) sequence where the torsion term has been annihilated. It contrasts sharply with the $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ computation that precedes it.
\dgi{Concrete example:} This diagram \emph{is} the concrete example, but note the phenomenon more sharply: $\times2\colon\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}$ has the inverse $\times\tfrac12$, so the tensored sequence is not merely exact but actually has $\times2$ as an isomorphism, making the sequence split.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} Students may think that when the right-hand term becomes $0$ after tensoring, something went wrong. In fact $\mathbb{Q}\otimes_\mathbb{Z}\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}=0$ is correct and expected: $\mathbb{Q}$ is divisible, and any torsion module tensored with $\mathbb{Q}$ collapses to zero.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that tensoring a SES with a flat module such as $\mathbb{Q}$ preserves full exactness, here visibly converting the original non-split sequence into a fully exact sequence with the torsion term annihilated.
\end{dgx}
Here $\times2\colon\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Q}$ is a bijection (invert by $\times\tfrac12$), so the sequence is
exact at every spot. Flatness of $\mathbb{Q}$ kept the left map injective, and indeed exact.
\textit{Check.} $\mathbb{Q}\otimes\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}=0$ matches $\mathbb{Q}$ being divisible (multiplication by $2$
surjective), so the cokernel collapses; consistent. Correct.
\end{wex}

\begin{pitfall}
Tensoring is only \emph{right} exact: $1\otimes\psi$ may fail to be injective even when
$\psi$ is. Do not assume $M\otimes_R(-)$ preserves submodules -- e.g. $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{Z}$ via
$\times2$ tensored with $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ collapses to the zero map. The fix is exactly flatness of
$M$. Dually, $\Hom$ is only \emph{left} exact, with the right-hand surjectivity governed by
projectivity (covariant slot) or injectivity (contravariant slot).
\end{pitfall}

\begin{remark}[The three dictionaries]
Projective, injective, flat are the modules that ``correct'' the one-sided exactness of the
three basic functors:
\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=small, column sep=large]
P \text{ projective} \arrow[r, leftrightarrow] & \Hom_R(P,-) \text{ exact} \\
Q \text{ injective} \arrow[r, leftrightarrow] & \Hom_R(-,Q) \text{ exact} \\
M \text{ flat} \arrow[r, leftrightarrow] & M\otimes_R- \text{ exact}
\end{tikzcd}\]
\begin{dgx}
\dgi{Objects:} The left column lists module-theoretic properties: $P$ projective, $Q$ injective, $M$ flat. The right column lists the corresponding functor-exactness properties for $\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,-)$, $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,Q)$, and $M\otimes_R-$, each of which is only partially exact in general.
\dgi{Arrows:} Each horizontal double-headed arrow $\leftrightarrow$ denotes a biconditional (if and only if). The three rows are three separate equivalences, not a commutative diagram in the traditional sense: no path-composition is being equated. Rather, this is a correspondences table displayed diagrammatically.
\dgi{What commutes:} The three equivalences hold simultaneously and independently: (i) $P$ projective $\iff$ $\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,-)$ carries every surjection to a surjection (i.e. is exact); (ii) $Q$ injective $\iff$ $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,Q)$ carries every injection to a surjection (i.e. is exact); (iii) $M$ flat $\iff$ $M\otimes_R-$ carries every injection to an injection (i.e. is exact).
\dgi{Why it commutes:} Each iff was established in the section: (i) the lifting property of $P$ is equivalent to exactness of $\operatorname{Hom}_R(P,-)$ because lifting is exactly preserving surjections. (ii) The extension property of $Q$ is equivalent to $\operatorname{Hom}_R(-,Q)$ preserving injections-to-surjections. (iii) The definition of flat is directly that $M\otimes_R-$ preserves injections.
\dgi{Why this matters here:} This diagram is the organizational capstone of the entire section. It collects the three module classes and their functor-exactness characterizations into one unified picture, clarifying that projective, injective, and flat are each the ``right'' hypothesis to add to the base functor to make it fully exact.
\dgi{Concrete example:} Over $\mathbb{Z}$: $\mathbb{Z}$ is projective (free) and flat (torsion-free); $\operatorname{Hom}_\mathbb{Z}(\mathbb{Z},-)=\operatorname{id}$ is trivially exact. $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is injective (divisible). $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ is neither projective, injective, nor flat, and all three functors applied to it can fail exactness.
\dgi{Common pitfall:} The implications run only one way downward: free $\Rightarrow$ projective $\Rightarrow$ flat, but not conversely in general. Students sometimes read the triple list as saying projective, injective, and flat are equivalent to each other; they are not -- they correspond to three different functors.
\dgi{Takeaway:} The point of this diagram is that projective, injective, and flat modules are precisely the three module classes that upgrade their associated functor from one-sided exact to fully exact, organizing the entire theory around a single unifying principle.
\end{dgx}
Implications: free $\Rightarrow$ projective $\Rightarrow$ flat (none reversible in general),
and over $\mathbb{Z}$: projective $=$ free for finitely generated, injective $=$ divisible,
flat $=$ torsion-free.
\end{remark}

\item Let $J$ be an $(R,R)$-bimodule, let $A$ be a left $R$-module and let $M = \Hom_R(J,A)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] For $r \in R$ and for $\varphi \in \Hom_R(J,A)$ define $r\varphi$ by $(r\varphi)(j) = \varphi(jr)$. Prove that $r\varphi$ is a homomorphism of left $R$-modules, and that this action of $R$ on $\Hom_R(J,A)$ makes it into a left $R$-module. (cf. Exercise 10.)
\item[(b)] If $A$ is an injective $R$-module and $J$ is flat as a right $R$-module, prove that $M = \Hom_R(J,A)$ is an injective $R$-module. [Use the natural isomorphism $\Hom_R(X,M)\cong\Hom_R(J\otimes_R X,A)$ for left $R$-modules $X$. Flatness cannot be dropped: $\Hom_{\mathbb{Z}}(\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z})\cong\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ is not an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module.]
\end{enumerate}
\item Show that if $R$ is a Noetherian ring (cf. Exercise 14 in Section 10.3) and $Q$ is an injective $R$-module then any direct sum of copies of $Q$ is also an injective $R$-module. [Use Baer's Criterion, Proposition 36.]
\item This exercise proves that $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module (cf. Corollary 35).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Prove that a quotient of a divisible group is again divisible.
\item[(b)] Prove that $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is a divisible group, hence is an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module.
\end{enumerate}
\item Let $M$ be any left $R$-module. This exercise proves that $M$ may be embedded in an injective $R$-module.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Show that $M$ is contained in an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module $Q$ (cf. Exercise 18 and Corollary~\ref{cor:divisible@c10}).
\item[(b)] Show that $\Hom_R(R,M) \subseteq \Hom_{\mathbb{Z}}(R,M) \subseteq \Hom_{\mathbb{Z}}(R,Q)$ as $R$-modules, and that $\Hom_{\mathbb{Z}}(R,Q)$ is an injective $R$-module by Exercise 15.
\item[(c)] Deduce that $M$ is contained in an injective $R$-module. [Use the $R$-module isomorphism $M \cong \Hom_R(R,M)$ of Exercise 10.]
\end{enumerate}
\item This exercise completes the proof of Proposition 34. Suppose that $Q$ is an $R$-module with the property that every short exact sequence $0 \to Q \to M_1 \to M_2 \to 0$ splits and suppose that the sequence $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\;\psi\;} B$ is exact. Prove that every $R$-module homomorphism $f$ from $A$ to $Q$ lifts to an $R$-module homomorphism $F$ from $B$ to $Q$ with $f = F \circ \psi$ (i.e., $Q$ has the injective property with respect to all injections). [Imitate the proof of Proposition 34 (and use the previous exercise) to embed $Q$ into an injective module $I$. Then the splitting property together with Exercise 4 using Exercise 1(b) gives an isomorphism from $Q$ to a direct summand of $I$. Use the fact that the property in Proposition 36 holds for injective modules.]
\item Prove that the injective hull of the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\mathbb{Z}$ is $\mathbb{Q}$ and that $\mathbb{Q}$ contains an isomorphic copy of $\mathbb{Z}$ as an essential submodule.
\item Prove that the injective hull of the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$ is the injective hull of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ and deduce that $\mathbb{Z}/p^n\mathbb{Z}$ has the Pr\"ufer group $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]/\mathbb{Z}$ (the $p$-primary part of $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$), not $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ itself, as its injective hull.
\item If $F$ is a field, prove that the injective hull of $F[x]$ is the rational function field $F(x)$.
\item Prove that the polynomial ring $R[x]$ in the indeterminate $x$ over the commutative ring $R$ is a flat $R$-module.
\item Let $R$ and $S$ be rings with $1$ and suppose $M$ is a right $R$-module, and $N$ is an $(R,S)$-bimodule. If $M$ is flat over $R$ and $N$ is flat as an $S$-module then prove that $M \otimes_R N$ is flat as a right $S$-module.
\item Suppose that $R$ is a commutative ring and that $M$ and $N$ are flat $R$-modules. Prove that $M \otimes_R N$ is a flat $R$-module. (See the previous exercise.)
\item Prove that the (right) module $M \otimes_R S$ obtained by changing the base from the ring $R$ to the ring $S$ by some homomorphism $f : R \to S$ with $f(1_R) = 1_S$ (cf. Example 6 following Corollary 12 in Section 4) of the flat (right) $R$-module $M$ is the flat (right) $S$-module $M \otimes_R S$.
\item Prove that $A$ is a flat $R$-module if and only if for every finitely generated ideal $I$ of $R$ the map from $A \otimes_R I$ to $A \otimes_R R \cong A$ induced by the inclusion $I \subseteq R$ is injective. [The image of $A \otimes_R I$ in $A \otimes_R R = A$ is $AI$, so this is equivalent to showing that the natural map $A \otimes_R I \to AI$ is injective.]
\item \emph{(A Flatness Criterion)} Parts (a)--(c) of this exercise prove that $A$ is a flat $R$-module if and only if (I) for every finitely generated ideal $I$ of $R$, the map from $A \otimes_R I \to A$ given by $a \otimes i \mapsto ai$ is injective (cf. the preceding exercise). By the previous two exercises it suffices to prove that (I) implies $A$ is flat, i.e., that $A \otimes_R B \to A \otimes_R C$ is injective for every injection of (left) $R$-modules $\iota : B \to C$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose that $L_2 \subseteq L_1$ are two left ideals of $R$. Show that if (I) is satisfied for both $L_1$ and $L_2$ then (I) is satisfied for $L_1/L_2$.
\item[(b)] Suppose $D_1 \subseteq D_2 \subseteq \cdots$ is an ascending chain of left ideals of $R$ and let $D = \bigcup_i D_i$. Show that if (I) is satisfied for each $D_i$ then (I) is satisfied for $D$.
\item[(c)] Use Zorn's Lemma to prove that (I) is satisfied for every left ideal of $R$. Prove that this implies $A$ is flat as follows. Let $B$ be a submodule of the $R$-module $C$. By the previous exercises it suffices to consider the case where $C = R^n$ is a finitely generated free module; use induction on $n$, the case $n = 1$ being the assumption that (I) holds, together with parts (a) and (b), to complete the proof. [Use the commutative diagram with exact rows obtained from $0 \to K \to R^n \to R \to 0$, where $K = R^{n-1}$, and apply the snake lemma.]
\end{enumerate}
\item \emph{(A Flatness Criterion for quotients)} Suppose $A = F/K$ where $F$ is flat (e.g., if $F$ is free) and $K$ is an $R$-submodule of $F$. Show that $A = F/K$ is flat if and only if $K \cap FI = KI$ for every finitely generated ideal $I$ of $R$. (Use the flatness criterion in the preceding exercise.) [Use the previous exercise. Since $F$ is flat, $F \otimes I \cong FI$, and the image of $K \otimes I$ in $FI$ is $KI$; tensoring $0 \to K \to F \to A \to 0$ with $I$ gives $A \otimes I \cong FI/KI$. Under this identification the map $A \otimes I \to A = F/K$ is $FI/KI \to F/K$, whose kernel is $(K \cap FI)/KI$.]
\item Let $M$ and $N$ be submodules of the $R$-module $L$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] Suppose $\alpha : A \to M$ and $\beta : A \to N$ are $R$-module homomorphisms. Prove that $X = \{(\alpha(a), -\beta(a)) \mid a \in A\}$ is an $R$-submodule of the direct sum $M \oplus N$ and prove that $\alpha$ and $\beta$ factor through the quotient $(M \oplus N)/X$ (called the \emph{pushout} or \emph{fiber sum} of $\alpha$ and $\beta$) and that there is a commutative diagram
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
A \arrow[r, "\beta"] \arrow[d, "\alpha"'] & N \arrow[d, "\pi_2"] \\
M \arrow[r, "\pi_1"'] & P
\end{tikzcd}
\]
where $\pi_1$ and $\pi_2$ are the natural maps to the quotient induced by the maps into the first and second components.
\item[(b)] Suppose $f : M \to D$ and $g : N \to D$ are $R$-module homomorphisms with $f \circ \alpha = g \circ \beta$. Prove that there is a unique $R$-module homomorphism from the pushout $P$ to $D$ making the natural diagram commute.
\item[(c)] If $M$ and $N$ are submodules of an $R$-module $L$, show that the pushout of the inclusion maps $M \cap N \hookrightarrow M$ and $M \cap N \hookrightarrow N$ is isomorphic to the submodule $M + N$ of $L$.
\end{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Schanuel's Lemma)} If $0 \to K \to P \xrightarrow{\;\varphi\;} M \to 0$ and $0 \to K' \to P' \xrightarrow{\;\varphi'\;} M \to 0$ are exact sequences of $R$-modules where $P$ and $P'$ are projective, prove that $K \oplus P' \cong K' \oplus P$ as $R$-modules. [Show that there is an exact sequence $0 \to \ker \pi \to X \xrightarrow{\;\pi\;} P \to 0$ where $X = \{(x,y) \in P \oplus P' \mid \varphi(x) = \varphi'(y)\}$ is the submodule that is the pullback (or fiber product) of $\varphi$ and $\varphi'$, and the map $\pi$ is the natural projection onto the first component. Show that $\ker \pi \cong K'$ and that this sequence splits since $P$ is projective. Deduce that $X \cong K' \oplus P$. Show similarly that $X \cong K \oplus P'$.] The $R$-modules $M$ and $N$ are said to be \emph{projectively equivalent} if $M \oplus P \cong N \oplus Q$ for some projective $R$-modules $P$ and $Q$. Similarly, $M$ and $N$ are \emph{injectively equivalent} if $M \oplus Q \cong N \oplus Q'$ for some injective modules $Q$, $Q'$. This exercise shows $K$ and $K'$ are projectively equivalent.
\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Practice problems.}
\item Show that a sequence $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\psi} B$ of $R$-modules is exact (at $A$) if and only if $\psi$ is injective. Dually, show that $B \xrightarrow{\varphi} C \to 0$ is exact (at $C$) if and only if $\varphi$ is surjective.

\item Let $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\psi} B \xrightarrow{\varphi} C \to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Prove that $C \cong B/\psi(A)$ as $R$-modules.

\item Determine whether the sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal] 0 \arrow[r] & \mathbb{Z} \arrow[r, "2"] & \mathbb{Z} \arrow[r] & \mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z} \arrow[r] & 0 \end{tikzcd}\]
of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules is exact, where the first map is multiplication by $2$ and the second is reduction mod $2$. Justify exactness at each of the three middle positions.

\item Consider the $\mathbb{Z}$-module homomorphisms in
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal] \mathbb{Z} \arrow[r, "f"] & \mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z} \arrow[r, "g"] & \mathbb{Z} \end{tikzcd}\]
where $f(n) = (n, -n)$ and $g(a,b) = a + b$. Verify that $\im f = \ker g$, i.e.\ the sequence is exact at $\mathbb{Z} \oplus \mathbb{Z}$.

\item Let $R$ be a ring with $1$. Prove that the free $R$-module $R^n$ is projective. More generally, prove that every free $R$-module is projective.

\item Prove that a finite direct sum $P_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus P_n$ of $R$-modules is projective if and only if each $P_i$ is projective.

\item Show that $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ is a projective $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$-module by exhibiting a $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$-module $Q$ with $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z} \oplus Q$ free. Conclude $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ is projective but not free over $\mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}$.

\item Show that $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ is \emph{not} a projective $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z}$-module. (Show the surjection $\mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ does not split, i.e.\ the identity map $\mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z}$ does not lift through it.)

\item Prove that the short exact sequence
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal] 0 \arrow[r] & \mathbb{Z} \arrow[r, hook, "2"] & \mathbb{Z} \arrow[r, two heads] & \mathbb{Z}/(2)\mathbb{Z} \arrow[r] & 0 \end{tikzcd}\]
of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules does not split. Compare with problem 8.

\item Let $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\psi} B \xrightarrow{\varphi} C \to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Prove the following are equivalent: (a) the sequence splits; (b) there is an $R$-module homomorphism $\lambda : B \to A$ with $\lambda \circ \psi = \id_A$; (c) there is an $R$-module homomorphism $\mu : C \to B$ with $\varphi \circ \mu = \id_C$. In each splitting case prove $B \cong A \oplus C$.

\item Prove that an $R$-module $P$ is projective if and only if every short exact sequence $0 \to A \to B \to P \to 0$ of $R$-modules splits.

\item Show that $\mathbb{Q}$ is an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module. (Use the criterion that a $\mathbb{Z}$-module $Q$ is injective if and only if it is divisible, i.e.\ $nQ = Q$ for every nonzero integer $n$.)

\item Show that $\mathbb{Z}$ is \emph{not} an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module by exhibiting an injection $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Q}$ and a homomorphism $\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}$ that does not extend to $\mathbb{Q}$.

\item Compute the following tensor products of $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, identifying each as a familiar abelian group:
\[ \mathbb{Z}/(4)\mathbb{Z} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Z}/(6)\mathbb{Z}, \qquad \mathbb{Z}/(m)\mathbb{Z} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z}, \qquad \mathbb{Q} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Z}/(n)\mathbb{Z} \ (n > 0), \qquad \mathbb{Q} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Q}. \]

\item Let $R$ be commutative with $1$ and let $I, J \sgr R$ be ideals. Prove that there is an $R$-module isomorphism $R/I \otimes_R R/J \cong R/(I+J)$.

\item Prove that every free $R$-module $R^{(A)}$ is flat. Deduce that every projective $R$-module is flat. (You may use that a direct summand of a flat module is flat.)

\end{exers}

\begin{exers}{Commutative-diagram exercises.}
\item (Lifting property of projectives) Let $P$ be a projective $R$-module, let $g : B \to C$ be a surjection of $R$-modules, and let $f : P \to C$ be any homomorphism. State and prove the existence of the dashed lift in
\[\begin{tikzcd}
& P \arrow[d, "f"] \arrow[dl, dashed, "\exists\,\tilde f"'] \\
B \arrow[r, two heads, "g"'] & C
\end{tikzcd}\]
Then show by example (over $R = \mathbb{Z}$) that the lift $\tilde f$ need not be unique.

\item (Extension property of injectives) Let $Q$ be an injective $R$-module, let $\iota : A \to B$ be an injection of $R$-modules, and let $f : A \to Q$ be any homomorphism. Prove the existence of the dashed extension $F$ making
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
A \arrow[r, hook, "\iota"] \arrow[dr, "f"'] & B \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists\,F"] \\
& Q
\end{tikzcd}\]
commute. Using this with $A = \mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow B = \mathbb{Q} = Q$, find all extensions of $f = \id_\mathbb{Z}$.

\item (Universal property of tensor product) Let $M, N, L$ be $R$-modules over a commutative ring $R$ and let $\varphi : M \times N \to L$ be $R$-bilinear. State the universal property realized by
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
M\times N \arrow[r, "\otimes"] \arrow[dr, "\varphi"'] & M\otimes_R N \arrow[d, dashed, "\exists!\,\Phi"] \\
& L
\end{tikzcd}\]
and use it to prove the canonical isomorphism $R \otimes_R N \cong N$ as $R$-modules.

\item (Snake Lemma) Given a commutative diagram of $R$-modules with exact rows
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=normal]
& A \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "a"] & B \arrow[r, two heads] \arrow[d, "b"] & C \arrow[r] \arrow[d, "c"] & 0 \\
0 \arrow[r] & A' \arrow[r, hook] & B' \arrow[r] & C' &
\end{tikzcd}\]
state the snake lemma (the existence of the connecting map $\delta : \ker c \to \coker a$ and the resulting six-term exact sequence $\ker a \to \ker b \to \ker c \xrightarrow{\delta} \coker a \to \coker b \to \coker c$), and prove that $\delta$ is well defined.

\item (Splitting via a section) Let $0 \to A \xrightarrow{\psi} B \xrightarrow{\varphi} C \to 0$ be a short exact sequence of $R$-modules. Suppose a homomorphism $\mu : C \to B$ exists with $\varphi \circ \mu = \id_C$, as in
\[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=large]
0 \arrow[r] & A \arrow[r, hook, "\psi"] & B \arrow[r, two heads, "\varphi"] & C \arrow[r] \arrow[l, dashed, bend left, "\mu"] & 0
\end{tikzcd}\]
Prove that $B = \psi(A) \oplus \mu(C)$ and hence $B \cong A \oplus C$.

\end{exers}

\item [DF 10.5.26] For rings $R, S$, a right $R$-module $M$ flat over $R$, and an $(R,S)$-bimodule $N$ flat as an $S$-module, prove $M \otimes_R N$ is flat as a right $S$-module.
\item [DF 10.5.27] Prove $A$ is flat iff for every finitely generated ideal $I$ the map $A \otimes_R I \to A \otimes_R R \cong A$ induced by $I \subseteq R$ is injective.
\item [DF 10.5.28] Prove the Flatness Criterion: $A$ is flat iff for every finitely generated ideal $I$ the map $A \otimes_R I \to A$, $a \otimes i \mapsto ai$, is injective; reduce via quotients, ascending unions, and Zorn's Lemma to free modules and conclude using the snake lemma.
\item [DF 10.5.29] For $A = F/K$ with $F$ flat, prove $A$ is flat iff $K \cap FI = KI$ for every finitely generated ideal $I$.
\item [DF 10.5.30] For submodules $M, N$ of $L$, construct the pushout (fiber sum) $(M \oplus N)/X$ of $\alpha, \beta$, verify its universal property, and show the pushout of the inclusions $M \cap N \hookrightarrow M$, $M \cap N \hookrightarrow N$ is isomorphic to $M + N$.
\item [DF 10.5.31] Prove Schanuel's Lemma: for exact $0 \to K \to P \to M \to 0$ and $0 \to K' \to P' \to M \to 0$ with $P, P'$ projective, $K \oplus P' \cong K' \oplus P$; conclude $K$ and $K'$ are projectively equivalent.
\item [Artin 2.2] Prove that a ring $R$ over which every finitely generated module is free is either a field or the zero ring.
\item [Artin 2.3] For the matrix $A$ of a homomorphism $\varphi : \mathbb{Z}^n \to \mathbb{Z}^m$ of free $\mathbb{Z}$-modules, prove $\varphi$ is injective iff $\mathrm{rank}(A) = n$ over $\mathbb{R}$, and surjective iff the gcd of the $m \times m$ minors of $A$ is $1$.
\item [Artin 9.5] For $R = \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ and the module $V$ presented by the matrix $A = \begin{psmallmatrix} 2 & 1-\sqrt{-5} \\ 1+\sqrt{-5} & 3 \end{psmallmatrix}$, prove the residue of $A$ in $R/P$ has rank $1$ for every prime ideal $P$, yet $V$ is not a free module.
\item [Artin M.5] Determine which matrices $A \in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{R})$ stabilize some lattice $L$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
\item [Artin M.6] (a) Describe the orbits of right multiplication by $G = \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z})$ on the space of $2 \times 2$ integer matrices. (b) Show that for any integer matrix $A$ there is an invertible integer matrix $P$ with $AP$ in Hermite normal form.
\item [Artin M.8] For a complex number $\alpha$, prove $\alpha$ is an algebraic integer iff $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha]$ is a finitely generated abelian group; deduce $\mathbb{Z}[\alpha, \beta]$ is finitely generated for algebraic integers $\alpha, \beta$, and hence the algebraic integers form a subring of $\mathbb{C}$.
\item [Artin M.9] For a lattice $L$ in Euclidean space with dual $L^* = \{w \mid (v \cdot w) \in \mathbb{Z}\ \forall v \in L\}$: show $L$ has a lattice basis, $L^*$ is a lattice, describe a basis of $L^*$ in terms of one for $L$, determine when $L \subseteq L^*$, and find $[L^* : L]$ when $L \subseteq L^*$.
\item [Artin M.10] Prove that the multiplicative group $\mathbb{Q}^\times$ is the direct sum of a cyclic group of order $2$ and a free abelian group of countable rank; prove the additive group $\mathbb{Q}$ is not a direct sum of two proper subgroups; and prove $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is not a direct sum of cyclic groups.
\end{exers}

Throughout, $F$ denotes a field; its elements are called \emph{scalars}. A vector space over $F$ is, axiomatically, just a unital module over $F$ (D\&F Chapter 10), but because $F$ is a field every such module behaves far better than a general module: it always has a basis, its ``size'' is a single well-defined number, and a linear map is pinned down by its action on a basis. The whole of linear algebra is the unwinding of these facts.

\begin{wex}{The one-step subspace test on $\mathbb{R}^3$}
Decide whether $W=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3 : x-2y+z=0\}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$, and whether $U=\{(x,y,z): x-2y+z=1\}$ is.
\wrec Use the one-step test: a nonempty subset is a subspace iff it is closed under $\alpha w_1+w_2$. A defining equation that is \emph{homogeneous} (right side $0$) survives this closure; an inhomogeneous one (right side $1$) does not, because it fails to contain $0$.
\wsol $W$ contains $0=(0,0,0)$ since $0-0+0=0$, so $W\neq\varnothing$. If $w_1=(x_1,y_1,z_1)$, $w_2=(x_2,y_2,z_2)$ lie in $W$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, then the coordinate satisfying the test is
\[
(x_1-2y_1+z_1)\alpha+(x_2-2y_2+z_2)=\alpha\cdot 0+0=0,
\]
so $\alpha w_1+w_2\in W$. Hence $W\sgr\mathbb{R}^3$. For $U$: $0\notin U$ because $0-0+0=1$ is false, so $U$ is not even nonempty-with-zero; concretely $(1,0,0)\in U$ but $2\cdot(1,0,0)=(2,0,0)$ has $2-0+0=2\neq 1$, so $U$ is not closed. \textit{Check.} $W$ is the kernel of the linear functional $(x,y,z)\mapsto x-2y+z$, a plane through the origin --- exactly the shape a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$ should have.
\end{wex}

\begin{definition}[Linear combination and span]
Let $A\subseteq V$. A \emph{linear combination} of $A$ is a vector $\alpha_1 v_1+\cdots+\alpha_n v_n$ with $n\geq 0$, $v_i\in A$, $\alpha_i\in F$. The \emph{span} of $A$,
\[
\Span(A)=\{\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i v_i : n\geq 0,\ v_i\in A,\ \alpha_i\in F\},
\]
is the set of all linear combinations of finitely many elements of $A$; it is the smallest subspace of $V$ containing $A$ (the empty combination gives $0$, so $\Span(\varnothing)=\{0\}$). We say $A$ \emph{spans} (or \emph{generates}) $V$ if $\Span(A)=V$.
\end{definition}
title: Linear combination and span

\begin{wex}{Independence over $\mathbb{R}$ via a determinant}
Are $v_1=(1,2,1)$, $v_2=(2,1,0)$, $v_3=(1,-1,1)$ linearly independent in $\mathbb{R}^3$?
\wrec In $F^n$ with $n$ vectors, independence is equivalent to the matrix with these columns being invertible, i.e.\ having nonzero determinant: $\det\neq 0\iff$ independent.
\wsol Form $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}1&2&1\\2&1&-1\\1&0&1\end{psmallmatrix}$ (columns $v_1,v_2,v_3$). Expanding along the bottom row,
\[
\det A=1\cdot\det\begin{psmallmatrix}2&1\\1&-1\end{psmallmatrix}-0+1\cdot\det\begin{psmallmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{psmallmatrix}=1(-2-1)+1(1-4)=-3-3=-6\neq 0.
\]
So the only solution of $\alpha_1 v_1+\alpha_2 v_2+\alpha_3 v_3=0$ is $\alpha=0$, and the set is independent. \textit{Check.} Since $\det A=-6\neq 0$, $A$ is invertible, so the three columns also \emph{span} $\mathbb{R}^3$; three independent vectors in a $3$-dimensional space ought to be a basis, as the next subsection confirms.
\end{wex}
title: Independence over $\mathbb{R}$ via a determinant

\begin{wex}{Dependence over $\F_2$ that would be independence over $\mathbb{Q}$}
In $\F_2^{\,3}$ ($\F_2=\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$) consider $v_1=(1,1,0)$, $v_2=(0,1,1)$, $v_3=(1,0,1)$. Are they independent?
\wrec The field matters: solve $\alpha_1 v_1+\alpha_2 v_2+\alpha_3 v_3=0$ with $\alpha_i\in\F_2$. A relation valid mod $2$ need not be valid over $\mathbb{Q}$, and vice versa.
\wsol Try $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=\alpha_3=1$:
\[
v_1+v_2+v_3=(1{+}0{+}1,\;1{+}1{+}0,\;0{+}1{+}1)=(0,0,0)\ \text{in }\F_2.
\]
This is a nontrivial relation (coefficients all $1\neq 0$), so the set is \emph{dependent} over $\F_2$. \textit{Check.} Over $\mathbb{Q}$ the same three vectors give $v_1+v_2+v_3=(2,2,2)\neq 0$, and one checks $\det\begin{psmallmatrix}1&0&1\\1&1&0\\0&1&1\end{psmallmatrix}=2\neq 0$, so they are \emph{independent} over $\mathbb{Q}$. The dependence appeared precisely because $2\equiv 0$ in $\F_2$ --- a vivid reminder that (in)dependence is relative to $F$.
\end{wex}
